# Roman invasion of Africa (204–201 BC)

The **Roman invasion of Africa** was a military campaign conducted by the Roman Republic against the Carthaginian Empire during the final phase of the Second Punic War. Lasting from 204 BC to 201 BC, the campaign was led by the Roman general Publius Cornelius Scipio (later known as Scipio Africanus). The invasion began with Roman landings near Utica and culminated in the decisive Battle of Zama in 202 BC, where Scipio defeated the Carthaginian general Hannibal.

Following the expulsion of Carthaginian forces from the Iberian Peninsula in 206 BC, Scipio proposed an invasion of the Carthaginian homeland in North Africa to force Hannibal to withdraw from Italy. Despite political opposition in the Roman Senate, Scipio was granted permission to launch the expedition from Sicily. Upon landing in Africa in 204 BC, the Roman forces, aided by the Numidian prince Masinissa, besieged the city of Utica. In 203 BC, Scipio destroyed the combined armies of Carthage and its Numidian ally, King Syphax, in the Battle of Utica and the Battle of the Great Plains.

These defeats prompted the Carthaginian Senate to recall Hannibal from Italy to defend the capital. The ensuing confrontation at Zama resulted in a complete Roman victory. The war concluded with the peace treaty of 201 BC, which stripped Carthage of its overseas territories, imposed a heavy war indemnity, and severely restricted its military capabilities. The invasion established Rome as the dominant power in the western Mediterranean and marked the end of Carthage as a major military threat .

## Background

The Second Punic War began in 218 BC with Hannibal's invasion of Italy. For over a decade, Roman forces suffered a series of defeats on the Italian peninsula, most notably at the Battle of Cannae in 216 BC. However, the strategic situation began to shift as Rome gradually regained control of Italian cities and launched successful offensives in other theaters .

### Scipio's Rise and Planning
In 210 BC, Publius Cornelius Scipio was appointed to command Roman forces in Iberia (modern Spain and Portugal). Over the next four years, he systematically dismantled Carthaginian power in the region, culminating in the decisive victory at the Battle of Ilipa in 206 BC . Following this success, Scipio returned to Rome and was elected consul for the year 205 BC. He advocated for an aggressive strategy to end the war by invading Africa, thereby forcing Carthage to recall Hannibal from Italy to defend its homeland .

### Senate Debate and Preparations
Scipio's plan faced significant opposition within the Roman Senate, particularly from the elder statesman Quintus Fabius Maximus, who favored a defensive strategy focused on defeating Hannibal in Italy. A political compromise was eventually reached: Scipio was assigned Sicily as his consular province, with permission to cross into Africa if he deemed it in the public interest. However, he was not permitted to conscript a new army through the standard levy. Instead, he was authorized to recruit volunteers and utilize the garrison troops already stationed in Sicily .

Scipio spent the year 205 BC in Sicily training his forces. His army consisted largely of the survivors of the Battle of Cannae, who had been exiled to Sicily as punishment for their defeat, and approximately 7,000 volunteers. Scipio implemented a rigorous training regime to integrate these disparate elements into a cohesive fighting force. Modern historians estimate the invasion force numbered between 25,000 and 35,000 men, comprising roughly 30,000 infantry and a cavalry contingent . During this period, Scipio also secured an alliance with Masinissa, a Numidian leader who had defected from Carthage following the Roman victories in Spain .

## Invasion of 204 BC

In the summer of 204 BC, likely in June or July, Scipio's fleet departed from Lilybaeum in Sicily. The armada consisted of approximately 400 transport ships escorted by 40 warships. The Roman force landed at Cape Farina (Promontory of Apollo), approximately 20 kilometers (12 miles) north of the major Carthaginian port of Utica .

### Initial Engagements
Upon landing, the Romans secured the immediate area and began pillaging the countryside. The initial Carthaginian response was led by a commander named Hanno, who led a scouting force of 500 cavalry to confront the invaders. Scipio's forces, augmented by Masinissa's Numidian cavalry, engaged and defeated this detachment; Hanno was killed, and the Romans captured or killed the majority of the Carthaginian patrol . Following this success, the Romans captured a nearby town, seizing substantial loot and sending thousands of captives back to Sicily as slaves .

### Siege of Utica
The primary strategic objective of the initial landing was the capture of Utica, which Scipio intended to use as a supply base and winter quarters. The Romans advanced on the city and launched a siege, utilizing siege engines and a naval blockade. However, the city's defenses proved resilient, and the garrison held out, expecting relief from Carthage .

Meanwhile, the Carthaginians mobilized a large relief army under Hasdrubal Gisco. He was joined by his son-in-law Syphax, the king of the Masaesyli (western Numidians), who had sided with Carthage. The combined Carthaginian and Numidian forces reportedly numbered over 30,000 men, significantly outnumbering the Romans. This army established two separate camps approximately 11 kilometers (7 miles) from the Roman position . Faced with this superior force and the approach of winter, Scipio was forced to abandon the direct siege of Utica. He withdrew his army to a fortified position on a promontory nearby, which became known as the *Castra Cornelia* (Cornelius's Camp), to wait out the winter of 204–203 BC .

## Campaign of 203 BC

During the winter truce, Scipio entered into prolonged peace negotiations with Syphax. These negotiations were largely a ruse employed by Scipio to gather intelligence. He sent centurions disguised as slaves into the enemy camps to map their layout and observe their defenses. The spies reported that the Numidian camp was composed chiefly of reed huts and the Carthaginian camp of timber, making them highly vulnerable to fire .

### Battle of Utica (Burning of the Camps)
In the spring of 203 BC, Scipio launched a surprise night attack. He divided his army, sending a force under his second-in-command Gaius Laelius and Masinissa to attack Syphax's camp, while he led the remainder against Hasdrubal's position. The Romans set fire to the reed huts in the Numidian camp; the fire spread rapidly, causing panic. Many Numidians, believing the fire to be accidental, were slaughtered by the Romans as they attempted to flee or extinguish the flames .

Seeing the fire in the neighboring camp, soldiers from Hasdrubal's camp rushed out unarmed to assist, only to be ambushed by Scipio's troops. The Romans then stormed the Carthaginian camp and set it ablaze as well. The double attack resulted in the near-total destruction of both armies. Ancient sources claim heavy casualties for the Carthaginians and Numidians, with estimates of up to 40,000 killed or captured, though Hasdrubal and Syphax managed to escape with a small fraction of their forces .

### Battle of the Great Plains
Following the disaster at Utica, Hasdrubal and Syphax regrouped at a location known as the Great Plains (*Campi Magni*), near the Bagradas River, approximately 120 kilometers (75 miles) from Utica. They were reinforced by 4,000 Celtiberian mercenaries newly arrived from Spain, raising their total strength to approximately 30,000 men .

Scipio marched to meet them, leaving a detachment to maintain the blockade of Utica. In the ensuing battle, the Roman cavalry, superior in quality and morale, quickly routed the Carthaginian and Numidian wings. The center, held by the Celtiberians, stood firm and fought to the death, allowing Hasdrubal and Syphax to escape, but the army itself was effectively destroyed .

### Defeat of Syphax
After the battle, Scipio dispatched Laelius and Masinissa to pursue Syphax back to his kingdom in Numidia. They engaged him at the Battle of Cirta, where Syphax was defeated and captured. This victory allowed Masinissa to unify Numidia under his rule and deprived Carthage of its most important source of cavalry, while simultaneously securing those resources for Rome .

### Failed Peace Negotiations
The catastrophic defeats in Africa caused panic in Carthage. The Carthaginian Senate sued for peace and simultaneously recalled Hannibal and his brother Mago from Italy. A preliminary treaty was agreed upon, and the Roman Senate ratified the terms. However, upon the arrival of Hannibal's veteran army in Africa in late 203 BC, confidence returned to the Carthaginian war party. Emboldened by Hannibal's presence, Carthage repudiated the truce by attacking a Roman supply fleet, leading to a resumption of hostilities .

## Campaign of 202 BC

The final phase of the invasion centered on the confrontation between the two greatest commanders of the war: Scipio and Hannibal.

### Hannibal's Return
Hannibal landed at Hadrumetum (modern Sousse) and spent the winter and spring gathering forces. His army consisted of his veterans from the Italian campaign, Mago's troops (Mago having died during the voyage), and new levies raised in Africa. He also secured a corps of 80 war elephants. However, his cavalry was significantly weaker than in previous campaigns, as he had been forced to leave his horses behind in Italy and Masinissa's defection had stripped Carthage of Numidian horsemen .

### Battle of Zama
The decisive engagement took place in October 202 BC near Zama Regia. The two commanders met for a parley prior to the battle, but failed to reach an agreement.

**Forces:**
* **Rome:** Approximately 30,000 infantry and 6,000 cavalry (including 4,000 Numidians under Masinissa) .
* **Carthage:** Approximately 40,000 to 50,000 infantry and 4,000 cavalry, plus 80 war elephants .

**Tactics:**
Hannibal opened the battle by charging with his elephants, intending to break the Roman lines. Scipio, anticipating this, had arranged his infantry in columns with wide lanes between them (rather than the traditional checkerboard formation), allowing the elephants to pass through harmlessly. Roman skirmishers and trumpeters panicked the beasts, causing many to turn back and disrupt the Carthaginian cavalry .

The Roman and Numidian cavalry then charged and drove the Carthaginian horsemen from the field. In the center, the infantry battle was fierce. The Roman *hastati* and *principes* engaged Hannibal's first two lines of mercenaries and levies. As the infantry fight reached a stalemate against Hannibal's veteran third line, the Roman cavalry returned from their pursuit and attacked the Carthaginian rear. This encirclement caused the Carthaginian army to collapse .

**Casualties:**
Carthage suffered approximately 20,000 killed and 20,000 captured. Roman losses were significantly lighter, estimated at around 1,500 to 2,500 killed .

## Aftermath

The defeat at Zama left Carthage defenseless. Hannibal, having escaped the battle, advised the Carthaginian Senate to accept peace terms. The war formally ended in 201 BC with the ratification of a treaty that fundamentally altered the balance of power in the Mediterranean .

### Treaty of 201 BC
The terms imposed by Rome were severe, designed to permanently reduce Carthage to a second-rate power:
* **Territorial Losses:** Carthage surrendered all territories outside of Africa, including its holdings in Spain and the Mediterranean islands. It also had to restore lands to Masinissa, effectively checking Carthaginian power in Africa .
* **Military Restrictions:** The Carthaginian navy was reduced to only 10 triremes, intended solely for protection against piracy. Carthage was forbidden from training war elephants .
* **Indemnity:** Carthage was required to pay a war indemnity of 10,000 silver talents over a period of 50 years .
* **Sovereignty:** Crucially, Carthage was prohibited from waging war, even in self-defense, without the express permission of the Roman Senate. This clause would eventually provide the pretext for the Third Punic War .

### Legacy
For his victory, Scipio was awarded a triumph in Rome and the agnomen *Africanus* . The success of the invasion validated Scipio's strategic vision and marked a turning point in Roman military history, demonstrating the Republic's ability to project power overseas and conduct complex logistical operations. Carthage ceased to be a military rival to Rome, and the Roman Republic emerged as the hegemon of the western Mediterranean .

Top Questions

*   Who was Scipio Africanus?
    
*   What important war did Scipio Africanus fight in?
    
*   Which famous enemy general did Scipio Africanus defeat?
    
*   How did Scipio Africanus help Rome win the Second Punic War?
    
*   What was the Battle of Zama, and why was it important for Scipio Africanus?
    
*   How did Scipio Africanus's actions influence the future of Rome?
    

**Scipio Africanus** (born 236 bce—died 183 bce, Liternum, [Campania](https://www.britannica.com/place/Campania-region-Italy) \[now Patria, Italy\]) was a [Roman](https://www.britannica.com/place/ancient-Rome) [general](https://www.britannica.com/topic/general) noted for his victory over the Carthaginian leader [Hannibal](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hannibal-Carthaginian-general-247-183-BCE) in the great [Battle of Zama](https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Zama-Roman-Carthaginian-history) (202 bce), ending the [Second Punic War](https://www.britannica.com/event/Second-Punic-War). For his victory he won the [surname](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/surname) Africanus (201 bce).

Family background
-----------------

[Publius Cornelius Scipio](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Publius-Cornelius-Scipio) was born into one of the great [patrician](https://www.britannica.com/topic/patrician) families in Rome; his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather had all been consuls in their day. In 218 bce Scipio’s father, also named Publius Cornelius Scipio, held the consulship in one of the most critical years of [Rome’s](https://www.britannica.com/place/Rome) [history](https://www.britannica.com/topic/history). While with him during an engagement on the [Ticinus River](https://www.britannica.com/place/Ticino-River), the young Scipio made his first appearance in history. According to the Roman historian [Livy](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Livy), the Roman force was outflanked by [Numidian](https://www.britannica.com/place/Numidia) cavalry. Seeing his father wounded, the younger Scipio charged forward, an action that allowed Scipio père to escape with his guard of cavalry officers and his young son. This [anecdote](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/anecdote) was also recounted by the historian [Polybius](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Polybius) on the authority of Scipio’s friend Laelius, and it may well be true.

Nothing is known of Scipio’s boyhood or the date of his marriage to Aemilia, daughter of Aemilius Paullus, [consul](https://www.britannica.com/topic/consul-ancient-Roman-official) of 216, who fell at Cannae. Scipio had two sons: Publius, who was debarred by ill health from a public career and who adopted the name [Scipio Africanus the Younger](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Scipio-Africanus-the-Younger), and Lucius, who became praetor in 174. Scipio’s physical appearance is shown on some coins minted at Carthago Nova (now [Cartagena](https://www.britannica.com/place/Cartagena-Spain), Spain)—which almost certainly bear his portrait—and also probably on a signet ring found near Naples.

Military career
---------------

According to Livy, Scipio served as a young [military](https://www.britannica.com/topic/armed-force) [tribune](https://www.britannica.com/topic/tribune-Roman-official) at the disastrous [Battle of Cannae](https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Cannae) in 216. He escaped after the defeat to Canusium (modern [Canosa di Puglia](https://www.britannica.com/place/Canosa-di-Puglia), Italy), where some 4,000 survivors rallied; there he boldly [thwarted](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/thwarted) a plot of some fainthearts to desert Rome. Then in 213 he returned to a civilian career by winning the position of curule (“higher”) [aedile](https://www.britannica.com/topic/aedile); the story is told that when the tribunes objected to his candidature because he was under the legal age, he replied, “If all the Roman people want to make me aedile, I am old enough.” Soon family and national disaster followed: his father and uncle were defeated and killed in [Spain](https://www.britannica.com/topic/history-of-Spain), where the Carthaginians swept forward to the [Ebro River](https://www.britannica.com/place/Ebro-River) (211).

In 210 the Romans decided to send reinforcements to Spain, but it is said that no senior general would undertake the task and that young Scipio offered himself as a candidate; at any rate, the Roman people decided to invest him with a command there, although he was technically a _privatus_ (not a magistrate). This grant of a military command outside [Italy](https://www.britannica.com/place/Italy) by the people to a man who had not been [praetor](https://www.britannica.com/topic/praetor) or [consul](https://www.britannica.com/topic/consul-government-official) created an important [constitutional](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/constitutional) precedent. Thus, Scipio was given the chance to avenge the deaths of his father and uncle in Spain, where he hoped not merely to hold the Carthaginian armies at bay and prevent their sending reinforcements to Hannibal in Italy but to resume his father’s offensive policy, to turn back the tide of war, and to drive the enemy out of the [Iberian Peninsula](https://www.britannica.com/place/Iberian-Peninsula). Such a task must have seemed fantastic in 210, but Scipio had the confidence and ability; it was achieved in the next four years.

From his headquarters at Tarraco ([Tarragona](https://www.britannica.com/place/Tarragona-province-Spain)) in 209, Scipio suddenly launched a combined military and naval assault on the enemy’s headquarters at [Carthago Nova](https://www.britannica.com/place/Cartagena-Spain), knowing that all three enemy armies in Spain were at least 10 days distant from the city. Polybius relates that Scipio had heard from Spanish fishermen at Tarraco that the water level around Carthago Nova varied daily and that it was especially low in the afternoon. Helped by a lowering of the water in a lagoon, which exposed the northern wall, he successfully stormed the city. This possibly tidal phenomenon, attributed to the help of [Neptune](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Neptune-Roman-god), was perhaps [enhanced](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/enhanced) by an offshore wind; at any rate, it increased the troops’ belief in their commander’s divine support. In Carthago Nova he gained stores and supplies, Spanish hostages, the local silver mines, a splendid harbour, and a base for an advance farther south.

After training his army in new tactics, Scipio defeated the Carthaginian commander [Hasdrubal Barca](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hasdrubal-Carthaginian-general-died-207-BCE) at Baecula (Bailen) in Baetica (208); whereas normally the two rear ranks of a Roman army closely supported the front line, Scipio in this battle, under a screen of light troops, divided his main forces, which fell upon the enemy’s flanks. When [Hasdrubal](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hasdrubal-Carthaginian-general-died-207-BCE) broke away, ultimately to join his brother Hannibal in Italy, Scipio wisely declined the impossible task of trying to stop him and decided rather to accomplish his mission in Spain—the defeat of the other two Carthaginian armies still there. This he brilliantly achieved in 206 at the [Battle of Ilipa](https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Ilipa) (Alcalá [del Río](https://www.britannica.com/place/Del-Rio), near [Sevilla](https://www.britannica.com/place/Sevilla-Spain)). Over several days of posturing and light skirmishing between the arrayed armies, Scipio lulled the Carthaginian commanders—[Hasdrubal](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hasdrubal-Carthaginian-general-died-circa-202-BCE) (son of Gisco) and [Mago](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Mago-Carthaginian-general)—into a sense of routine. On the day of the battle, Scipio dramatically altered that routine, arriving in full force at dawn and changing the order of his troops so that where he was strong the Carthaginians were weak. He used his Roman veterans to execute a series of [audacious](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/audacious) flanking maneuvers while his fickle Spanish allies held the enemy’s main forces in place. The Carthaginian armies were destroyed, and Hasdrubal and Mago fled the field. Scipio then secured Gades ([Cádiz](https://www.britannica.com/place/Cadiz-Spain)), thus making Roman control of Spain complete.

Quick Facts

Also called:

Scipio Africanus the Elder

Latin:

Scipio Africanus Major

In full:

Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus

Died:

183 bce, Liternum, [Campania](https://www.britannica.com/place/Campania-region-Italy) \[now Patria, Italy\]

After he was elected consul for 205, Scipio boldly determined to disregard Hannibal—already largely contained in southern Italy—and to strike instead at Africa. Once he had beaten down political opposition in the Senate, he crossed to [Sicily](https://www.britannica.com/place/Sicily) with an army consisting partly of volunteers, some of whom had also survived the disaster of Cannae and sought to redeem themselves. While preparing his troops, he boldly [snatched](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/snatched) [Locri Epizephyrii](https://www.britannica.com/place/Locri-Epizephyrii), in the toe of Italy, from Hannibal’s grasp, though the subsequent misconduct of Pleminius, the man he left in command of the town, gave Scipio’s political opponents cause to criticize him. In 204 he landed with perhaps 35,000 men in Africa, where he besieged [Utica](https://www.britannica.com/place/Utica-Tunisia). Early in 203, with the help of Rome’s new Numidian ally [Masinissa](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Masinissa), he burned the camps of [Hasdrubal](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hasdrubal-Carthaginian-general-died-circa-202-BCE) (son of Gisgo) and his Numidian ally [Syphax](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Syphax). Then, sweeping down on the forces that the enemy was trying to muster at the [Great Plains](https://www.britannica.com/place/Great-Plains) on the upper Bagradas (modern Sūq al Khamīs, on the Majardah in [Tunisia](https://www.britannica.com/place/Tunisia)), he smashed that army by a double [flanking](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/flanking) movement.

The Great Numidian cavalry leader, Masinissa, has gone over to the Roman side.While the siege continues, the Carthaginians raise a large, but untried army. Rashly, the Carthaginians advance to raise the siege. Scipio leaves a siege force and meets the larger Carthaginian army on the Great Plains. After two days of skirmishing, Scipio initiates the battle, sending Masinissa and his crack cavalry against the Carthaginian right while the superbly trained legionary infantry moves to envelop the Carthaginian left. Initially, the poorly trained Carthaginian center holds, but Scipio's better-trained troops quickly overwhelm both flanks. Sensing approaching disaster, the Carthaginian center breaks. The entire Carthaginian army disintegrates and suffers heavy losses as the survivors stream back to Carthage. Scipio returns to the siege of Utica, and the desperate Carthaginians turn to their last hope—Hannibal. They recall their greatest general from Italy. The following year, the final battle of the Second Punic War (Zama) will be fought by its two greatest generals, Hannibal and Scipio. _The stage is set. The battle lines are drawn and you are in command. The rest is history._ ![Image 4](https://www.commandsandcolors.net/ancients/images/014_Great_Plains.png)

[Dionysius of Omaha](https://www.commandsandcolors.net/ancients/forum-main.html?view=user&userid=1787 "View Dionysius of Omaha's Profile") replied the topic: [#41100](https://www.commandsandcolors.net/ancients/forum-main.html?view=topic&catid=18&id=30#41100) 2 years 4 weeks ago [![Image 30](https://www.commandsandcolors.net/ancients/media/kunena/avatars/resized/size120/users/avatar1787.jpg?1658009442)](https://www.commandsandcolors.net/ancients/forum-main.html?view=user&userid=1787 "View Dionysius of Omaha's Profile") Great Plains – 203 B.C. Turn 1: Masinissa’s Numidians conduct a mounted charge against the Carthaginian right. The Carthaginians are pushed back and suffer a few casualties. But Hasdrubal Gisco’s leadership forms up the Punic line and the infantry force the Numidian cavalry to retire. Turn 2: The Carthaginian commander, Bostar, in charge of the Punic the center, double times his Carthaginian troops forward and engages the Roman light infantry. The Romans successfully evade with few losses. Turn 3: Bostar double times again trying to smash through the Roman light infantry screen, but the Roman light infantry actually hold their own and the Carthaginians only have marginal success. Turn 4: Roman Legate, Gaius Laelius, hits the Punic left with medium infantry and horse. Bostar’s forces stagger under the attack. On the Carthaginian right, Hasdrubal and Hanno move forward scattering the light Numidian cavalry before them… Victory Banner Count: Carthage 2, Rome 1. Turn 5: Roman Legate, Gaius Laelius, commanding the Roman center, orders a coordinated attack that concentrates on Bostar’s weakened auxiliaries. A Punic unit is lost and Bostar is forced to find refuge with another Carthaginian battalion. He then motivates that unit to attack forward into the teeth of the Roman center. A Roman light infantry unit is shattered. Carthage 3, Rome 2. Turn 6: Fighting in the center is hot! Bostar and Laelius are facing each other and both sides suffer losses; the Carthaginians lose another infantry unit. All tied up. Carthage 3, Rome 3. Turn 7: Both sides have little luck… But then a Roman cavalry unit foolishly tries to cut off a Carthaginian infantry unit only to be surrounded itself. It is destroyed between three Carthaginian infantry formations. Carthage 4, Rome 3. Turn 8: Romans surge forward in the center and destroy the last Carthaginian medium and heavy infantry in the Punic center-left! On the other side of the battlefield, Hanno finally begins to move toward the Roman left flank with his fresh troops… but is it too late? Carthage 4, Rome 4. Turn 10: The stubborn Bostar orders all his remaining light troops and they unleash a swarm of sling bullets and javelins. This is enough to eliminate an exhausted Roman infantry unit. Now the Roman right is perilously close to collapsing! Carthage 5, Rome 4. Turns 11-13: Both sides go on the defensive and reposition for a final strike. Turn 14: Both sides reform their lines. Hasdrubal and Hanno, after they’ve reset a firm line of infantry, finally order the double time and the Carthaginians crash into the Roman left line… a line that has fresh heavy and medium infantry legionary troops. The Punic forces take horrendous casualties as the Romans battle back. The Roman line holds. Turn 15: Publius Cornelius Scipio oversees a clash of shields as his Romans converge on Hasdrubal’s veteran heavy infantry. The Carthaginians lose another infantry unit and Scipio has tied things up 5 to 5. In a gamble for the ages, Hasdrubal with impressive leadership urges on his exhausted Carthaginians forward for one last charge against the Roman line. His men hit a Roman infantry unit with a devastating attack (Rolled four leadership symbols on a roll of four dice!) and eliminates the Roman unit which breaks Scipio’s line for the sixth and final victory banner! Carthage 6, Rome 5. Very close game! We’ll run this one again… [clavain](https://www.commandsandcolors.net/ancients/forum-main.html?view=user&userid=1685 "View clavain's Profile") replied the topic: [#3870](https://www.commandsandcolors.net/ancients/forum-main.html?view=topic&catid=18&id=30#3870) 4 years 8 months ago [](https://www.commandsandcolors.net/ancients/forum-main.html?view=user&userid=1685 "View clavain's Profile") 6-5 Carthage, very close and tense match. Romans (me) managed to move their foot forward in an extended line, while Carthage ate up the Roman light troops and went to a quick 3-0 lead. As soon as the lines met that went back to 3-3, and then it was trading units one for one each turn until the end almost. Rome could likely have won it if they had managed to draw a single card allowing them to activate two units in the centre, but the hand was full of less useful cards for the most part. We also did not pick up on the error in the Vassal module mentioned below (HI vs HC with Hasdrubal, dooh!) [DanieleC](https://www.commandsandcolors.net/ancients/forum-main.html?view=user&userid=1638 "View DanieleC's Profile") replied the topic: [#3708](https://www.commandsandcolors.net/ancients/forum-main.html?view=topic&catid=18&id=30#3708) 4 years 11 months ago [](https://www.commandsandcolors.net/ancients/forum-main.html?view=user&userid=1638 "View DanieleC's Profile") the map and the Vassal's scenario are wrong. In GMT officil scenario book the unit attached with Hasdrubal is an Heavy Infantry not an Heavy Cavalry. Also the list of the units below the map states 1 HC and 1 HI. How the Vassal's module can be correct? [Valvorik](https://www.commandsandcolors.net/ancients/forum-main.html?view=user&userid=1394 "View Valvorik's Profile") replied the topic: [#1991](https://www.commandsandcolors.net/ancients/forum-main.html?view=topic&catid=18&id=30#1991) 8 years 8 months ago [](https://www.commandsandcolors.net/ancients/forum-main.html?view=user&userid=1394 "View Valvorik's Profile") Romans win at last 6:4, despite Carthage's heavy cavalry being used to good effect, line commands and double times move the roman foot with leaders in their midst come forward resulting in heavy Carthaginian losses in the centre. [Valvorik](https://www.commandsandcolors.net/ancients/forum-main.html?view=user&userid=1394 "View Valvorik's Profile") replied the topic: [#1990](https://www.commandsandcolors.net/ancients/forum-main.html?view=topic&catid=18&id=30#1990) 8 years 8 months ago [](https://www.commandsandcolors.net/ancients/forum-main.html?view=user&userid=1394 "View Valvorik's Profile") Another 6:4 Carthage win, this time the turning point being a "clash of shields" that takes out key Roman units in centre, and heavy infantry well-commanded doing well. Carthage's heavy cavalry never came into action. Solo play. [Valvorik](https://www.commandsandcolors.net/ancients/forum-main.html?view=user&userid=1394 "View Valvorik's Profile") replied the topic: [#1982](https://www.commandsandcolors.net/ancients/forum-main.html?view=topic&catid=18&id=30#1982) 8 years 9 months ago [](https://www.commandsandcolors.net/ancients/forum-main.html?view=user&userid=1394 "View Valvorik's Profile") Carthage was taking a beating, Rome 4:2, its centre having been driven into and its heavy cavalry destroyed, when a coordinated strike saw it wipe out two Roman units with their officers to get 4 banners, for a 6:4 win for Carthage - statistical fluke but such is war. [alecrespi](https://www.commandsandcolors.net/ancients/forum-main.html?view=user&userid=223 "View alecrespi's Profile") replied the topic: [#1516](https://www.commandsandcolors.net/ancients/forum-main.html?view=topic&catid=18&id=30#1516) 9 years 10 months ago [![Image 31](https://www.commandsandcolors.net/ancients/media/kunena/avatars/resized/size120/users/avatar223.png?1714554199)](https://www.commandsandcolors.net/ancients/forum-main.html?view=user&userid=223 "View alecrespi's Profile") Just played it tonight: Rome 6 - Carthage 5 Carthaginians had the chance to win with an all-or-nothing "mounted charge" on Heavy Cavalry... but dice rolls conceeded the victory to Romans. [badweasel](https://www.commandsandcolors.net/ancients/forum-main.html?view=user&userid=413 "View badweasel's Profile") replied the topic: [#392](https://www.commandsandcolors.net/ancients/forum-main.html?view=topic&catid=18&id=30#392) 17 years 1 month ago [![Image 32](https://www.commandsandcolors.net/ancients/media/kunena/avatars/resized/size120/aurelia/nophoto.png)](https://www.commandsandcolors.net/ancients/forum-main.html?view=user&userid=413 "View badweasel's Profile") Solo Play: Carthage was completely outmatched in this battle. Rome spent the first several turns laying down harassing fire that weakened the Carthaginian line. A combination of Move-Fire-Move, Green Units, and Darken the Sky really made this an effective move. Once the actual battle was joined, Carthage took the lead through a shock attack that pushed back Scipio's legion. Unfortunately, here and throughout the rest of the battle, Carthage could not eliminate many units but instead sent them retreating several hexes away. The other bright spot for them was Hasdrubal was again a powerful commander using his heavy infantry to crush Laelius and scatter his legion. This was not enough however to counteract the superior Roman fighting force. Rome 6 - Carthage 3 Carthage opted to push against the Roman left this time, keeping themselves away from the bulk of the Roman force. It was quite effective as their medium units were able to cut off and then eliminate units, while Rome was struggling to respond. Hasdrubal was again an excellent leader. Though his heavies were cut to pieces, the back up medium infantry filled the role and cut through the Roman line. In my games, it seems that Carthaginian leaders named Hasdrubal are absolutely unstoppable. Rome fought back for a long time and protected its units, but the continuous onslaught broke them before the larger right legion could come into play.
