| | | The **Battle of Zama** was fought in 202 BC in what is now Tunisia between a [Roman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Republic "Roman Republic") army commanded by [Scipio Africanus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scipio_Africanus "Scipio Africanus") and a [Carthaginian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Carthage "Ancient Carthage") army commanded by [Hannibal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal "Hannibal"). The battle was part of the [Second Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Punic_War "Second Punic War") and resulted in such a severe defeat for the Carthaginians that they [capitulated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitulation_/(surrender/) "Capitulation (surrender)"), while Hannibal was forced into exile. The Roman army of approximately 30,000 men was outnumbered by the Carthaginians who fielded either 40,000 or 50,000; the Romans were stronger in cavalry, but the Carthaginians had 80 [war elephants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_elephant "War elephant"). At the outset of the Second Punic War, in 218 BC, a Carthaginian army led by Hannibal invaded [mainland Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Italy "Mainland Italy"), where it [campaigned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_campaign "Military campaign") for the next 16 years. In 210 BC Scipio took command of the faltering Roman war effort in [Iberia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberia "Iberia") (modern Spain and Portugal) and cleared the peninsula of Carthaginians in five years. He returned to Rome and was appointed [consul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_consul "Roman consul") in 205 BC. The following year [his army landed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_invasion_of_Africa_/(204%E2%80%93201_BC/) "Roman invasion of Africa (204–201 BC)") near the Carthaginian port of [Utica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utica,_Tunisia "Utica, Tunisia"). The Carthaginians and their [Numidian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numidians "Numidians") allies were repeatedly beaten in battle and the Roman ally [Masinissa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masinissa "Masinissa") became the leading Numidian ruler. Scipio and Carthage entered into peace negotiations, while Carthage recalled armies from Italy commanded by Hannibal and [Mago Barca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mago_Barca "Mago Barca"). The [Roman Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Senate "Roman Senate") ratified a draft treaty, but when Hannibal arrived from Italy, Carthage repudiated it. Hannibal marched inland to confront the Romans and a battle quickly ensued. The fighting opened with a charge by the Carthaginian elephants. These were repulsed, some retreating through the Carthaginian cavalry on each wing and disorganising them. The Roman cavalry units on each wing took advantage to charge their counterparts, rout them and pursue them off the battlefield. The two armies' close-order infantry were each deployed in three lines. The first two lines engaged each other and after a hard-fought combat the Carthaginians were routed. The second Carthaginian line then fanatically assaulted the Roman first line, inflicting heavy losses and pushing it back. After the Romans committed their second line the Carthaginians were forced to withdraw. There was a pause, during which the Romans formed a single extended line, to match that of the Carthaginians. These two lines charged each other, according to the near-contemporary historian [Polybius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polybius "Polybius") "with the greatest fire and fury". The fight continued for some time, neither side gaining the advantage. The Roman cavalry then returned to the battlefield and charged the Carthaginian line in the rear, routing and destroying it. Carthage was left with no army with which to continue the war. The [peace treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_treaty "Peace treaty") dictated by Rome stripped Carthage of its non-African territories and some of its African ones. Thereafter, it was clear that Carthage was politically subordinate to Rome. [![Image 5: A monochrome relief stele depicting a man in classical Greek clothing raising one arm](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/Stele_des_Polybios.jpg/120px-Stele_des_Polybios.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Stele_des_Polybios.jpg) Polybius The main source for almost every aspect of the Punic Wars[\[note 1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-2) is the historian [Polybius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polybius "Polybius") (c. 200 – c. 118 BC), a Greek sent to Rome in 167 BC as a hostage.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200620%E2%80%9321-3) His works include a now largely lost manual on military tactics,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShutt193853-4) but he is best known for [_The Histories_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Histories_/(Polybius/) "The Histories (Polybius)"), written sometime after 146 BC.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200620%E2%80%9321-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWalbank199011%E2%80%9312-5) Polybius's work is considered broadly objective and largely neutral as between [Carthaginian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Carthage "Ancient Carthage") and [Roman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Republic "Roman Republic") points of view.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996x%E2%80%93xi-6)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHau201623%E2%80%9324-7) Polybius was an analytical historian and wherever possible interviewed participants, from both sides, in the events he wrote about.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShutt193855-8)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200620%E2%80%9321-3)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChampion201598,_101-9) The accuracy of Polybius's account has been much debated over the past 150 years. Modern historians consider Polybius to have treated the relatives of [Scipio Aemilianus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scipio_Aemilianus "Scipio Aemilianus"), his patron and friend, unduly favourably but the consensus is to accept his account largely at face value and the details of the wars in modern sources are largely based on interpretations of Polybius's account.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200620%E2%80%9321-3)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996x%E2%80%93xi,_82%E2%80%9384-10) The modern historian Andrew Curry sees Polybius as being "fairly reliable";[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECurry201234-11) [Craige Champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craige_B._Champion "Craige B. Champion") describes him as "a remarkably well-informed, industrious, and insightful historian".[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChampion2015102-12) Much of Polybius's account of the Second Punic War is missing, or only exists in fragmentary form.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby199887-13) The account of the Roman historian [Livy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Livy "Livy"), who relied heavily on Polybius, is used by modern historians where Polybius's account is not extant.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby199887-13)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChampion201595-14) The classicist [Adrian Goldsworthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrian_Goldsworthy "Adrian Goldsworthy") says Livy's "reliability is often suspect",[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006222-15) and the historian [Philip Sabin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Sabin "Philip Sabin") refers to Livy's "military ignorance".[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTESabin199662-16) Dexter Hoyos describes Livy's account of Zama as "bizarrely at odds with Polybius’ which he seems not to understand fully".[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos20153-17) Other, later, ancient histories of the war exist, although often in fragmentary or summary form.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200621%E2%80%9323-18)[\[note 2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-20) Modern historians usually take into account the writings of [Appian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appian "Appian") and [Cassius Dio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassius_Dio "Cassius Dio"), two Greek authors writing during the [Roman era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece_in_the_Roman_era "Greece in the Roman era"); they are described by John Lazenby as "clearly far inferior" to Livy. Hoyos accuses Appian of bizarre invention in his account of Zama; Michael Taylor states that it is "idiosyncratic". But some fragments of Polybius can be recovered from their texts.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby199887-13)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200620%E2%80%9321-3)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaylor2019312-21) The Greek moralist [Plutarch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plutarch "Plutarch") wrote several biographies of Roman commanders in his _[Parallel Lives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parallel_Lives "Parallel Lives")_.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMineo2015111%E2%80%93127-19)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos20153-17) Other sources include coins, inscriptions, archaeological evidence and empirical evidence from reconstructions such as the [trireme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trireme "Trireme") [_Olympias_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympias_/(trireme/) "Olympias (trireme)").[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200623,_98-22) The [First Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Punic_War "First Punic War") was fought between the two main powers of the western [Mediterranean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean "Mediterranean") in the 3rd century BC: Carthage and Rome.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200682-23) The war lasted for 23 years, from 264 to 241 BC, before the Carthaginians were defeated.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996157-24)[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199997-25) It took place primarily on the Mediterranean island of [Sicily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicily "Sicily"), its surrounding waters and in [North Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Africa "North Africa").[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200682-23) [![Image 6: a map of the western Mediterranean region showing the territory controlled by Rome and Carthage in 218 BC](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/62/Map_of_Rome_and_Carthage_at_the_start_of_the_Second_Punic_War_Modified.svg/500px-Map_of_Rome_and_Carthage_at_the_start_of_the_Second_Punic_War_Modified.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Map_of_Rome_and_Carthage_at_the_start_of_the_Second_Punic_War_Modified.svg) The approximate extent of territory controlled by Rome and Carthage immediately before the start of the Second Punic War [Carthage expanded its territory in Iberia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthaginian_Iberia "Carthaginian Iberia") (modern Spain and Portugal) from 236 BC,[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011220-26) in 226 BC agreeing the [Ebro Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ebro_Treaty "Ebro Treaty") with Rome which established the [Ebro River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ebro_River "Ebro River") as the northern boundary of the Carthaginian [sphere of influence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere_of_influence "Sphere of influence"). A little later Rome made a separate treaty of association with the city of [Saguntum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saguntum "Saguntum"), well south of the Ebro. [Hannibal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal "Hannibal"), the de facto ruler of Carthaginian Iberia, led an army to Saguntum in 219 BC and [besieged, captured and sacked it](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Saguntum "Siege of Saguntum"). Early the following year Rome [declared war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declaration_of_war "Declaration of war") on Carthage, starting the [Second Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Punic_War "Second Punic War").[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006143%E2%80%93145-27)[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECollins199813-28)[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2015281-29) Hannibal led a large Carthaginian army from Iberia, through [Gaul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaul "Gaul"), [over the Alps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal%27s_crossing_of_the_Alps "Hannibal's crossing of the Alps") and invaded [mainland Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_Italy "Mainland Italy") in 218 BC. During the next three years Hannibal inflicted heavy defeats on the Romans at the battles of [the Trebia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Trebia "Battle of the Trebia"), [Lake Trasimene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lake_Trasimene "Battle of Lake Trasimene") and [Cannae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cannae "Battle of Cannae").[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTE%C3%91aco_del_Hoyo2015377-30) At the last of these alone, at least 67,500 Romans were killed or captured.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999192%E2%80%93194-31) The historian Toni Ñaco del Hoyo describes these as "great military calamities",[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTE%C3%91aco_del_Hoyo2015377-30) and Brian Carey writes that they brought Rome to the brink of collapse.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey20072-32) Hannibal's army campaigned in Italy for 14 years.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015322-33) There was also extensive fighting in [Iberia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberia "Iberia") from 218 BC. In 210 BC [Publius Cornelius Scipio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scipio_Africanus "Scipio Africanus") arrived to take command of Roman forces in Iberia.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015323-34) During the following four years Scipio repeatedly defeated the Carthaginians, driving them out of Iberia in 206 BC.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006277%E2%80%93285-35) One of Carthage's allies in Iberia was the [Numidian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numidians "Numidians") prince [Masinissa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masinissa "Masinissa"), who led a force of [light cavalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numidian_cavalry "Numidian cavalry") in several battles.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015330-36)[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999233-37) In 206 BC Scipio left Iberia and returned to Italy.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006285-38) There he was elected to the senior position of [consul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_consul "Roman consul") in early 205 BC, despite being aged 31 when the minimum age for the office was 42.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey200799-39) Scipio was already anticipating an invasion of North Africa and while still in Iberia had been negotiating with the Numidian leaders Masinissa and [Syphax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syphax "Syphax"). He failed to win over the latter, but made an ally of the former.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006285%E2%80%93286-40) Opinion was divided in Roman political circles as to whether an invasion of North Africa was an excessive risk. Hannibal was still on Italian soil; there was the possibility of further Carthaginian invasions,[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006286-41) shortly to be realised when Hannibal's youngest brother [Mago Barca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mago_Barca "Mago Barca") landed in [Liguria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liguria "Liguria") with an army from Iberia;[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011306-42) the practical difficulties of an amphibious invasion and its logistical follow up were considerable; and when the Romans had invaded North Africa in 256 BC during the First Punic War they had been driven out with heavy losses, which had re-energised the Carthaginians.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006286%E2%80%93287-43) Eventually a compromise was agreed: Scipio was given Sicily as his consular province,[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998194-44) which was the best location for the Romans to launch an invasion of the Carthaginian homeland from and then logistically support it, and permission to cross to Africa on his own judgement.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006286-41) However, Roman commitment was less than wholehearted; Scipio could not [conscript troops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscription "Conscription") for his consular army, as was usual, but only call for volunteers.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011306-42)[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998195-45) In 216 BC the survivors of the Roman defeat at Cannae had been formed into two legions and sent to Sicily.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006218-46) They formed the core of the Roman expeditionary force.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006287-47)[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaylor2019316-48) Modern historians estimate a combat strength of 25,000–30,000, of whom more than 90 per cent were infantry.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006287-47)[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007100-49) With up to half of the complement of his legions being fresh volunteers, and with no fighting having taken place on Sicily for the past five years, Scipio instigated a rigorous training regime. This extended from drills by individual [centuries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centuria "Centuria") – the basic Roman army manoeuvre unit of 80 men – to exercises by the full army. This lasted for approximately a year. At the same time Scipio assembled a vast quantity of food and [materiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Materiel "Materiel"), [merchant ships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merchant_ship "Merchant ship") to transport it and his troops, and warships to escort the transports.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006287%E2%80%93288-50) Also during 205 BC, 30 Roman ships under Scipio's second-in-command, the [legate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legatus "Legatus") [Gaius Laelius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaius_Laelius "Gaius Laelius"), raided North Africa around [Hippo Regius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hippo_Regius "Hippo Regius"), gathering large quantities of loot and many captives.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007100-49)[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006288-51) The Carthaginians initially believed this was the anticipated invasion by Scipio and his full invasion force; they hastily strengthened fortifications and raised troops. Reinforcements were sent to Mago in an attempt to distract the Romans in Italy.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998194%E2%80%93195-52) Meanwhile a succession war had broken out in Numidia between the Roman-supporting Masinissa and the Carthaginian-inclined Syphax. Laelius re-established contact with Masinissa during his raid. Masinissa expressed dismay regarding how long it was taking the Romans to complete their preparations and land in Africa.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998198%E2%80%93199-53) [![Image 7: a photograph of an inverted, polished, slightly tarnished, battered bronze hemisphere](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a8/Helmet_typ_Montefortino_01.jpg/250px-Helmet_typ_Montefortino_01.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Helmet_typ_Montefortino_01.jpg) The bowl of a [Montefortino-type helmet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montefortino_helmet "Montefortino helmet"), which was used by Roman infantry between c. 300 BC and 100 AD. The cheek guards are missing. Most male Roman citizens were liable for military service and would serve as [infantry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infantry "Infantry"); a [better-off minority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equites "Equites") provided a [cavalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalry "Cavalry") component. Historically, when at war the Romans would raise two [legions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_legion "Roman legion"), each of 4,200 infantry – this could be increased to 5,000 in some circumstances,[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199923-54) or, rarely, even more (6,200 being the largest number recorded)[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006287-47) – and 300 cavalry. Approximately 1,200 of the infantry – poorer or younger men unable to afford the armour and equipment of a standard [legionary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legionary "Legionary") – served as [javelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Javelin "Javelin")\-armed [skirmishers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skirmisher "Skirmisher") known as _[velites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velites "Velites")_; they each carried several javelins, which would be thrown from a distance, a short sword and a 90-centimetre (3 ft) shield.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200648-55) The balance were equipped as [heavy infantry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_infantry "Heavy infantry"), with [body armour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body_armor "Body armor"), large [shields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scutum_/(shield/) "Scutum (shield)") and [short thrusting swords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gladius "Gladius"). They were divided into three ranks, of which the _[hastati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hastati "Hastati")_ and _[principes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principes "Principes")_ in the first two ranks also carried two javelins each; the _[triarii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triarii "Triarii")_, in the third rank, had [thrusting spears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasta_/(spear/) "Hasta (spear)") instead. A standard-size legion at full strength would have 1,200 _velites_, 1,200 _hastati_, 1,200 _principes_, 600 _triarii_ and 300 _equites_.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199922%E2%80%9325-56)[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200650-57) Both legionary [sub-units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maniple_/(military_unit/) "Maniple (military unit)") and individual legionaries fought in relatively open order. It was the long-standing Roman procedure to elect two men each year as senior [magistrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_magistrate "Roman magistrate"), known as consuls, who in time of war would each lead an army. An army was usually formed by combining a Roman legion with a similarly sized and equipped legion provided by their [Latin allies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socii "Socii"); allied legions usually had a larger attached complement of cavalry than Roman ones.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199922%E2%80%9325-56)[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200650-57) By this stage of the war, Roman armies were generally larger, typically consisting of four legions, two Roman and two provided by its allies, for a total of approximately 20,000 men. The Roman army which invaded Africa consisted of four legions, each of the Roman pair reinforced to an unprecedented 6,200 infantry and with a more usual 300 cavalry each. Modern historians estimate the invading army to have totalled 25,000–30,000 men, including perhaps 2,500 cavalry.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006227,_287-58)[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007100-49)[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011309-59) Goldsworthy describes the army as being "superbly trained" when it left Sicily.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200476-60) [![Image 8: a pen and ink sketch of a man on a horse waving a spear](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c2/Numidian_cavalry.png/250px-Numidian_cavalry.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Numidian_cavalry.png) A Numidian cavalryman as imagined in 1891 Carthaginian citizens served in their army only if there was a direct threat to the city of [Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthage "Carthage").[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby19989-61)[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2006494-62) When they did they fought as well-armoured heavy infantry armed with long thrusting spears, although they were notoriously ill-trained and ill-disciplined. In most circumstances Carthage recruited foreigners to make up its army.[\[note 3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-64) Many were from North Africa and these were frequently referred to as "Libyans". The region provided several types of fighters, including: [close-order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Close_order_formation "Close order formation") infantry equipped with large shields, helmets, short swords and long thrusting [spears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spear "Spear"); javelin-armed [light infantry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_infantry "Light infantry") skirmishers; close-order shock cavalry[\[note 4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-66) (also known as "heavy cavalry") carrying spears; and light cavalry skirmishers who threw javelins from a distance and avoided close combat – the latter were usually Numidians.)[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200632%E2%80%9334-67)[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKoon201579%E2%80%9387-68) The close-order African infantry and the citizen-militia both fought in a tightly packed formation known as a [phalanx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phalanx "Phalanx").[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKoon201593-69) On occasion some of the infantry would wear captured Roman armour, especially those who served with Hannibal.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTERawlings2015305-70) Both Iberia and Gaul provided experienced but unarmoured infantry who would charge ferociously, but had a reputation for breaking off if combat was protracted. [Slingers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balearic_slinger "Balearic slinger") were frequently recruited from the [Balearic Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balearic_Islands "Balearic Islands").[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200632%E2%80%9334-67)[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall19998%E2%80%939-71) The Carthaginians also employed [war elephants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_elephant "War elephant"); North Africa had indigenous [African forest elephants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_forest_elephant "African forest elephant") at the time.[\[note 5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-73)[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall19999-74)[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby199627-75) The sources are not clear as to whether they carried towers containing fighting men.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTESabin199670,_n._76-76) [![Image 9: A relief map of part of north Africa, showing the site of the battle and the movements of Scipio's forces during the campaign](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/Publius_Scipio%27s_Invasion_of_Africa%2C_204%E2%80%93201_BC.png/500px-Publius_Scipio%27s_Invasion_of_Africa%2C_204%E2%80%93201_BC.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Publius_Scipio%27s_Invasion_of_Africa,_204%E2%80%93201_BC.png) In 204 BC, probably in June or July, the Roman army left Sicily and disembarked three days later at [Cape Farina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Farina "Cape Farina") 20 kilometres (12 mi) north of the large Carthaginian port of [Utica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utica,_Tunisia "Utica, Tunisia").[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007103-77)[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006291-78) Carthaginian scouting parties were repulsed and the area was pillaged. Masinissa joined the Romans with either 200 or 2,000 men, the sources differ. Masinissa had been recently defeated by his Numidian rival Syphax, who had decided to act in support of Carthage.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006290%E2%80%93292-79) Wanting a more permanent base and a port more resilient to the bad weather to be expected when winter came, Scipio [besieged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Besiege "Besiege") Utica. Although the Romans were well supplied with [siege engines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_engine "Siege engine") the siege dragged on.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006291-78)[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998206-80) A Carthaginian army under the experienced commander [Hasdrubal Gisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasdrubal_Gisco "Hasdrubal Gisco") and a Numidian one under Syphax set up separate fortified camps nearby. The size of both of these armies is uncertain, but it is accepted that the Romans were considerably outnumbered, especially in terms of cavalry.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006292%E2%80%93293-81)[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996207-82) The Romans pulled back from Utica.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006294-83) Both sides were reluctant to commit to a [pitched battle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitched_battle "Pitched battle").[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999277-84) [![Image 10: a photograph of a marble bust of a man, with the nose broken off](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a6/Bust_of_Sulla_%28loan_from_Ny_Carlsberg_Glyptotek%29_-_Glyptothek_-_Munich_-_Germany_2017.jpg/250px-Bust_of_Sulla_%28loan_from_Ny_Carlsberg_Glyptotek%29_-_Glyptothek_-_Munich_-_Germany_2017.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bust_of_Sulla_/(loan_from_Ny_Carlsberg_Glyptotek/)_-_Glyptothek_-_Munich_-_Germany_2017.jpg) Marble bust of the younger Scipio[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoarelli200273%E2%80%9374-85)[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEtcheto2012274%E2%80%93278-86) Scipio sent [emissaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambassador "Ambassador") to Syphax to attempt to persuade him to defect. Syphax in turn offered to broker peace terms.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006292%E2%80%93293-81) A series of exchanges of negotiating parties followed, during which Scipio obtained information on the layout and construction of the Numidian camp, as well as the size and composition of the Numidian army and the most frequented routes in and out of the camp.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006292%E2%80%93293-81)[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999277-84)[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999278-87) As the weather improved Scipio made conspicuous preparations to assault Utica.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999278%E2%80%93279-88) Instead, he marched his army out late one evening and divided it in two.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006293-89)[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998208-90) One part [launched a night attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Utica_/(203_BC/) "Battle of Utica (203 BC)") on the Numidian camp, setting fire to their reed [barracks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barracks "Barracks"). In the ensuing panic and confusion the Numidians were dispersed with heavy casualties.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007105%E2%80%93106-91) Not realising what was happening, the Carthaginians were also taken by surprise when Scipio attacked them with the remaining Romans. Again the Romans inflicted heavy casualties in the dark.[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006293%E2%80%93294-92)[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007105%E2%80%93106-91) Hasdrubal fled 40 kilometres (25 mi) to Carthage with 2,500 survivors, pursued by Scipio. Syphax escaped with a few cavalry and regrouped 11 kilometres (7 mi) away.[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998208-90)[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007106-93) When word of the defeat reached Carthage there was panic, and some wanted to renew the peace negotiations. The Carthaginian Senate also heard demands for Hannibal's army to be recalled. A decision was reached to fight on with locally available resources.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006294-83) A force of 4,000 Iberian warriors arrived in Carthage, and Hasdrubal raised further local troops with whom to reinforce the survivors of Utica;[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2003162-94) Syphax remained loyal and joined Hasdrubal with what was left of his army.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006294%E2%80%93295-95) The combined force is estimated at 30,000 and they established a strong camp in an area by the [Bagradas River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bagradas_River "Bagradas River") known as the Great Plains within 30–50 days of the defeat at Utica.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006295-96)[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2003162-94) Scipio immediately marched most of his army to the scene. The size of his army is not known, but it was outnumbered by the Carthaginians.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007106-93) After several days of skirmishing both armies committed to a pitched battle.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006295-96) Upon being charged by the Romans and Masinissa's Numidians, those Carthaginians who had been involved in the debacle at Utica turned and fled; morale had not recovered.[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015333-97)[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006295-96)[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007108-98) Only the Iberians stood and fought. They were enveloped by the well-drilled Roman legions and wiped out.[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTERawlings199690-99)[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006295%E2%80%93296-100) Hasdrubal fled to Carthage, where he was demoted and exiled.[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2015b205-101) [![Image 11: A monochrome photograph of both sides of a crude, ancient coin; one showing the head of a bearded man, the other a horse](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/94/MASSINISSA_-_MAA_23_-_87000716.jpg/330px-MASSINISSA_-_MAA_23_-_87000716.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MASSINISSA_-_MAA_23_-_87000716.jpg) A coin issued by King Masinissa Syphax withdrew as far as his capital, [Cirta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cirta "Cirta"), where he recruited more troops to supplement those survivors who had stayed with him.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015334-102) Masinissa's Numidians pursued their fleeing countrymen accompanied by part of the Roman force, under Laelius.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015334-102) The armies met in the [battle of Cirta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cirta "Battle of Cirta"), where Syphax's army initially gained the upper hand.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015334-102) Laelius fed groups of Roman infantry into the battle line and Syphax's troops broke and fled.[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200648,_50-103)[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015334-102) Syphax was captured[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2015b205-101)[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999282-104) and paraded beneath the city walls in chains, which caused Cirta to surrender to Masinissa, who then took over much of Syphax's kingdom and joined it to his own.[\[note 6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-107)[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998212-105)[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007110-108) Scipio and Carthage entered into peace negotiations.[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007111-109) Carthage built up its naval strength and prepared the city of Carthage for a siege.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015334-102) The Carthaginian Senate recalled both Hannibal and Mago from Italy.[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007111-109)[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006296%E2%80%93297-110) After Scipio overran all of Carthaginian Iberia in 205 BC, Mago had left with those forces still loyal and sailed to Liguria in northern Italy[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarcel%C3%B32015362-111)[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007111-109) where he recruited Gallic and Ligurian reinforcements. In 203 BC Mago marched into [Cisalpine Gaul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cisalpine_Gaul "Cisalpine Gaul") in an attempt to draw Roman attention away from North Africa, but was defeated at the [battle of Insubria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Insubria "Battle of Insubria").[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999286%E2%80%93287-112) His army retreated and sailed for Carthage from [Genua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genoa "Genoa"). Mago died of wounds on the voyage and some of his ships were intercepted by the Romans,[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011312-113) but 12,000 of his troops reached Carthage.[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999289-114) By 207 BC, after 12 years of campaigning in Italy, Hannibal's forces had been compelled to withdraw to [Bruttium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruttium "Bruttium"), the "toe" of Italy, where they remained undefeated but were ineffective.[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007111-109)[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2015289%E2%80%93290-115)[\[110\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011304%E2%80%93305-116) When recalled the limited number of ships available meant that few horses could be taken and that many newer recruits were left in Italy.[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007111%E2%80%93112-117)[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoberts2017228%E2%80%93229-118) Hannibal's army sailed from [Croton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crotone "Crotone") and landed at [Leptis Minor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leptis_Parva "Leptis Parva"), some 140 kilometres (87 mi) south of Carthage, with 15,000–20,000 experienced veterans. Hannibal was appointed to command the new army and consolidated his forces at [Hadrumetum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadrumetum "Hadrumetum").[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007111%E2%80%93112-117)[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011312-113)[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006244-119) The Roman Senate ratified a draft treaty, but because of mistrust and a surge in confidence when Hannibal arrived from Italy, Carthage repudiated it.[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999287%E2%80%93291-120) The Romans retaliated by methodically capturing Carthaginian-controlled towns in Carthage's [hinterland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hinterland "Hinterland") and selling their inhabitants into slavery, regardless of whether they had surrendered before being attacked or not. Scipio probably anticipated that these attacks would create pressure on the Carthaginians to dispatch an army to face him as soon as possible, rather than wait until it had recruited to maximum strength and was fully trained. Scipio was himself under time pressure, as he was concerned that his political opponents in the Roman Senate might appoint a new consul to replace him. The Carthaginian Senate repeatedly ordered Hannibal to advance from his base at Hadrumetum and deal with Scipio's army, but Hannibal delayed until he had been reinforced by 2,000 Numidian cavalry led by a relative of Syphax – they were reputed to be elite troops.[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998216%E2%80%93218-121) Hannibal believed, correctly, that the Roman army had not yet been joined by its Numidian auxiliaries under Masinissa and so had the Carthaginian army march inland for five days and camp not far from the town of [Zama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zama_/(Tunisia/) "Zama (Tunisia)"), just 3 kilometres (1.9 mi) from the Roman army. This proximity all but guaranteed that a battle would result. While the Carthaginians were en route Masinissa arrived at the Roman camp with 10,000 Numidians.[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998219-122) The site of the battle is generally, but not universally, believed to be a flat area to the south of Sicca (modern [El Kef](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Kef "El Kef")), the Draa el Metnan.[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaylor2019313%E2%80%93314-123) [![Image 12: a photograph of a white marble head depicting Hannibal](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/Hannibal_Slodtz_Louvre_MR2093_%28cropped2%29.png/250px-Hannibal_Slodtz_Louvre_MR2093_%28cropped2%29.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hannibal_Slodtz_Louvre_MR2093_/(cropped2/).png) 1704 French bust of Hannibal Little is known of the number of men Scipio commanded at Zama.[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015336-124) An estimated 25,000–30,000 men had landed in Africa the year before and there is no record of any reinforcements arriving from Italy. However, the strength of the force left to guard their camp and continue the siege of Utica is not known, nor is the level of attrition suffered in the three major battles and several skirmishes the legions had so far been involved in.[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998221-125)[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011309-59) The ancient sources agree that the Romans were supported by 6,000 Numidian infantry and 4,000 cavalry under Masinissa. The ancient historian Appian, writing 350 years after the event, states that the Numidians brought the total to 34,500 troops, but modern historians do not accept this.[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006301%E2%80%93302-126)[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015336-124) They usually give a total of 29,000[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011316-127)[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaylor2019316-48) or 30,000,[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998219-122)[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaylor2019316-48) although [Nigel Bagnall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigel_Bagnall "Nigel Bagnall") gives 40,000.[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999291-128) Of these, slightly more than 6,000 were cavalry.[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998221-125) Appian states that the Carthaginian army at the battle of Zama consisted of 50,000 men; this is discounted by many modern historians,[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006302-129) although some accept it with provisos.[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaylor2019317,_317_n._24-130) Most give 40,000, based on Polybius. Of these, all but 4,000 were infantry. Hannibal's army had abandoned its horses in Italy because of a lack of shipping space and Masinissa's defeat of Syphax had dried up the supply of Numidian cavalry; thus, even with the recent addition of 2,000 Numidians the Carthaginians fielded only 4,000 cavalry.[\[125\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998220%E2%80%93221-131)[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBahmanyar201641-132)[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007115-133) Hannibal also deployed 80 war elephants, the first time these are recorded as being used since Scipio invaded. Hannibal delayed seeking battle to give his army time to train up a force of elephants. Such forces had been fielded earlier in the war in both Italy and Iberia. Hannibal had famously taken elephants over the Alps in 218 BC. It is unclear why Carthage was not able to field a force of fully trained war elephants at Zama, or at any time since Scipio invaded.[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwards2001903-134)[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006163%E2%80%93166,_250,_279-135)[\[130\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBahmanyar201653-136) ### Initial dispositions \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Battle_of_Zama&action=edit§ion=13 "Edit section: Initial dispositions")\] [![Image 13: A map showing the initial dispositions of both armies](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/Mohammad_adil_rais-battle_of_zama-1.PNG/330px-Mohammad_adil_rais-battle_of_zama-1.PNG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mohammad_adil_rais-battle_of_zama-1.PNG) The initial deployment of the Roman and Carthaginian armies The Roman army formed up with the heavy infantry of its two Roman legions in the centre and with allied legions on each side of them.[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006302-129)[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBahmanyar201641-132) As usual, the _hastati_ formed the front rank with the _principes_ and then the _triarii_ behind them. Instead of organising each legion's maniples – the basic Roman infantry manoeuvre unit of 120 men each – in the usual "checkerboard" or _[quincunx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincunx "Quincunx")_ formation, Scipio arranged a _principes_ maniple directly behind each maniple of _hastati_. This left broad avenues through the Roman lines, which were occupied by the Roman light infantry, the _velites_. Masinissa's 4,000 Numidian cavalry were on the right of the infantry. Laelius led 1,500 Roman and allied cavalry positioned on the left. There were a further 600 Numidian cavalry under Dacamas, but it is not known whether they were attached to Masinissa's or Laelius's force.[\[131\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998221%E2%80%93222-137) It is not stated in the ancient sources what role or roles the 6,000 Numidian infantry took up. Modern suggestions include operating in close support of their cavalry, guarding the Roman camp, supplementing the _velites_ as skirmishers or forming up as close-order infantry to one side of the legions.[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaylor2019322-138) The Carthaginian deployment reflected the fact that Hannibal's command was made up of the survivors of three different armies. Hannibal had not had time to integrate the forces he had been allocated into a unified command and so felt it wisest to deploy them separately.[\[133\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006303-139) The Carthaginian infantry, like the Romans', went in the centre. Its first line was made up largely of veterans of Mago's failed expedition to northern Italy. The close-order troops were [Iberians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberians "Iberians"), [Gauls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauls "Gauls") and [Ligurians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ligurians "Ligurians"). In front of these heavy infantry were light-infantry skirmishers consisting of Balearic slingers, [Moor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauri "Mauri") archers and Moor and Ligurian javelin-men. The total strength of this component was 12,000 men. In front of these infantry were the 80 war elephants, evenly spaced along the line, approximately 30 metres (98 ft) apart.[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998222-140)[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999291-128)[\[135\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBahmanyar201655-141) The modern historian José Lago states that the Carthaginian light infantry were sent out in front of the whole Carthaginian army, as was usual, including in front of the elephants,[\[136\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELago201360-142)[\[137\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200657-143) for the several hours it took the army to form up.[\[138\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006304-144) Carthaginians and other Africans made up the second line. They were either survivors of the earlier campaigns whose morale was poor or freshly raised recruits who had received little training. They probably fought as close-order infantry; Polybius describes them as adopting phalanx formations, but there is modern debate as to just what this describes. The strength of the second line is not known, but it is sometimes assumed by modern historians to have consisted of a further 12,000 men.[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998222-140)[\[139\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBahmanyar201656-145)[\[140\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDaly200287-146) About 200 metres (700 ft) behind the Carthaginian second line were the infantry Hannibal had brought back from Italy. Most of them were [Bruttians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruttians "Bruttians"), but they included some Africans and Iberians who had left Iberia with Hannibal more than 17 years before, and Gauls recruited in northern Italy in 218 and 217 BC. All were battle-hardened veterans.[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998222-140)[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007117-147) This third line is variously estimated at 12,000,[\[142\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007116-148) 15,000–20,000[\[133\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006303-139) or 20,000[\[143\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011317-149)[\[144\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaylor2019318-150) men by modern historians. The Carthaginians are believed to have fielded approximately 4,000 cavalry. Hannibal placed the Numidians among them on his left flank, facing Masinissa's Numidians; and the other African cavalry on the right. How many of the total of 4,000 cavalry were in each of these contingents is not known, although Lazenby suggests that the Numidians on the left would have been the stronger.[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998222-140) [![Image 14: A diagram showing the usual deployment of a legionary maniple and how that fitted within a legion and a typical army](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/Roman_Consular_Army.png/330px-Roman_Consular_Army.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Roman_Consular_Army.png) How a consular army would usually deploy, at Zama each maniple of _principes_ deployed slightly to the left, leaving nine broad avenues through each legion.[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999292-151) The armies advanced towards each other, the first clashes occurring on the Carthaginian left flank, the Roman right, between the 2,000 or more Carthaginian-supporting Numidian cavalry and the 4,000 – or possibly 4,600 – siding with the Romans. Each force sent detachments to hurl javelins at the other and then withdraw. Lazenby describes these skirmishes as "desultory". Hannibal then ordered a charge against the Roman infantry by his 80 elephants, with the whole of his first two lines moving forward in support.[\[146\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007117%E2%80%93118-152)[\[147\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998223-153) The modern historian Jacob Edwards, in a study of Hannibal's use of elephants during the war, describes their deployment at Zama as "an ill-advised practice which departed from the successful tactics used previously". He suggests that they would have been better employed against the superior Roman cavalry on the flanks, rather than directly charging the Roman infantry.[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwards2001903-134) It is possible that Hannibal believed the elephants would have brought an element of surprise, as their previous use in the war had been limited.[\[148\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDoreyDudley1971144-154) Most modern accounts have the elephants in front of the Carthaginian infantry,[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998222-140)[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999291-128)[\[135\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBahmanyar201655-141) but Lago has the Carthaginian light infantry in front of the whole Carthaginian army,[\[136\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELago201360-142) skirmishing with their opposite numbers, as was usual before armies were formed up and ready to commence the battle proper.[\[137\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200657-143) Lago states that they stayed in front of and between the elephants, protecting them from the javelins of the Roman _velites_ until the elephants charged.[\[136\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELago201360-142) As the elephants advanced, the _velites_ moved forward into the gap between the armies, hurled javelins at the elephants, and fell back.[\[138\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006304-144) The Roman heavy infantry then sounded their bugles, and possibly rhythmically banged their weapons against their shields – swashbuckling.[\[note 7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-156)[\[150\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999293-157) This startled some of the elephants and several of those on the left turned and fled, past the end of the line of infantry behind them. Edwards expresses amazement that war elephants should be so easily panicked and again suggests that at least some of the animals were "young and inexperienced at battle" making them "a liability rather than an asset". These out-of-control elephants trampled their way through the Carthaginian-backing Numidian cavalry, thoroughly disordering them.[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007115-133)[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwards2001903-134) Masinissa took advantage of the situation by ordering a charge. This routed the disordered cavalry and they fled, pursued by Masinissa's force.[\[150\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999293-157) Most of the rest of the elephants charged into the Roman infantry, amid showers of javelins. Terrified by the swashbuckling infantry and their bugles the majority stampeded into the broad gaps the Romans had left between their maniples. Many of the _velites_ were killed as they ran back in front of the elephants and into the gaps between the ranks of the heavy infantry. From there they hurled javelins into the elephants' flanks. Those elephants, which emerged into the rear of the Roman army, were all wounded and now cut off. They were subsequently hunted down and killed. Some elephants did charge into the _hastati_ as planned, where they caused heavy casualties before being driven off. This causes Mir Bahmanyar to suggest that the elephants accomplished what Hannibal expected of them. Some elephants balked at charging the _hastati_ on the Roman left and attacked the cavalry alongside them, who also showered the elephants with javelins. Most of these elephants were badly wounded and had lost their crews by this point; those that could flee avoided the line of Carthaginian infantry, but not the Carthaginian cavalry on the right flank. This cavalry force became disorganised by the out-of-control elephants and like Masinissa, Laelius ordered his cavalry to take advantage of this and charge. The Carthaginian cavalry were swept from the field and the Roman cavalry closely pursued them.[\[151\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007118,_122-158)[\[138\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006304-144)[\[150\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999293-157)[\[152\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKoon201584-159)[\[153\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBahmanyar201667-160) ### Infantry engagement \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Battle_of_Zama&action=edit§ion=15 "Edit section: Infantry engagement")\] With the battlefield cleared of both elephants and cavalry, all three ranks of the Roman heavy infantry and the first two ranks of the Carthaginians advanced towards each other. The Carthaginian third rank, Hannibal's Italian veterans, remained in place. The two front ranks charged enthusiastically and violently into each other and commenced a hard-fought, close-quarter, hand-to-hand combat. The Romans' superior weaponry and organisation eventually told and despite the _hastati_ taking further heavy losses, the Carthaginian front rank broke and fled. They attempted to make their way through the Carthaginian second rank, but these men refused to let them pass; according to Polybius to the point of fighting them off. The survivors of the front rank were forced to make their escape around the flanks of the second rank. Many of these then rallied and rejoined the fight by extending the flanks of the Carthaginian second rank.[\[154\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBahmanyar201670-161)[\[155\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006305%E2%80%93306-162) The _hastati_, despite having taken casualties from the elephants and the Carthaginian first rank, now attacked the Carthaginian second rank. Polybius reports that the Carthaginian and other African spearmen who made up this force fought "fanatically and in an extraordinary manner".[\[156\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998224-163) The Romans were pushed back in disorder. Bahmanyar opines that the Roman front rank came close to being broken at this stage.[\[157\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBahmanyar201671-164) The Romans were forced to commit their second line, the _principes_, to the fight.[\[158\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999293%E2%80%93294-165)[\[159\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007124-166) [Liddell Hart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B._H._Liddell_Hart "B. H. Liddell Hart") writes that even the _principes_ struggled to hold the line,[\[160\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELiddell_Hart1976182-167) but eventually this reinforcement was sufficient to break the Carthaginian second line; they fled, pursued impetuously by the _hastati_.[\[161\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006306-168) Both Bahmanyar and Goldsworthy suggest this was an opportunity for the Carthaginian third line to counter-attack the disorganised _hastati_, but that Hannibal decided against it because his third line was some distance back, the fleeing Carthaginians from the first two lines were inadvertently blocking a clean charge and because the ground over which the third line would have attacked was strewn with corpses.[\[161\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006306-168)[\[162\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBahmanyar201676-169) According to Polybius the gap between the fighting lines "was now covered with blood, slaughter, and dead bodies ... slippery corpses which were still soaked in blood and had fallen in heaps".[\[163\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKoon201591%E2%80%9392-170) Bagnall suggests the withdrawal of the Carthaginian second line was more deliberate and orderly than the ancient sources portray.[\[164\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999294-171) Taylor believes that Hannibal had hoped that the Romans would rush forward in pursuit at this stage and that he had prepared an infantry envelopment in anticipation of this. In the event, Scipio saw the potential trap and his troops were disciplined enough to break off their pursuit when recalled.[\[165\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaylor2019324%E2%80%93327-172) The Romans recalled the pursuing _hastati_ by sounding bugles and reformed their line. The Carthaginian third line – Hannibal's veterans supplemented by some of the survivors of the first and second lines – was longer than the Roman formation and outflanked it on both sides. The _hastati_ formed up in the centre and the _principes_ and _triarii_ moved to each side to make a single, longer line. There was a prolonged pause while this was taking place. The Carthaginians took advantage of the hiatus to rally some of their first and second line troops, using them to extend the length of their own fighting line. This enabled Roman close-order infantry to match the length of the Carthaginian's third line, but correspondingly thinned their line, preventing them from using their habitual tactic of feeding new, less-fatigued men into the fighting line as a combat wore on.[\[161\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006306-168)[\[166\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaylor2019324%E2%80%93326-173) The surviving heavy infantry of each side were roughly equal in numbers. Most of the original Carthaginian were equipped in the same manner as the Romans they faced. They were veterans of many years' experience and they were fresh, having not yet fought. Many of the Romans were veterans, some having fought at Cannae and almost all having taken part in the two, or for some three, major victories the previous year. Many of the Romans were tired from the two immediately preceding fierce combats, but their victories in both would have boosted their morale.[\[167\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006306%E2%80%93307-174) Having satisfactorily reorganised, the two lines charged each other, according to Polybius "with the greatest fire and fury".[\[164\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999294-171) The fight continued for some time, neither side gaining the advantage.[\[168\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007125-175) Lazenby describes this fighting as "a grim business".[\[169\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998225-176) The cavalry commanded by Masinissa and Laelius then returned to the battlefield, apparently at more or less the same time.[\[170\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006307-177) Philip Sabin states that they arrived "in the nick of time".[\[171\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTESabin199667_n._52-178) Being fiercely engaged to their front, the Carthaginian infantry were helpless to prevent the Roman cavalry from charging into their rear. Their line collapsed and there was a great massacre.[\[170\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006307-177) Hannibal was one of the few Carthaginians to escape.[\[172\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999295-179) Polybius states that 20,000 Carthaginians were killed and as many again taken prisoner, which accounts for the entire Carthaginian army. He gives Roman losses as 1,500 killed. This is five per cent or more of their total force; Goldsworthy considers this fatality rate "a substantial loss for a victorious army, testimony to the hard fighting" and that the battle as a whole was "a slogging match". The number of wounded is not known, although the ancient sources refer to many wounded Roman soldiers being carried to the rear during the pause before the final engagement.[\[167\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006306%E2%80%93307-174)[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200476-60) At least 11 Carthaginian elephants survived the battle to be captured by the Romans.[\[168\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007125-175) Hannibal and his surviving companions reached the main Carthaginian base at Hadrumetum, where they mustered 6,000 infantry and 500 cavalry. Considering this too few with which to continue the war, Hannibal advised the Carthaginian Senate to make peace on whatever terms they could.[\[173\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTETaylor2019326%E2%80%93327-180) The Romans looted the Carthaginian camp and Scipio marched his legions back to Tunis. The Carthaginians again [sued for peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suing_for_peace "Suing for peace"). Given the difficulty of ending the war by storming or starving the city of Carthage, and his continuing fear that he might be superseded in command, Scipio entered into negotiations. During these Scipio received word that a Numidian army under Syphax's son [Vermina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vermina "Vermina") was marching to Carthage's assistance. This was intercepted and surrounded by a Roman force largely made up of cavalry and defeated. The number of Numidians involved is not known, but Livy records that more than 16,000 were killed or captured. This was the last battle of the Second Punic War.[\[174\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007131-181)[\[175\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999296%E2%80%93297-182) The peace treaty the Romans subsequently imposed on the Carthaginians stripped them of their overseas territories and some of their African ones. An indemnity of 10,000 silver [talents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talent_/(measurement/) "Talent (measurement)")[\[note 8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-184) was to be paid over 50 years, hostages were taken, Carthage was forbidden to possess war elephants and its fleet was restricted to 10 warships. It was prohibited from waging war outside Africa and in Africa only with Rome's express permission. Many senior Carthaginians wanted to reject it, but Hannibal spoke strongly in its favour and it was accepted in spring 201 BC. Henceforth it was clear Carthage was politically subordinate to Rome.[\[177\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007132-185)[\[178\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2015295-186) Scipio was awarded a [triumph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_triumph "Roman triumph") and received the _[agnomen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnomen "Agnomen")_ "Africanus".[\[179\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011318-187) Masinissa exploited the prohibition on Carthage waging war to repeatedly raid and seize Carthaginian territory with impunity. Carthage appealed to Rome, which always backed its Numidian ally.[\[180\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKunze2015398,_407-188) In 149 BC, fifty years after the end of the Second Punic War, Carthage sent an army, under [Hasdrubal the Boetharch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasdrubal_the_Boetharch "Hasdrubal the Boetharch"), against Masinissa,[\[note 9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-191) the treaty notwithstanding. The campaign ended in disaster at the [Battle of Oroscopa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Oroscopa "Battle of Oroscopa") and anti-Carthaginian factions in Rome used the illicit military action as a pretext to prepare a punitive expedition.[\[183\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKunze2015399,_407-192) The [Third Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War "Third Punic War") began later in 149 BC when a large Roman army landed in North Africa[\[184\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurcell1995134-193) and [besieged Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Carthage_/(Third_Punic_War/) "Siege of Carthage (Third Punic War)").[\[185\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006341-194) In the spring of 146 BC the Romans launched their final assault,[\[note 10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-196) systematically destroying the city and killing its inhabitants;[\[187\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015441-197) 50,000 survivors were sold into slavery.[\[188\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2002316-198) The formerly Carthaginian territories were annexed by Rome and reconstituted to become the [Roman province of Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa_Province "Africa Province"), with Utica as its capital.[\[189\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015443-199)[\[190\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2002310,_316-200) | Punic Wars | | --- | | [![Image 1: An animated display showing the territory controlled by Rome and Carthage at different times during the Punic Wars](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f9/Domain_changes_during_the_Punic_Wars_BC.gif/250px-Domain_changes_during_the_Punic_Wars_BC.gif)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Domain_changes_during_the_Punic_Wars_BC.gif) Territory controlled by Rome and Carthage at different times during the Punic WarsCarthaginian possessions Roman possessions | |

changes		Roman conquest of all Carthaginian territories (except Numidia)
| | Belligerents | | [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Republic "Roman Republic") | [Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Carthage "Ancient Carthage") | The **Punic Wars** were a series of wars fought between the [Roman Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Republic "Roman Republic") and the [Carthaginian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Carthage "Ancient Carthage") during the period 264 to 146 BC. Three such wars took place, involving a total of forty-three years of warfare on both land and sea across the [western Mediterranean](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Western_Mediterranean&action=edit&redlink=1 "Western Mediterranean (page does not exist)") region, and a four-year-long [revolt against Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercenary_War "Mercenary War"). The [First Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Punic_War "First Punic War") broke out on the Mediterranean island of [Sicily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicily "Sicily") in 264 BC as a result of Rome's expansionary attitude combined with Carthage's proprietary approach to the island. At the start of the war Carthage was the dominant power of the western Mediterranean, with an extensive maritime empire (a [thalassocracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thalassocracy "Thalassocracy")), while Rome was a rapidly expanding power in [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Italy "Roman Italy"), with a strong [army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_army_of_the_mid-Republic "Roman army of the mid-Republic") but no navy. The fighting took place primarily on Sicily and its surrounding waters, as well as in [North Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Africa "North Africa"), [Corsica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corsica "Corsica") and [Sardinia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sardinia "Sardinia"). It lasted twenty-three years, until 241 BC, when the Carthaginians were defeated. By the terms of the [peace treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Lutatius "Treaty of Lutatius") Carthage paid large [reparations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_reparations "War reparations") and Sicily was annexed as the [first Roman province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicilia_/(Roman_province/) "Sicilia (Roman province)"). The end of the war sparked a major but eventually unsuccessful revolt within Carthaginian territory known as the [Mercenary War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercenary_War "Mercenary War"). The [Second Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Punic_War "Second Punic War") began in 218 BC and witnessed the Carthaginian general [Hannibal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal "Hannibal")'s [crossing of the Alps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal%27s_crossing_of_the_Alps "Hannibal's crossing of the Alps") and invasion of mainland Italy. This expedition enjoyed considerable early success and campaigned in Italy for fourteen years before the survivors withdrew. There was also extensive fighting in [Iberia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberians "Iberians") (modern Spain and Portugal), Sicily, Sardinia and North Africa. The successful [Roman invasion of the Carthaginian homeland in Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_invasion_of_Africa_/(204%E2%80%93201_BC/) "Roman invasion of Africa (204–201 BC)") in 204 BC led to Hannibal's recall. He was defeated in the [battle of Zama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama "Battle of Zama") in 202 BC and Carthage [sued for peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suing_for_peace "Suing for peace"). A treaty was agreed in 201 BC which stripped Carthage of its overseas territories and some of its African ones, imposed a large indemnity, severely restricted the size of [its armed forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_of_Carthage "Military of Carthage") and prohibited Carthage from waging war without Rome's express permission. This caused Carthage to cease to be a military threat to Rome. In 151 BC Carthage attempted to defend itself against [Numidian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numidia "Numidia") encroachments; Rome used this as a justification to declare war in 149 BC, starting the [Third Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War "Third Punic War").
