This conflict was fought entirely on Carthaginian territory in what is now Tunisia and centred on the [siege of Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Carthage_/(Third_Punic_War/) "Siege of Carthage (Third Punic War)"). In 146 BC the Romans stormed the city of [Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthage "Carthage"), [sacked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Looting "Looting") it, slaughtered or enslaved its population and completely demolished the city. The Carthaginian territories were taken over as the [Roman province of Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa_/(Roman_province/) "Africa (Roman province)"). The ruins of the city lie east of modern [Tunis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunis "Tunis") on the North African coast. Primary sources --------------- [![Image 2: A monochrome relief stele depicting a man in classical Greek clothing raising one arm](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/Stele_des_Polybios.jpg/250px-Stele_des_Polybios.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Stele_des_Polybios.jpg) Polybius[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMelfi2017192-1) The most reliable source for the Punic Wars[\[note 1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-3) is the historian [Polybius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polybius "Polybius") (c. 200 – c. 118 BC), a Greek sent to Rome in 167 BC as a hostage.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200620%E2%80%9321-4) He is best known for [_The Histories_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Histories_/(Polybius/) "The Histories (Polybius)"), written sometime after 146 BC.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200620%E2%80%9321-4)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWalbank199011%E2%80%9312-5) Polybius was an [analytical historian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historian#History_analysis "Historian") and wherever possible interviewed participants from both sides in the events he wrote about.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200620%E2%80%9321-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShutt193855-6)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChampion201598,_101-7) He accompanied his [patron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patronage_in_ancient_Rome "Patronage in ancient Rome") and friend,[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAstin20065-8) the Roman general [Scipio Aemilianus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scipio_Aemilianus "Scipio Aemilianus"), in North Africa during the Third Punic War;[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChampion201596,_108-9) modern historians consider Polybius to have treated Scipio and his relatives unduly favourably, but the consensus is to accept his account largely at face value.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200620%E2%80%9321-4)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996x%E2%80%93xi,_82%E2%80%9384-10) [Craige Champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Craige_B._Champion "Craige B. Champion") describes him as "a remarkably well-informed, industrious and insightful historian",[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChampion2015102-11) while the classicist [Adrian Goldsworthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrian_Goldsworthy "Adrian Goldsworthy") states that "Polybius' account is usually to be preferred when it differs with any of our other accounts".[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200621-12) Polybius's work is considered broadly objective in spite of his pro-Roman point of view.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996x%E2%80%93xi-13)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles201116-14)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHau201623%E2%80%9324-15) The details of the wars in modern sources are largely based on interpretations of Polybius's account.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200620%E2%80%9321-4)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996x%E2%80%93xi,_82%E2%80%9384-10)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTETipps1985432-16) The other major source commonly used by modern historians, particularly where Polybius's account is not extant, is the Roman historian [Livy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Livy "Livy"). Livy relied heavily on Polybius, but wrote in a more structured way, with more details about Roman politics, as well as being openly pro-Roman.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby199887-17)[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200622-18)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChampion201595-19)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBriscoeHornblower20208%E2%80%9313-20) His accounts of military encounters are often demonstrably inaccurate; the classicist [Adrian Goldsworthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrian_Goldsworthy "Adrian Goldsworthy") says Livy's "reliability is often suspect",[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006222-21) and the historian [Philip Sabin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Sabin "Philip Sabin") refers to Livy's "military ignorance".[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTESabin199662-22) Other, later ancient histories of the wars also exist, often in fragmentary or summary form.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200621%E2%80%9323-23) Modern historians usually take into account the writings of various Roman [annalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annalists "Annalists"), some contemporary; the [Sicilian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicily "Sicily") Greek [Diodorus Siculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diodorus_Siculus "Diodorus Siculus"); and later writers such as[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChampion201595-19) [Plutarch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plutarch "Plutarch"), [Appian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appian "Appian"), and [Dio Cassius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassius_Dio "Cassius Dio").[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMineo2015111%E2%80%93127-24)[\[note 2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-25) No primary sources written from a Carthaginian point of view have survived,[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles20117-26) although elements of some – such as [Philinus of Agrigentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philinus_of_Agrigentum "Philinus of Agrigentum") – can be found in the works of some of the pro-Roman writers, especially Polybius.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChampion201599-27) Other sources include coins, inscriptions, archaeological evidence and empirical evidence from reconstructions, such as the [trireme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trireme "Trireme") [_Olympias_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympias_/(trireme/) "Olympias (trireme)").[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200623,_98-28) Background and origin --------------------- [![Image 3: a colour of the western Mediterranean region showing the areas under Roman and Carthaginian control in 264 BC](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/First_Punic_War_264_BC_v3.png/500px-First_Punic_War_264_BC_v3.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:First_Punic_War_264_BC_v3.png) The map shows the approximate extent of territory controlled by Rome, Carthage and Syracuse immediately before the start of the First Punic War. Rome is shown in red, Carthage in grey, and Syracuse in green. The [Roman Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Republic "Roman Republic") had been [aggressively expanding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_expansion_in_Italy "Roman expansion in Italy") in the southern Italian mainland for a century before the [First Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Punic_War "First Punic War").[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011157%E2%80%93158-29) By 270 BC, when the last Greek cities of southern Italy ([Magna Graecia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magna_Graecia "Magna Graecia")) submitted after the conclusion of the [Pyrrhic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrrhic_War "Pyrrhic War"), it had conquered all of peninsular Italy south of the [Arno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arno "Arno") River.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199921%E2%80%9322-30) During this period of Roman expansion Carthage, with its capital in what is now [Tunisia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunisia "Tunisia"), had come to dominate southern [Iberia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberians "Iberians") (modern Spain and Portugal), much of the coastal regions of North Africa, the [Balearic Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balearic_Islands "Balearic Islands"), [Corsica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corsica "Corsica"), [Sardinia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sardinia "Sardinia") and the western half of Sicily in a maritime empire (a [thalassocracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thalassocracy "Thalassocracy")).[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200629%E2%80%9330-31) Beginning in 480 BC Carthage fought a [series of inconclusive wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicilian_Wars "Sicilian Wars") against the Greek [city-states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City-state "City-state") of Sicily, led by [Syracuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syracuse,_Sicily "Syracuse, Sicily").[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011115,_132-32) By 264 BC Carthage was in control of much of the island, especially in the south and the west. Carthage and Rome were the preeminent powers in the western Mediterranean.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200625%E2%80%9327-33) Relations were good and the two states had several times declared their mutual friendship in [formal alliances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaties_between_Rome_and_Carthage "Treaties between Rome and Carthage"): in 509 BC, 348 BC and around 279 BC. There were strong commercial links. During the Pyrrhic War of 280–275 BC, against a king of [Epirus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epirus "Epirus") who alternately fought Rome in Italy and Carthage on Sicily, Carthage provided [materiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Materiel "Materiel") to the Romans and on at least one occasion provided its navy to ferry a Roman force.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles201194,_160,_163,_164%E2%80%93165-34)[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200669%E2%80%9370-35) As Rome and Carthage came closer to sharing a joint border the chances of misunderstandings and hostilities increased. In the event they stumbled into war more by accident than design, with neither anticipating a prolonged conflict.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011175%E2%80%93176-36)[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2015c145%E2%80%93147-37)[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200671%E2%80%9372-38) Opposing forces --------------- ### Armies [![Image 4: A monochrome relief stele depicting two figures dressed as Roman legionaries](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/Altar_Domitius_Ahenobarbus_Louvre_n3_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Altar_Domitius_Ahenobarbus_Louvre_n3_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Altar_Domitius_Ahenobarbus_Louvre_n3_/(cropped/).jpg) Detail from the second century BC [Ahenobarbus relief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altar_of_Domitius_Ahenobarbus "Altar of Domitius Ahenobarbus") showing two Roman foot-soldiers Male Roman citizens who met a property requirement were liable for military service. Most were eligible and would serve as infantry, with a [better-off minority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equites "Equites") providing a cavalry component.[\[note 3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-40) Traditionally, when at war the Romans would raise two [legions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_legion "Roman legion"), each of 4,200 infantry[\[note 4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-43) and 300 cavalry. Approximately 1,200 members of the infantry – poorer or younger men unable to afford the armour and equipment of a standard [legionary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legionary "Legionary") – served as [javelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Javelin "Javelin")\-armed [skirmishers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skirmisher "Skirmisher") known as [velites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Velites "Velites"); they each carried several javelins, which would be thrown from a distance, as well as a short sword and a large circular shield.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200648-44) The rest of the soldiers were equipped as [heavy infantry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heavy_infantry "Heavy infantry"), with [body armour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body_armor "Body armor"), a large [shield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scutum_/(shield/) "Scutum (shield)") and [short thrusting swords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gladius "Gladius"). They were divided into three ranks: the [front rank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hastati "Hastati") also carried two javelins, while the [second](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principes "Principes") and [third](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triari "Triari") ranks had a [thrusting spear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasta_/(spear/) "Hasta (spear)") instead. Both legionary [sub-units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maniple_/(military_unit/) "Maniple (military unit)") and individual legionaries fought in relatively open order. It was the long-standing Roman procedure to elect two men each year as senior [magistrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_magistrate "Roman magistrate"), known as [consuls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_consul "Roman consul"), who in a time of war would each lead an army. An army was usually formed by combining a Roman legion with a similarly sized and equipped legion provided by their [Italian allies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socii "Socii"); allied legions usually had a larger attached complement of cavalry than Roman ones.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199922%E2%80%9325-45)[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200650-46)[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200141-47) Carthaginian citizens only served in their army if there was a direct threat to the city of [Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthage "Carthage").[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby19989-48)[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2006494-49) When they did they fought as well-armoured heavy infantry armed with long thrusting spears, although they were notoriously ill-trained and ill-disciplined. In most circumstances Carthage recruited foreigners to make up its army.[\[note 5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-51) Many were from North Africa and these are usually referred to as Libyans. The region provided several types of fighters, including: [close-order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Close_order_formation "Close order formation") infantry equipped with large shields, helmets, short swords and long thrusting [spears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spear "Spear"); javelin-armed [light-infantry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light-infantry "Light-infantry") skirmishers; close-order [shock cavalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shock_cavalry "Shock cavalry")[\[note 6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-53) (also known as heavy cavalry) carrying spears; and [light cavalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_cavalry "Light cavalry"), skirmishers who threw javelins from a distance and avoided close combat; the latter were usually [Numidians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numidians "Numidians").[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200631%E2%80%9334-54)[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKoon201579%E2%80%9387-55) The close-order African infantry and the citizen-militia both fought in a tightly-packed formation known as a [phalanx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phalanx "Phalanx").[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKoon201593-56) On occasion some of the infantry would wear captured Roman armour, especially among the troops of the Carthaginian general [Hannibal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal "Hannibal").[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTERawlings2015305-57) In addition both [Iberia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iberians "Iberians") and [Gaul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaul "Gaul") provided many experienced infantry and cavalry. The infantry from these areas were unarmoured troops who would charge ferociously, but had a reputation for breaking off if a combat was protracted.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200632%E2%80%9334-58)[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall19999-59) The Gallic cavalry, and possibly some of the Iberians, wore armour and fought as close-order troops; most or all of the mounted Iberians were light cavalry.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey200713-60) [Slingers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balearic_slinger "Balearic slinger") were frequently recruited from the Balearic Islands.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200632-61)[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall19998-62) The Carthaginians also employed [war elephants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_elephant "War elephant"); North Africa had indigenous [African forest elephants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_forest_elephant "African forest elephant") at the time.[\[note 7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-64)[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall19999-59)[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby199627-65) Garrison duty, [foraging](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Forage_\(militaty\)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Forage (militaty) (page does not exist)") and land [blockades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blockade "Blockade") were the most common operations.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200682,_311,_313%E2%80%93314-66)[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999237-67) When armies were campaigning, surprise attacks, [ambushes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambush "Ambush") and [stratagems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruse_de_guerre "Ruse de guerre") were common.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKoon201593-56)[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200655-68) Armies of the time consumed large amounts of resources, in particular food.[\[note 8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-70) This could be supplied from stockpiles, either continuously taken to an army by pack animals or by army marching to its supply base at frequent intervals. Stockpiling the necessary quantities posed its own problems given the limited means of transportation of the time. Moving such bulk cargos was easier and swifter by sea, and was much preferred. The alternative, especially favoured in enemy territory, was to gather in what resources were locally available, which is known as foraging. If enemy forces were near this needed to be carried out in a controlled way, to prevent presenting easy opportunities for them to attack. Cavalry superiority made it much easier to protect ones own foragers or harass the enemy's. A large force relying on foraging would need to move frequently as they stripped the local countryside bare.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEErdkamp201569%E2%80%9370-71) [Formal battles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitched_battle "Pitched battle") were usually preceded by the two armies camping two–twelve kilometres (1–7 miles) apart for days or weeks; sometimes both forming up in battle order each day. If either commander felt at a disadvantage, he might march off without engaging; in such circumstances it was difficult to force a battle.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200656-72)[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTESabin199664-73) Forming up in battle order was a complicated and premeditated affair, which took several hours. Infantry were usually positioned in the centre of the battle line, with light-infantry skirmishers to their front and cavalry on each flank.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200657-74) Many battles were decided when one side's infantry force was [attacked in the flank or rear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flanking_maneuver "Flanking maneuver") and it was partially or wholly [enveloped](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Envelopment "Envelopment").[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKoon201593-56)[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTESabin199666-75) ### Navies [![Image 5: A diagram showing the location and usage of a corvus on a Roman galley.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/Corvus.svg/250px-Corvus.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Corvus.svg) [Quinqueremes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quinqueremes "Quinqueremes") were large and powerful-for-their-time warships[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200698-76) which provided the main components of the Roman and Carthaginian fleets throughout the Punic Wars.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby199627%E2%80%9328-77) So ubiquitous was the type that Polybius uses it as a shorthand for "warship" in general.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006104-78) A quinquereme carried a crew of 300: 280 oarsmen and 20 deck crew and officers.[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006100-79) It would also normally carry a complement of 40 marines;[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTETipps1985435-80) if battle was thought to be imminent this would be increased to as many as 120.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson1995121-81)[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006102%E2%80%93103-82) In 260 BC the Romans set out to construct a [fleet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_navy "Roman navy") and used a shipwrecked Carthaginian quinquereme as a blueprint for their own.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200697,_99%E2%80%93100-83)[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTETipps1985436_n._6-84) The Romans and their allies were unaccustomed to building quinqueremes and their early efforts were heavier than the Carthaginian vessels; thus they were slower and less manoeuvrable.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMurray201169-85) Getting the oarsmen to row as a unit, let alone to execute more complex battle manoeuvres, required long and arduous training.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson1995278%E2%80%93280-86)[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEde_Souza2008359-87) As a result, the Romans were initially at a disadvantage against the more experienced Carthaginians. To counter this, the Romans introduced the [corvus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corvus_/(weapon/) "Corvus (weapon)"), a bridge 1.2 metres (4 feet) wide and 11 metres (36 feet) long, with a heavy spike on the underside, designed to pierce and anchor into an enemy ship's deck.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTECasson1995121-81) This allowed Roman legionaries acting as marines to [board enemy ships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_boarding "Naval boarding") and capture them, rather than employing the previously [more common tactic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_tactics_in_the_Age_of_Galleys "Naval tactics in the Age of Galleys") of [ramming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramming "Ramming").[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011178-88) All warships were equipped with rams, a triple set of 60-centimetre-wide (2 ft) bronze blades weighing up to 270 kilograms (600 lb) positioned at the waterline. In the century prior to the Punic Wars, boarding had become increasingly common and ramming had declined, as the [larger and heavier vessels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellenistic-era_warships "Hellenistic-era warships") adopted in this period increasingly lacked the speed and manoeuvrability necessary to ram effectively, while their sturdier construction reduced a ram's effect on them even in case of a successful attack. The Roman adaptation of the corvus was a continuation of this trend and compensated for their initial disadvantage in ship-manoeuvring skills. The added weight in the prow compromised both the ship's manoeuvrability and its seaworthiness, and in rough sea conditions the corvus became useless; part way through the First Punic War the Romans ceased using it.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011178-88)[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWallinga195677%E2%80%9390-89)[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006100%E2%80%93101,_103-90) First Punic War, 264–241 BC --------------------------- ### Course Much of the First Punic War was fought on or in the waters near Sicily.[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006310-91) Away from the coasts its hilly and rugged terrain made manoeuvring large forces difficult, which encouraged defensive strategies. Land operations were largely confined to [raids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raid_/(military/) "Raid (military)"), [sieges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege "Siege") and [interdiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interdiction "Interdiction"); in twenty-three years of war on Sicily there were only two full-scale pitched battles.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200682-92) #### Sicily, 264–257 BC [![Image 6: A relief map of Sicily showing the main cities at the time of the First Punic War](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1f/Sicilia_-_prima_guerra_punica_key_en.svg/500px-Sicilia_-_prima_guerra_punica_key_en.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sicilia_-_prima_guerra_punica_key_en.svg) Sicily, the main theatre of the First Punic War The spark that ignited the First Punic War in 264 BC was the issue of control of the independent Sicilian city-state of Messana (modern Messina),[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200674%E2%80%9375-93)[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWarmington1993168-94) with the Romans gaining control of the city and a foothold on Sicily at the [battle of Messana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Messana "Battle of Messana").[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199952%E2%80%9353-95) They then pressed Syracuse, the only substantial independent power on the island, into allying with them[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAmeling201556-96)[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarcel%C3%B32015368-97) and laid siege to Carthage's main base, Agrigentum (modern [Agrigento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agrigento "Agrigento")) on the south coast.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011179-98) A Carthaginian army of 50,000 infantry, 6,000 cavalry and 60 elephants attempted to lift the siege in 262 BC, but was badly defeated at the [battle of Agrigentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Agrigentum "Battle of Agrigentum"). The Carthaginian garrison escaped during the night after the battle and the Romans seized the city and its inhabitants, selling 25,000 of them [into slavery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_ancient_Rome "Slavery in ancient Rome").[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011179%E2%80%93180-99) After this the land war on Sicily reached a stalemate as the Carthaginians focused on defending their well-fortified towns and cities; these were mostly on the coast and so could be supplied and reinforced without the Romans being able to use their superior army to interfere.[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199964%E2%80%9366-100)[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200697-101) The focus of the war shifted to the sea, where the Romans had less experience. On the few occasions they had previously felt the need for a naval presence greater than anti-piracy squadrons they had relied on their Latin or Greek allies for larger warships.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011179-98)[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199966-102)[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200691%E2%80%9392,_97-103) But the Romans did have extensive commercial maritime experience and access to a large pool of experienced sailors and [shipwrights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shipwright "Shipwright") enabling them to rapidly build a navy to challenge Carthage's,[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarris201724%E2%80%9326-104)[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPotter201464%E2%80%9365-105)[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011180%E2%80%93181-106) Using this navy and the corvus the Romans won a major victory at the [battle of Mylae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mylae "Battle of Mylae") in 260 BC.[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006109%E2%80%93110-107)[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199965-108)[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby199673%E2%80%9374-109) A Carthaginian base on Corsica was seized, but an attack on Sardinia was repulsed; the base on Corsica was then lost.[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199963%E2%80%9365-110) In 258 BC a Roman fleet defeated a smaller Carthaginian fleet at the [battle of Sulci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Sulci "Battle of Sulci") off the western coast of Sardinia.[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199965-108) #### Africa, 256–255 BC Taking advantage of their naval victories the Romans launched an invasion of North Africa in 256 BC,[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTERankov2015155-111) which the Carthaginians intercepted at the [battle of Cape Ecnomus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cape_Ecnomus "Battle of Cape Ecnomus") off the southern coast of Sicily. The Carthaginians' superior seamanship was not as effective as they had hoped, while the Romans' corvuses gave them an edge as the battle degenerated into a shapeless brawl.[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006102%E2%80%93103-82)[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTETipps1985435,_459-112) The Carthaginians were again beaten[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTERankov2015155%E2%80%93156-113) in what was possibly the [largest naval battle in history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Largest_naval_battle_in_history "Largest naval battle in history") by the number of combatants involved.[\[note 9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-117)[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006110%E2%80%93111-114)[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby199687-115)[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTETipps1985436-116) The invasion initially went well and in 255 BC the Carthaginians [sued for peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suing_for_peace "Suing for peace"); the proposed terms were so harsh they decided to fight on.[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200687-118) At the [battle of Tunis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Bagradas_River_/(255_BC/) "Battle of the Bagradas River (255 BC)") in spring 255 BC a combined force of infantry, cavalry and war elephants under the command of the [Spartan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sparta "Sparta") mercenary [Xanthippus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xanthippus_of_Carthage "Xanthippus of Carthage") crushed the Romans.[\[110\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011188-119) The Romans sent a fleet to evacuate their survivors and the Carthaginians opposed it at the [battle of Cape Hermaeum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cape_Hermaeum "Battle of Cape Hermaeum") (modern [Cape Bon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Bon "Cape Bon")); the Carthaginians were again heavily defeated.[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTETipps2003382-120) The Roman fleet, in turn, [was devastated by a storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sinking_of_the_Roman_fleet_/(255_BC/) "Sinking of the Roman fleet (255 BC)") while returning to Italy, losing most of its ships and more than 100,000 men.[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTETipps1985438-121)[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011189-122)[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEErdkamp201566-123) It is possible that the presence of the corvus, making the Roman ships unusually [unseaworthy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unseaworthy "Unseaworthy"), contributed to this disaster; there is no record of their being used again.[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2006557-124)[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996112,_117-125) #### Sicily, 255–241 BC [![Image 7: A small, white statuette of an elephant with a mahout](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ee/Pompeii%2C_Statuette_of_a_war_elephant.jpg/250px-Pompeii%2C_Statuette_of_a_war_elephant.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pompeii,_Statuette_of_a_war_elephant.jpg) The war continued, with neither side able to gain a decisive advantage.[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2006559-127) The Carthaginians attacked and recaptured Akragas in 255 BC, but not believing they could hold the city they razed and abandoned it.[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996114%E2%80%93116,_169-128)[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTERankov2015158-129) The Romans rapidly rebuilt their fleet, adding 220 new ships, and captured Panormus (modern [Palermo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palermo "Palermo")) in 254 BC.[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199980-130) The next year they lost another 150 ships to a storm.[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011189%E2%80%93190-131) On Sicily the Romans avoided battle in 252 and 251 BC, according to Polybius because they feared the war elephants which the Carthaginians had shipped to the island.[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996118-132)[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTERankov2015159-133) In 250 BC the Carthaginians advanced on Panormus, but in a [battle outside the walls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Panormus "Battle of Panormus") the Romans drove off the Carthaginian elephants with javelins. The elephants routed through the Carthaginian infantry, who were then charged by the Roman infantry to complete their defeat.[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTERankov2015159-133)[\[125\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996169-134) Slowly the Romans had occupied most of Sicily; in 250 BC they besieged the last two Carthaginian strongholds – [Lilybaeum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lilybaeum "Lilybaeum") and [Drepana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drepana "Drepana") in the extreme west.[\[126\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011190-135) Repeated attempts to storm Lilybaeum's strong walls failed, as did attempts to block access to its harbour, and the Romans [settled down to a siege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Lilybaeum_/(250%E2%80%93241_BC/) "Siege of Lilybaeum (250–241 BC)") which was to last nine years.[\[127\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996127-136)[\[128\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199984%E2%80%9386-137) They launched a surprise attack on the Carthaginian fleet, but were defeated at the [battle of Drepana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Drepana "Battle of Drepana"); Carthage's greatest naval victory of the war.[\[129\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006117%E2%80%93121-138) Carthage turned to the maritime offensive, inflicting another heavy naval defeat at the [battle of Phintias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Phintias "Battle of Phintias") and all but swept the Romans from the sea.[\[130\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199988%E2%80%9391-139) It was to be seven years before Rome again attempted to field a substantial fleet, while Carthage put most of its ships into [reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reserve_fleet "Reserve fleet") to save money and free up manpower.[\[131\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006121%E2%80%93122-140)[\[132\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTERankov2015163-141) #### Roman victory, 243–241 BC After more than 20 years of war, both states were financially and demographically exhausted.[\[133\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBringmann2007127-142) Evidence of Carthage's financial situation includes their request for a 2,000-talent loan[\[note 10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-145) from [Ptolemaic Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ptolemaic_Egypt "Ptolemaic Egypt"), which was refused.[\[136\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199992-146)[\[137\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011193-147) Rome was also close to [bankruptcy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign_default "Sovereign default") and the number of adult male citizens, who provided the manpower for the navy and the legions, had declined by 17 per cent since the start of the war.[\[138\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199991-148) Goldsworthy describes Roman manpower losses as "appalling".[\[139\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006131-149) The Romans rebuilt their fleet again in 243 BC after the Senate approached Rome's wealthiest citizens for loans to finance the construction of one ship each, repayable from the [reparations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_reparations "War reparations") to be imposed on Carthage once the war was won.[\[140\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby199649-150) This new fleet effectively blockaded the Carthaginian garrisons.[\[135\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2006565-144) Carthage assembled a fleet which attempted to relieve them, but it was destroyed at the [battle of the Aegates Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Aegates_Islands "Battle of the Aegates Islands") in 241 BC,[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011196-151)[\[142\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199996-152) forcing the cut-off Carthaginian troops on Sicily to negotiate for peace.[\[135\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2006565-144)[\[143\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996157-153) The [Treaty of Lutatius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Lutatius "Treaty of Lutatius") was agreed by which Carthage paid 3,200 talents of silver[\[note 11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-154) in reparations and [Sicily was annexed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicilia_/(Roman_province/) "Sicilia (Roman province)") as the first [Roman province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_province "Roman province").[\[141\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011196-151) Polybius regarded the war as "the longest, most continuous and most severely contested war known to us in history".[\[144\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2002178-155) Henceforth Rome considered itself the leading military power in the western Mediterranean and increasingly the Mediterranean region as a whole.[\[145\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006128%E2%80%93129,_357,_359%E2%80%93360-156) Interbellum, 241–218 BC ----------------------- ### Mercenary War [![Image 8: A map of the western Mediterranean showing the territory ceded to Rome by Carthage under the treaty.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e8/First_Punic_War_237_BC.jpg/500px-First_Punic_War_237_BC.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:First_Punic_War_237_BC.jpg) Territory ceded to Rome by Carthage under the treaty is shown in pink The [Mercenary, or Truceless, War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercenary_War "Mercenary War") began in 241 BC as a dispute over the payment of wages owed to 20,000 foreign soldiers who had fought for Carthage on Sicily during the First Punic War. This erupted into full-scale mutiny under the leadership of [Spendius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spendius "Spendius") and [Matho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mathos "Mathos"); 70,000 Africans from Carthage's oppressed dependent territories and towns flocked to join the mutineers, bringing supplies and finance.[\[146\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999112%E2%80%93114-157)[\[147\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006133%E2%80%93134-158) Rome initially declined to take advantage of Carthage's troubles. Italians were prohibited from trading with the rebels[\[148\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006135%E2%80%93136-159)[\[149\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996173-160) and [Hiero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiero_II_of_Syracuse "Hiero II of Syracuse"), the king of the Roman satellite kingdom of [Syracuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syracuse,_Sicily "Syracuse, Sicily"), was allowed to supply Carthage with the large amounts of food it needed and was no longer able to obtain from its hinterland.[\[149\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996173-160)[\[150\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2006568-161) War-weary Carthage fared poorly in the initial engagements, especially under the generalship of [Hanno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanno_II_the_Great "Hanno II the Great").[\[151\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEckstein20176-162)[\[152\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999115-163) [Hamilcar Barca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamilcar_Barca "Hamilcar Barca"), a veteran of the campaigns in Sicily, was given joint command of the army in 240 BC and supreme command in 239 BC.[\[152\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999115-163) He campaigned successfully, initially demonstrating leniency in an attempt to woo the rebels over.[\[153\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999118-164) To prevent this, in 240 BC Spendius tortured 700 Carthaginian prisoners to death and henceforth the war was pursued with great brutality.[\[154\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011208-165)[\[155\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEckstein20177-166) By early 237 BC, after numerous setbacks, the rebels were defeated and their towns brought back under Carthaginian rule.[\[156\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2000377-167) An expedition was prepared to reoccupy Sardinia, where mutinous soldiers had slaughtered all Carthaginians. The Roman Senate stated they considered the preparation of this force an act of war and demanded Carthage cede Sardinia and Corsica and pay an additional 1,200-talent indemnity.[\[note 12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-168)[\[157\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2006569-169)[\[158\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011209,_212%E2%80%93213-170) Weakened by 30 years of war, Carthage agreed rather than again enter into conflict with Rome.[\[159\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996175-171) Polybius considered this "contrary to all justice" and modern historians have variously described the Romans' behaviour as "unprovoked aggression and treaty-breaking",[\[157\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2006569-169) "shamelessly opportunistic"[\[160\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006136-172) and an "unscrupulous act".[\[161\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999124-173) These events fuelled resentment of Rome in Carthage, which was not reconciled to Rome's perception of its situation. This breach of the recently signed treaty was to be one the greatest causes of war with Carthage breaking out again in 218 BC in the [Second Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Punic_War "Second Punic War").[\[162\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTECollins199813-174)[\[163\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2015211-175)[\[164\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011213-176) ### Carthaginian expansion in Iberia [![Image 9: Image of both sides of a coin: one depicting a man's head; the other an elephant](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Carthage%2C_quarter_shekel%2C_237-209_BC%2C_SNG_BM_Spain_102.jpg/250px-Carthage%2C_quarter_shekel%2C_237-209_BC%2C_SNG_BM_Spain_102.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Carthage,_quarter_shekel,_237-209_BC,_SNG_BM_Spain_102.jpg) With the suppression of the rebellion, Hamilcar understood that Carthage needed to strengthen its economic and military base if it were to again confront Rome.[\[166\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos201577-178) After the First Punic War, Carthaginian possessions in Iberia were limited to a handful of prosperous coastal cities in the south.[\[167\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos201580-179) Hamilcar took the army which he had led in the Mercenary War to Iberia in 237 BC and carved out a [quasi-monarchicial, autonomous state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthaginian_Iberia "Carthaginian Iberia") in its south east.[\[168\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011220-180) This gave Carthage the silver mines, agricultural wealth, [manpower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manpower "Manpower"), military facilities such as [shipyards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shipyard "Shipyard") and territorial depth to stand up to future Roman demands with confidence.[\[169\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011219%E2%80%93220,_225-181)[\[170\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEckstein2006173%E2%80%93174-182) Hamilcar ruled as a [viceroy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viceroy "Viceroy") and was succeeded by his son-in-law, [Hasdrubal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasdrubal_the_Fair "Hasdrubal the Fair"), in the early 220s BC and then his son, [Hannibal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal "Hannibal"), in 221 BC.[\[171\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011222,_225-183) In 226 BC the [Ebro Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ebro_Treaty "Ebro Treaty") was agreed with Rome, specifying the [Ebro River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ebro_River "Ebro River") as the northern boundary of the Carthaginian [sphere of influence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sphere_of_influence "Sphere of influence").[\[172\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006143%E2%80%93144-184) At some time during the next six years Rome made a separate agreement with the city of [Saguntum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saguntum "Saguntum"), which was situated well south of the Ebro.[\[173\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006144-185) Second Punic War, 218–201 BC ---------------------------- In 219 BC a Carthaginian army under Hannibal [besieged, captured and sacked Saguntum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Saguntum "Siege of Saguntum")[\[note 13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-186)[\[162\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTECollins199813-174)[\[174\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006144%E2%80%93145-187) and in spring 218 BC Rome [declared war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declaration_of_war "Declaration of war") on Carthage.[\[175\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006145-188) There is scholarly debate as to whether Hannibal deliberately provoked the Romans with this attack or if the Romans were not concerned with any perceived impact on their amour propre as much as using the episode as a pretext to militarily curb Carthaginian expansion.[\[176\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011234-189) There were three main [military theatres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theater_/(military/) "Theater (military)") in the [Second Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Punic_War "Second Punic War"): Italy, where Hannibal defeated the Roman legions repeatedly, with occasional subsidiary campaigns in Sicily, Sardinia and Greece; Iberia, where [Hasdrubal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasdrubal_/(Barcid/) "Hasdrubal (Barcid)"), a younger brother of Hannibal, defended the Carthaginian colonial cities with mixed success before moving into Italy; and Africa, where the war was decided.[\[177\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006310%E2%80%93311-190) ### Italy #### Hannibal crosses the Alps, 218–217 BC [![Image 10: a map of the western Mediterranean region showing the territory and allies of Rome and Carthage in 218 BC](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/62/Map_of_Rome_and_Carthage_at_the_start_of_the_Second_Punic_War_Modified.svg/500px-Map_of_Rome_and_Carthage_at_the_start_of_the_Second_Punic_War_Modified.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Map_of_Rome_and_Carthage_at_the_start_of_the_Second_Punic_War_Modified.svg) The territory and allies of Rome and Carthage immediately before the start of the Second Punic War. In 218 BC there was some naval skirmishing in the waters around Sicily; the Romans [defeated a Carthaginian attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lilybaeum "Battle of Lilybaeum")[\[178\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBriscoe200661-191)[\[179\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015327-192) and [captured the island of Malta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capture_of_Malta_/(218_BC/) "Capture of Malta (218 BC)").[\[180\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTECastillo200625-193) In [Cisalpine Gaul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cisalpine_Gaul "Cisalpine Gaul") (modern northern Italy), the major [Gallic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauls "Gauls") tribes attacked the Roman colonies there, causing the Roman settlers to flee to their previously established colony of Mutina (modern [Modena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modena "Modena")), where they were besieged. A Roman relief force broke through the siege, but was then ambushed and itself besieged.[\[181\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006151-194) A Roman army had been assembled to campaign in Iberia; one Roman and one allied legion was detached from it and sent to northern Italy. Raising fresh troops to replace these delayed the army's departure for Iberia until September.[\[182\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006151%E2%80%93152-195) Meanwhile, Hannibal assembled a Carthaginian army in New Carthage (modern [Cartagena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartagena,_Spain "Cartagena, Spain")) in Iberia and led it northwards along the coast in May or June. It entered Gaul and took an inland route, to avoid the Roman allies to the south.[\[183\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBriscoe200647-196) At the [battle of the Rhône crossing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Rh%C3%B4ne_Crossing "Battle of the Rhône Crossing") Hannibal defeated a force of local Gauls which sought to bar his way.[\[184\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999161%E2%80%93162-197) A Roman fleet carrying the Iberian-bound army landed at Rome's ally Massalia (modern [Marseille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marseille "Marseille")) at the mouth of the Rhône,[\[185\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFronda2011252-198) but Hannibal evaded the Romans and they continued to Iberia.[\[186\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2011291-199)[\[187\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015321-200) The Carthaginians reached the foot of the Alps by late autumn and [crossed them](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal%27s_crossing_of_the_Alps "Hannibal's crossing of the Alps") in 24 days, surmounting the difficulties of climate, terrain[\[188\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEErdkamp201572-201) and the [guerrilla tactics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guerrilla_warfare "Guerrilla warfare") of the native tribes. The Carthaginians arrived in what is now [Piedmont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piedmont "Piedmont"), northern Italy, in early November. They comprised 20,000 infantry, 6,000 cavalry and an unknown number of elephants – the survivors of the 37 with which they left Iberia. The Romans were still in their winter quarters. The Carthaginians' surprise entry into the Italian peninsula led to the cancellation of Rome's planned campaign for the following year: an invasion of Africa.[\[189\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2011283%E2%80%93284-202)[\[190\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEErdkamp201571-203)[\[191\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2015b107-204) #### Roman defeats, 217–216 BC [![Image 11: a photograph of a marble head depicting Hannibal](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/Hannibal_Slodtz_Louvre_MR2093_%28cropped2%29.png/250px-Hannibal_Slodtz_Louvre_MR2093_%28cropped2%29.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hannibal_Slodtz_Louvre_MR2093_/(cropped2/).png) Hannibal, as envisaged in 1704 The Carthaginians captured the chief settlement of the hostile [Taurini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taurini "Taurini") Gauls (in the area of modern [Turin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turin "Turin")) and seized its food stocks.[\[192\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999171-205)[\[193\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006168-206) In late November the Carthaginian cavalry routed a Roman force of cavalry and light infantry at the [battle of Ticinus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Ticinus "Battle of Ticinus").[\[194\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFronda2011243-207) As a result, most of the Gallic tribes declared for the Carthaginian cause and Hannibal's army grew to 37,000 men.[\[195\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006177%E2%80%93178-208) A large Roman army was lured into combat by Hannibal at the [battle of the Trebia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Trebia "Battle of the Trebia"), encircled and destroyed.[\[196\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFronda2011243%E2%80%93244-209)[\[197\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999175%E2%80%93176-210) Some 10,000 Romans out of 42,000 were able to fight their way to safety; most of their comrades were killed or captured. Gauls now joined Hannibal's army in large numbers.[\[198\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999175%E2%80%93176,_193-211)[\[199\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011270-212) The Romans stationed an army at [Arretium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arretium "Arretium") and one on the [Adriatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adriatic "Adriatic") coast to block Hannibal's advance into central Italy.[\[200\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2011285-213)[\[201\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006182-214) In early spring 217 BC the Carthaginians crossed the [Apennines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apennine_Mountains "Apennine Mountains") unopposed, taking a difficult but unguarded route.[\[202\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006184-215) Hannibal attempted to draw the westernmost of the two Roman armies into a pitched battle by devastating the area it had been sent to protect.[\[203\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFronda2011244-216) This provoked its commander into ordering a hasty pursuit without proper reconnaissance. Hannibal set an ambush and in the [battle of Lake Trasimene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lake_Trasimene "Battle of Lake Trasimene") completely defeated this Roman army, killing 15,000 Romans, including their commander, and taking 15,000 [prisoners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prisoner_of_war "Prisoner of war"). A cavalry force of 4,000 from the Roman army based at Arretium was also engaged and wiped out.[\[204\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006189%E2%80%93190-217)[\[203\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFronda2011244-216) The prisoners were badly treated if they were Romans, but released if they were from one of Rome's allies. Hannibal wished to stir up disaffection in the states which made up many of Rome's allies in Italy.[\[199\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011270-212) These allied states provided more than half of Rome's military manpower.[\[205\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTERawlings2015311%E2%80%93312-218) The Carthaginians marched deeper into Italy, hoping that the ethnic Greek and [Italic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_peoples_of_Italy "Ancient peoples of Italy") states of southern Italy in particular could be persuaded to [defect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defection "Defection").[\[206\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby199886-219) The Romans, panicked by these heavy defeats, appointed [Fabius Maximus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quintus_Fabius_Maximus_Verrucosus "Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus") as [dictator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_dictator "Roman dictator"), with sole charge of the war effort.[\[207\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999183-220) Fabius introduced the [Fabian strategy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabian_strategy "Fabian strategy") of avoiding open battle with his opponent, but constantly skirmishing with small detachments of the enemy. This was not popular with parts of the Roman army, public and Senate, since he avoided battle while Italy was being devastated by the enemy.[\[200\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2011285-213)[\[208\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006195%E2%80%93196-221) Hannibal marched through the richest and most fertile parts of Italy, hoping the devastation would draw Fabius into battle, but Fabius refused.[\[209\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999184%E2%80%93188-222) In the 216 BC elections [Terentius Varro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaius_Terentius_Varro "Gaius Terentius Varro") and [Aemilius Paullus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucius_Aemilius_Paullus_/(consul_219_BC/) "Lucius Aemilius Paullus (consul 219 BC)") were elected as consuls; both were more aggressively minded than Fabius.[\[210\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2011286-223)[\[211\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006199%E2%80%93200-224) The Roman Senate authorised the raising of a force of 86,000 men, the largest in Roman history to that point.[\[212\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999191,_194-225)[\[213\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006198%E2%80%93199-226) Paullus and Varro marched southward to confront Hannibal, who accepted battle on the open plain near [Cannae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannae "Cannae") in south-east Italy. In the [battle of Cannae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cannae "Battle of Cannae") the Roman legions forced their way through Hannibal's deliberately weak centre, but Libyan heavy infantry on the wings swung around their advance, menacing their flanks. Another Carthaginian commander named [Hasdrubal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasdrubal,_commander_of_the_service_corps "Hasdrubal, commander of the service corps") – not the same man as Hasdrubal Barca, one of Hannibal's younger brothers[\[214\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey200764-227) – led the Carthaginian cavalry on the left wing which routed the Roman cavalry opposite. It then swept around the rear of the Romans to attack the cavalry on the other wing, before charging into the legions from behind. As a result, the Roman infantry was surrounded with no means of escape.[\[215\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFronda2011245-228) At least 67,500 Romans were killed or captured.[\[216\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999192%E2%80%93194-229) The historian Richard Miles describes Cannae as "Rome's greatest military disaster".[\[217\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011279-230) Toni Ñaco del Hoyo considers the Trebia, Lake Trasimene and Cannae to be the three "great military calamities" suffered by the Romans in the first three years of the war.[\[218\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTE%C3%91aco_del_Hoyo2015377-231) Brian Carey writes that these three defeats brought Rome to the brink of collapse.[\[219\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey20072-232) Within a few weeks of Cannae a Roman army of 25,000 was ambushed by [Boii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boii "Boii") Gauls at the [battle of Silva Litana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Silva_Litana "Battle of Silva Litana") and annihilated.[\[220\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTERoberts2017vi%E2%80%931x-233) Fabius was elected consul in 215 BC and re-elected in 214 BC.[\[221\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006227-234)[\[222\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby199894,_99-235) #### Roman allies defect, 216–207 BC Little survives of Polybius's account of Hannibal's army in Italy after Cannae and Livy is the best surviving source for this part of the war.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby199887-17)[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006222-21)[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTESabin199662-22) Several of the city-states in southern Italy allied with Hannibal or were captured when pro-Carthaginian factions betrayed their defences. These included the large city of [Capua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capua "Capua") and the major port city of Tarentum (modern [Taranto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taranto "Taranto")). Two of the major [Samnite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samnium "Samnium") tribes also joined the Carthaginian cause. By 214 BC the bulk of southern Italy had turned against Rome, although there were many exceptions. The majority of Rome's allies in central Italy remained loyal. All except the smallest towns were too well fortified for Hannibal to take by assault and blockade could be a long-drawn-out affair, or, if the target was a port, impossible. Carthage's new allies felt little sense of community with Carthage, or even with each other. The new allies increased the number of places that Hannibal's army was expected to defend from Roman retribution, but provided relatively few fresh troops to assist him in doing so. Such Italian forces as were raised resisted operating away from their home cities and performed poorly when they did.[\[223\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006222%E2%80%93226-236)[\[224\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTERawlings2015313-237) [![Image 12: a map of southern peninsular Italy showing the maximum extent of Carthaginian control](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/61/Second_Punic_war_%28cropped%29.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Second_Punic_war_/(cropped/).png) Hannibal's allies in southern Italy c. 213 BC, shown in light blue When the port city of [Locri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Locri "Locri") defected to Carthage in the summer of 215 BC it was immediately used to reinforce the Carthaginian forces in Italy with soldiers, supplies and war elephants.[\[225\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby199898-238) It was the only time during the war that Hannibal received reinforcements from Carthage.[\[226\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEErdkamp201575-239) A second force, under Hannibal's youngest brother [Mago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mago_Barca "Mago Barca"), was meant to land in Italy in 215 BC but was diverted to Iberia after the Carthaginian defeat there at the [battle of Dertosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Dertosa "Battle of Dertosa").[\[225\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby199898-238)[\[227\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarcel%C3%B32015370-240) Meanwhile, the Romans took drastic steps to raise new legions: enrolling slaves, criminals and those who did not meet the usual property qualification.[\[228\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006226-241) By early 215 BC they were fielding at least 12 legions; two years later they had 18; and a year after that, 22. By 212 BC the full complement of the legions deployed would have been in excess of 100,000 men, plus, as always, a similar number of allied troops. The majority were deployed in southern Italy in field armies of approximately 20,000 men each. This was insufficient to challenge Hannibal's army in open battle, but sufficient to force him to concentrate his forces and to hamper his movements.[\[221\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006227-234) The war surged around southern Italy as cities went over to the Carthaginians or were taken by subterfuge and the Romans recaptured them by siege or by the support of pro-Roman factions.[\[229\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006222%E2%80%93235-242) Hannibal repeatedly defeated Roman armies; in 208 BC both consuls were killed in a cavalry skirmish. But wherever his main army was not active the Romans threatened Carthaginian-supporting towns or sought battle with Carthaginian or Carthaginian-allied detachments; frequently with success.[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996158-143)[\[230\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006236-243) By 207 BC Hannibal had been confined to the extreme south of Italy and many of the cities and territories which had joined the Carthaginian cause had returned to their Roman allegiance.[\[231\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006237%E2%80%93238-244) #### Greece, Sardinia and Sicily During 216 BC the Macedonian king, [Philip V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_V_of_Macedon "Philip V of Macedon"), [pledged his support](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macedonian%E2%80%93Carthaginian_Treaty "Macedonian–Carthaginian Treaty") to Hannibal,[\[232\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999199%E2%80%93200-245) initiating the [First Macedonian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Macedonian_War "First Macedonian War") against Rome in 215 BC. In 211 BC Rome contained this threat by allying with the [Aetolian League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aetolian_League "Aetolian League"), a coalition of Greek city-states which was hostile towards Macedonia, and persuading them to participate in the war. In 205 BC this war ended with a [negotiated peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Phoenice "Treaty of Phoenice").[\[233\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006253%E2%80%93260-246) A rebellion in support of the Carthaginians broke out on Sardinia in 213 BC, but it was quickly put down by the Romans.[\[234\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011288-247) [![Image 13: a colourful mosaic of a sword-armed soldier gesturing to a seated man in ancient-style robes](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/Archimedes_before_his_death_with_the_Roman_soldier%2C_Roman_mosaic.jpg/330px-Archimedes_before_his_death_with_the_Roman_soldier%2C_Roman_mosaic.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Archimedes_before_his_death_with_the_Roman_soldier,_Roman_mosaic.jpg) Archimedes before being killed by the Roman soldier – an early-modern mosaic Up to 215 BC Sicily remained firmly in Roman hands, preventing the easy seaborne reinforcement and resupply of Hannibal from Carthage. [Hiero II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiero_II_of_Syracuse "Hiero II of Syracuse"), the tyrant of Syracuse for the previous sixty years and a staunch Roman ally since 263 BC, died in 215 BC and his successor [Hieronymus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hieronymus_of_Syracuse "Hieronymus of Syracuse") was discontented with his situation. Hannibal negotiated a treaty whereby Syracuse defected to Carthage, in exchange for a Carthaginian pledge to allow the whole of Sicily to become a Syracusan possession. The Syracusan army proved no match for a Roman army led by [Claudius Marcellus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Claudius_Marcellus "Marcus Claudius Marcellus") and by spring 213 BC [Syracuse was besieged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Syracuse_/(213%E2%80%93212_BC/) "Siege of Syracuse (213–212 BC)").[\[235\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011327-248)[\[236\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999200-249) The siege was marked by the ingenuity of [Archimedes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archimedes "Archimedes") in inventing war machines to counteract the traditional siege warfare methods of the Romans.[\[237\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011328-250) A large Carthaginian army led by [Himilco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himilco_/(fl._3rd_century_BC/) "Himilco (fl. 3rd century BC)") was sent to relieve the city in 213 BC.[\[234\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011288-247)[\[238\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011329-251) It captured several Roman-garrisoned towns on Sicily; many Roman garrisons were either expelled or massacred by Carthaginian partisans. In spring 212 BC the Romans stormed Syracuse in a surprise night assault and captured several districts of the city. Meanwhile, the Carthaginian army was crippled by [plague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plague_/(disease/) "Plague (disease)"). After the Carthaginians failed to resupply the city, Syracuse fell that autumn; Archimedes was killed by a Roman soldier.[\[238\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011329-251) Carthage sent more reinforcements to Sicily in 211 BC and went on the offensive. A fresh Roman army attacked the main Carthaginian stronghold on the island, [Agrigentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agrigentum "Agrigentum"), in 210 BC and the city was betrayed to the Romans by a discontented Carthaginian officer. The remaining Carthaginian-controlled towns then surrendered or were taken through force or treachery[\[239\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011330-252)[\[240\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006266%E2%80%93267-253) and the Sicilian grain supply to Rome and its armies was secured.[\[241\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTERawlings2015311-254) #### Italy, 207–203 BC In the spring of 207 BC [Hasdrubal Barca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasdrubal_Barca "Hasdrubal Barca") repeated the feat of his elder brother by marching an army of 35,000 men across the Alps and invading Italy. His aim was to join his forces with those of Hannibal, but Hannibal was unaware of his presence. The Romans facing Hannibal in southern Italy tricked him into believing the whole Roman army was still in camp, while a large portion marched north under the consul [Claudius Nero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaius_Claudius_Nero "Gaius Claudius Nero") and reinforced the Romans facing Hasdrubal, who were commanded by the other consul, [Marcus Salinator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Livius_Salinator "Marcus Livius Salinator"). The combined Roman force attacked Hasdrubal at the [battle of the Metaurus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Metaurus "Battle of the Metaurus") and destroyed his army, killing Hasdrubal. This battle confirmed Roman dominance in Italy and marked the end of their Fabian strategy.[\[242\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2011290-255)[\[243\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011304%E2%80%93306-256) In 205 BC Mago landed in Genua (modern [Genoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genoa "Genoa")) in north-west Italy with the remnants of his Spanish army where it received Gallic and [Ligurian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liguria "Liguria") reinforcements. Mago's arrival in the north of the Italian peninsula was followed by Hannibal's inconclusive [battle of Crotona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Crotona "Battle of Crotona") in 204 BC in the far south of the peninsula. Mago marched his reinforced army towards the lands of Carthage's main Gallic allies in the [Po Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Po_Valley "Po Valley"), but was checked by a large Roman army and defeated at the [battle of Insubria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Insubria "Battle of Insubria") in 203 BC.[\[244\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999286%E2%80%93287-257) After a Roman army invaded the Carthaginian homeland in 204 BC, defeated the Carthaginians in two major battles and won the allegiance of the Numidian kingdoms of North Africa, Hannibal and the remnants of his army were recalled.[\[245\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011310-258) They sailed from Croton (modern [Crotone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crotone "Crotone"))[\[246\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006244-259) and landed at Carthage with 15,000–20,000 experienced veterans. Mago was also recalled; he died of wounds on the voyage and some of his ships were intercepted by the Romans,[\[247\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011312-260) but 12,000 of his troops reached Carthage.[\[248\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999289-261) ### Iberia #### Iberia, 218–209 BC The Roman fleet continued on from Massala in the autumn of 218 BC, landing the army it was transporting in north-east Iberia, where it won support among the local tribes.[\[186\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2011291-199) A rushed Carthaginian attack in late 218 BC was beaten back at the [battle of Cissa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cissa "Battle of Cissa").[\[186\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2011291-199)[\[249\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011321-262) In 217 BC 40 Carthaginian warships were defeated by 55 Roman and Massalian vessels at the [battle of the Ebro River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Ebro_River "Battle of Ebro River"), with 29 Carthaginian ships lost.
