The Romans' [lodgement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lodgement "Lodgement") between the Ebro and the [Pyrenees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyrenees "Pyrenees") blocked the route from Iberia to Italy and greatly hindered the despatch of reinforcements from Iberia to Hannibal.[\[249\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011321-262) The Carthaginian commander in Iberia, Hannibal's brother Hasdrubal, marched into this area in 215 BC, offered battle and was [defeated at Dertosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Ibera "Battle of Ibera"), although both sides suffered heavy casualties.[\[250\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011322-263) The Carthaginians suffered a wave of defections of local [Celtiberian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celtiberians "Celtiberians") tribes to Rome.[\[186\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2011291-199) The Roman commanders captured Saguntum in 212 BC and in 211 BC hired 20,000 Celtiberian mercenaries to reinforce their army. Observing that the three Carthaginian armies were deployed apart from each other, the Romans split their forces.[\[250\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011322-263) This strategy resulted in two separate battles in 211 BC, usually referred to jointly as the [battle of the Upper Baetis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Upper_Baetis "Battle of the Upper Baetis"). Both battles ended in complete defeat for the Romans, as Hasdrubal had bribed the Romans' mercenaries to desert. The Romans pulled back to their coastal stronghold north of the Ebro, from which the Carthaginians again failed to expel them.[\[186\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2011291-199)[\[250\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011322-263) Reinforcements arrived in 210 BC and stabilised the situation.[\[250\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011322-263) [![Image 14: a black and white photograph of a marble bust of a man, with the nose broken off](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a6/Bust_of_Sulla_%28loan_from_Ny_Carlsberg_Glyptotek%29_-_Glyptothek_-_Munich_-_Germany_2017.jpg/250px-Bust_of_Sulla_%28loan_from_Ny_Carlsberg_Glyptotek%29_-_Glyptothek_-_Munich_-_Germany_2017.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bust_of_Sulla_/(loan_from_Ny_Carlsberg_Glyptotek/)_-_Glyptothek_-_Munich_-_Germany_2017.jpg) 2nd century BC marble bust, identified as Scipio Africanus[\[251\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTECoarelli200273%E2%80%9374-264)[\[252\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEtcheto2012274%E2%80%93278-265) In 210 BC [Publius Cornelius Scipio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scipio_Africanus "Scipio Africanus") arrived in Iberia with further Roman reinforcements.[\[253\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011323-266) In a carefully planned assault in 209 BC [he captured New Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cartagena_/(209_BC/) "Battle of Cartagena (209 BC)"), the lightly-defended centre of Carthaginian power in Iberia.[\[253\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011323-266)[\[254\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2011292-267) Scipio seized a vast booty of gold, silver and siege artillery, but released the captured population. He also liberated the Iberian hostages, who had been held there by the Carthaginians to ensure the loyalty of their tribes.[\[253\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011323-266)[\[255\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarcel%C3%B32015362-268) Even so, many of them later fought against the Romans.[\[253\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011323-266) #### Roman victory in Iberia, 208–205 BC In the spring of 208 BC Hasdrubal moved to engage Scipio at the [battle of Baecula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Baecula "Battle of Baecula").[\[256\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015323-269) The Carthaginians were defeated, but Hasdrubal was able to withdraw the majority of his army and prevent any Roman pursuit; most of his losses were among his Iberian allies. Scipio was not able to prevent Hasdrubal from leading his depleted army through the western passes of the Pyrenees into Gaul. In 207 BC, after recruiting heavily in Gaul, Hasdrubal crossed the Alps into Italy in an attempt to join his brother, Hannibal, but was defeated before he could.[\[256\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2015323-269)[\[257\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey200786%E2%80%9390-270)[\[258\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999211-271) In 206 BC at the [battle of Ilipa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Ilipa "Battle of Ilipa"), Scipio with 48,000 men, half Italian and half Iberian, defeated a Carthaginian army of 54,500 men and 32 elephants. This sealed the fate of the Carthaginians in Iberia.[\[253\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011323-266)[\[259\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZimmermann2011293-272) The last Carthaginian-held city in Iberia, Gades (modern [Cádiz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%A1diz "Cádiz")), defected to the Romans.[\[260\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011303-273) Later the same year a [mutiny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutiny_at_Sucro "Mutiny at Sucro") broke out among Roman troops, which attracted support from Iberian leaders, disappointed that Roman forces had remained in the peninsula after the expulsion of the Carthaginians, but it was effectively put down by Scipio. In 205 BC a last attempt was made by Mago to recapture New Carthage when the Roman occupiers were shaken by another mutiny and an Iberian uprising, but he was repulsed. Mago left Iberia for Cisalpine Gaul with his remaining forces.[\[255\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarcel%C3%B32015362-268) In 203 BC Carthage succeeded in recruiting at least 4,000 mercenaries from Iberia, despite Rome's nominal control.[\[261\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011333-274) ### Africa In 213 BC [Syphax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syphax "Syphax"), a powerful [Numidian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numidians "Numidians") king in North Africa, declared for Rome. In response, Roman advisers were sent to train his soldiers and he waged war against the Carthaginian ally [Gala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gala_/(king/) "Gala (king)").[\[250\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEdwell2011322-263) In 206 BC the Carthaginians ended this drain on their resources by dividing several Numidian kingdoms with him. One of those disinherited was the Numidian prince [Masinissa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masinissa "Masinissa"), who was thus driven into the arms of Rome.[\[262\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBarcel%C3%B32015372-275) #### Scipio's invasion of Africa, 204–201 BC [![Image 15: a terrain map of northern Tunisia, with the manoeuvres of Scipio's army in 204–203 BC superimposed on it](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/65/Publius_Scipio%27s_Invasion_of_Africa%2C_204%E2%80%93201_BC.png/500px-Publius_Scipio%27s_Invasion_of_Africa%2C_204%E2%80%93201_BC.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Publius_Scipio%27s_Invasion_of_Africa,_204%E2%80%93201_BC.png) In 205 BC Publius Scipio was given command of the legions in Sicily and allowed to enrol volunteers for his plan to end the war by an invasion of Africa.[\[263\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006286%E2%80%93288-276) Preparations were extensive: including thorough training of the soldiers involved and the stockpiling of a vast quantity of food. Scipio intended to largely feed his army from stockpiles in Sicily, [Sardinia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sardinia "Sardinia") and southern Italy, thus freeing it from the need to forage. War [materiel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Materiel "Materiel") was also prepared in great quantities.[\[264\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006287%E2%80%93288,_294-277) After [landing in Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_invasion_of_Africa_/(204%E2%80%93201_BC/) "Roman invasion of Africa (204–201 BC)") in 204 BC he was joined by Masinissa and a force of Numidian cavalry.[\[265\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006291%E2%80%93292-278) The ships which had landed the Roman army returned to Sicily to pick up supplies; Scipio wished to build up a large stock of food and materiel in Africa.[\[266\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007103-279) In spring and summer 203 BC the Romans gave battle to two large Carthaginian armies and destroyed both.[\[245\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011310-258) After the second of these, Syphax was pursued and taken prisoner by Masinissa at the [battle of Cirta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cirta "Battle of Cirta"); Masinissa then seized most of Syphax's kingdom with Roman help.[\[267\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999282%E2%80%93283-280) Rome and Carthage entered into peace negotiations and Carthage recalled Hannibal from Italy.[\[268\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006298%E2%80%93300-281) The Roman Senate ratified a draft treaty, but because of mistrust and a surge in confidence when Hannibal arrived from Italy Carthage repudiated it.[\[269\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999287%E2%80%93291-282) Hannibal was placed in command of an army formed from his and Mago's veterans from Italy and newly raised troops from Africa, but with few cavalry.[\[270\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006302-283) The decisive [battle of Zama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama "Battle of Zama") followed in October 202 BC.[\[271\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011315-284)[\[272\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTECarey2007119-285) Unlike most battles of the Second Punic War, the Romans had superiority in cavalry and the Carthaginians in infantry.[\[270\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006302-283) Hannibal attempted to use 80 elephants to break into the Roman infantry formation, but the Romans countered them effectively and they routed back through the Carthaginian ranks.[\[273\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999291%E2%80%93293-286) The Roman and allied Numidian cavalry then pressed their attacks and drove the Carthaginian cavalry from the field. The two sides' infantry fought inconclusively until the Roman cavalry returned and attacked the Carthaginian rear. The Carthaginian formation collapsed; Hannibal was one of the few to escape the field.[\[271\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011315-284) The new peace treaty dictated by Rome stripped Carthage of all of its overseas territories and some of its African ones; an indemnity of 10,000 silver talents[\[note 14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-288) was to be paid over 50 years; hostages were to be taken; Carthage was forbidden to possess war elephants and its fleet was restricted to 10 warships; it was prohibited from waging war outside Africa and in Africa only with Rome's express permission. Many senior Carthaginians wanted to reject it, but Hannibal spoke strongly in its favour and it was accepted in spring 201 BC.[\[275\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006308%E2%80%93309-289) Henceforth it was clear that Carthage was politically subordinate to Rome.[\[276\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEckstein2006176-290) Scipio was awarded a [triumph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_triumph "Roman triumph") and received the _[agnomen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnomen "Agnomen")_ "Africanus".[\[277\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011318-291) Under the pressure of the war, the Romans developed an increasingly effective system of logistics to equip and feed the unprecedented numbers of soldiers they fielded. During the last three years of the war this was extended to the transporting by sea from Sicily to Africa of almost all the requirements of Scipio's large army. These developments made possible the subsequent Roman overseas wars of conquest.[\[278\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006359%E2%80%93360-292) Interbellum, 201–149 BC ----------------------- At the end of the war, Masinissa emerged as by far the most powerful ruler among the Numidians.[\[279\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKunze2015398-293) Over the following 48 years he repeatedly took advantage of Carthage's inability to protect its possessions. Whenever Carthage petitioned Rome for redress, or permission to take military action, Rome backed its ally, Masinissa, and refused.[\[280\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKunze2015398,_407-294) Masinissa's seizures of and raids into Carthaginian territory became increasingly flagrant. In 151 BC Carthage raised an army, the treaty notwithstanding, and [counterattacked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterattack "Counterattack") the Numidians. The campaign ended in disaster for the Carthaginians at the [battle of Oroscopa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Oroscopa "Battle of Oroscopa") when their army surrendered.[\[281\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKunze2015407-295) Carthage had paid off its indemnity and was prospering economically, but was no military threat to Rome.[\[282\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKunze2015408-296)[\[283\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015434-297) However, elements in the Roman Senate, led by [Cato the Elder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cato_the_Elder "Cato the Elder"), had long wished to destroy Carthage and with the breach of the treaty as a _[casus belli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casus_belli "Casus belli")_, war was declared in 149 BC.[\[281\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKunze2015407-295) Third Punic War, 149–146 BC --------------------------- In 149 BC a Roman army of approximately 50,000 men, jointly commanded by both consuls, landed near [Utica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utica,_Tunisia "Utica, Tunisia"), 35 kilometres (22 mi) north of Carthage.[\[284\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015436%E2%80%93437-298) Rome demanded that if war were to be avoided, the Carthaginians must hand over all of their armaments. Vast amounts of materiel were delivered, including 200,000 sets of armour, 2,000 [catapults](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballista#Early_Roman_ballistae "Ballista") and a large number of warships.[\[285\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015438-299) This done, the Romans demanded the Carthaginians burn their city and relocate at least 16 kilometres (10 mi) from the sea; the Carthaginians broke off negotiations and set to recreating their [armoury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsenal "Arsenal").[\[286\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999309%E2%80%93310-300) ### Siege of Carthage [![Image 16: a bronze head, believed by some experts to depict Scipio Aemilianus](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/64/Bronze_statue_of_a_Hellenistic_prince%2C_1st_half_of_2nd_century_BC%2C_found_on_the_Quirinal_in_Rome%2C_Palazzo_Massimo_alle_Terme%2C_Rome_%2831479801364%29.jpg/250px-Bronze_statue_of_a_Hellenistic_prince%2C_1st_half_of_2nd_century_BC%2C_found_on_the_Quirinal_in_Rome%2C_Palazzo_Massimo_alle_Terme%2C_Rome_%2831479801364%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bronze_statue_of_a_Hellenistic_prince,_1st_half_of_2nd_century_BC,_found_on_the_Quirinal_in_Rome,_Palazzo_Massimo_alle_Terme,_Rome_/(31479801364/).jpg) As well as manning the walls of Carthage, the Carthaginians formed a [field army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_army "Field army") under [Hasdrubal the Boetharch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasdrubal_the_Boetharch "Hasdrubal the Boetharch"), which was based 25 kilometres (16 mi) to the south.[\[288\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015439-302)[\[289\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011343-303) The Roman army moved to lay siege to Carthage, but its walls were so strong and its citizen militia so determined it was unable to make any impact, while the Carthaginians struck back effectively. Their army raided the Roman [lines of communication](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_of_communication "Line of communication"),[\[289\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011343-303) and in 148 BC Carthaginian [fire ships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_ship "Fire ship") destroyed many Roman vessels. The main Roman camp was in a swamp, which caused an outbreak of disease during the summer.[\[290\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999314-304) The Romans moved their camp, and their ships, further away – so they were now more blockading than closely besieging the city.[\[291\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999315-305) The war dragged on into 147 BC.[\[289\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011343-303) In early 147 BC [Scipio Aemilianus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scipio_Aemilianus "Scipio Aemilianus"), an adopted grandson of Scipio Africanus who had distinguished himself during the previous two years' fighting, was elected consul and took control of the war.[\[281\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKunze2015407-295)[\[292\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015440-306) The Carthaginians continued to resist vigorously: they constructed warships and, during the summer, twice gave battle to the Roman fleet, losing both times.[\[292\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015440-306) The Romans launched an assault on the walls; after confused fighting they broke into the city, but, becoming disoriented in the dark, withdrew. Hasdrubal and his army retreated into the city to reinforce the garrison.[\[293\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006348%E2%80%93349-307) Hasdrubal had Roman prisoners tortured to death on the walls, in view of the Roman army. He was reinforcing the will to resist in the Carthaginian citizens; from this point there could be no possibility of negotiations. Some members of the city council denounced his actions and Hasdrubal had them put to death and took control of the city.[\[292\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015440-306)[\[294\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006349-308) With no Carthaginian army in the field, those cities which had remained loyal went over to the Romans or were captured.[\[295\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999318-309) Scipio moved back to a close blockade of the city and built a [mole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mole_/(architecture/) "Mole (architecture)") which cut off supply from the sea.[\[296\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles20112-310) In the spring of 146 BC the Roman army managed to secure a foothold on the fortifications near the harbour.[\[297\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015441-311)[\[298\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011346-312) Scipio launched a major assault which quickly captured the city's main square, where the legions camped overnight.[\[299\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles20113-313) The next morning, the Romans started systematically working their way through the residential part of the city, killing everyone they encountered and burning the buildings behind them.[\[297\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015441-311) At times, the Romans progressed from rooftop to rooftop, to prevent missiles being hurled down on them.[\[299\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles20113-313) It took six days to clear the city of resistance; only on the last day did Scipio take prisoners. The last holdouts, including Roman [deserters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deserter "Deserter") in Carthaginian service, fought on from the Temple of [Eshmoun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eshmun "Eshmun") and burnt it down around themselves when all hope was gone.[\[300\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles20113%E2%80%934-314) There were 50,000 Carthaginian prisoners, a small proportion of the pre-war population, who were sold into slavery.[\[301\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2002316-315) There is a tradition that Roman forces then [sowed the city with salt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salting_the_earth "Salting the earth"), but this has been shown to have been a 19th-century invention.[\[302\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTERidley1986144%E2%80%93145-316)[\[303\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBaker201450-317) Aftermath --------- [![Image 17: a colour photograph of a semi-urban area by the sea on a sunny day](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0e/Carthage-1958-PortsPuniques.jpg/330px-Carthage-1958-PortsPuniques.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Carthage-1958-PortsPuniques.jpg) The site of Carthage in 1958, showing the circular war harbour capable of holding 170 galleys.[\[296\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles20112-310) Rome was determined that the city of Carthage remain in ruins. The Senate despatched a ten-man commission and Scipio was ordered to carry out further demolitions. A curse was placed on anyone who might attempt to resettle the site in the future.[\[304\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011353-318) The former site of the city was confiscated as _[ager publicus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ager_publicus "Ager publicus")_, public land.[\[305\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015443-319) The remaining Carthaginian territories were annexed by Rome and reconstituted to become the [Roman province of Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa_Province "Africa Province") with Utica as its capital.[\[306\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2002310,_316-320) The province became a major source of grain and other foodstuffs for Rome.[\[307\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWhittaker1996596-321) Numerous large Punic cities, such as those in [Mauretania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauretania "Mauretania"), were taken over by the Romans,[\[308\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollard2015249-322) although they were permitted to retain their Punic system of government and culture.[\[309\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFantar2015455%E2%80%93456-323) The Romans did not interfere in the locals' private lives and Punic culture, language and religion survived, and is known to modern scholars as "Neo-Punic civilization".[\[310\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015443%E2%80%93445-324)[\[311\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFantar2015454-325) The [Punic language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_language "Punic language") continued to be spoken in north Africa until the 7th century AD.[\[312\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJouhaud196822-326)[\[313\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard1955105-327) A century after the end of the Punic Wars, the site of Carthage was [rebuilt as a Roman city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Carthage "Roman Carthage") by [Julius Caesar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar "Julius Caesar"); it became one of the main cities of Roman Africa by the time of the [Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire").[\[314\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTERichardson2015480%E2%80%93481-328)[\[315\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011363%E2%80%93364-329) Rome still exists as the capital of Italy; the ruins of Carthage lie 24 kilometres (15 mi) east of [Tunis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunis "Tunis") on the North African coast.[\[316\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006296-330)[\[317\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEUNESCO2020-331) Notes, citations and sources ---------------------------- ### Notes 1. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_ref-3)** The term _Punic_ comes from the [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin "Latin") ancestry.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTESidwellJones199816-2) 2. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_ref-25)** Sources other than Polybius are **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_ref-40)** Those who did not meet the property requirement could be required to serve in the navy. At times of national emergency the property requirement might be waived and these poorer citizens conscripted into the army.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199922-39) 4. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_ref-43)** This could be increased to 5,000 in some circumstances,[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199923-41) or, rarely, even more.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006287-42) 5. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_ref-51)** Roman and Greek sources refer to these foreign fighters derogatively as "mercenaries", but the modern historian Adrian Goldsworthy describes this as "a gross oversimplification". (Carthaginian citizenship was largely reserved for inhabitants of the city of Carthage.)[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200633-50) 6. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_ref-53)** ["Shock" troops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shock_troops "Shock troops") are those trained and used to close rapidly with an opponent, with the intention of breaking them before, or immediately upon, contact.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJones19871-52) 7. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_ref-64)** These elephants were typically about 2.5 m (8 ft 2 in) high at the shoulder and should not be confused with the larger [African bush elephant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_bush_elephant "African bush elephant").[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011240-63) 8. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_ref-70)** For example, a typical Roman army of two Roman and two allied legions would consume 60 tons of grain each day. That supplied to the men would need to be [milled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mill_/(grinding/) "Mill (grinding)") by them.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEErdkamp201568-69) 9. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_ref-117)** Polybius gives 140,000 personnel in the Roman fleet and 150,000 in the Carthaginian; these figures are broadly accepted by modern historians of the conflict.[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006110%E2%80%93111-114)[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby199687-115)[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTETipps1985436-116) 10. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_ref-145)** Several different "talents" are known from antiquity. The ones referred to in this article are all Euboic (or Euboeic) talents, of approximately 26 kilograms (57 lb).[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996158-143)[\[135\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2006565-144) 2,000 talents was approximately 52,000 kilograms (51 long tons) of silver.[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996158-143) 11. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_ref-154)** 3,200 talents was approximately 82,000 kg (81 long tons) of silver.[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996158-143) 12. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_ref-168)** 1,200 talents was approximately 30,000 kg (30 long tons) of silver.[\[134\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1996158-143) 13. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_ref-186)** There is scholarly debate as to whether Saguntum was a formal Roman ally, in which case attacking it may have been a breach of the clause in the Treaty of Lutatius prohibiting attacking each other's allies; or whether the city had less formally requested Rome's protection, and possibly been granted it. In either case, the Carthaginians argued that relationships entered into after the signing of the treaty were not covered by it.[\[173\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006144-185) 14. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars#cite_ref-288)** 10,000 talents was approximately [Battle of Great Plains](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/battles/battle-of-great-plains/)
=======================================================================================

(203 BCE)

This post is also available in: **[Polish](https://imperiumromanum.pl/bitwy/bitwa-na-wielkich-rowninach/)** ([polski](https://imperiumromanum.pl/bitwy/bitwa-na-wielkich-rowninach/))

17 March 2023

![Image 4: Hastatus](https://imperiumromanum.pl/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/hastatus-1086x270.jpg)[](https://imperiumromanum.pl/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/hastatus.jpg "Hastatus")

Hastatus

Chapters

*   [African warfare](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/battles/battle-of-great-plains/#african-warfare)
*   [Battle of the Great Plains in 203 BCE](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/battles/battle-of-great-plains/#battle-of-the-great-plains-in-203-bce)
*   [The meaning of the battle](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/battles/battle-of-great-plains/#the-meaning-of-the-battle)

The fighting of the Second Punic War had been going on for over a decade. The scales of victory were tipping to the Roman side. In Italy, after his first victories, Hannibal became entangled in arduous fights which he could not win. In Spain and Sicily, the Romans defeated the Carthaginians. To successfully end the war, the Sons of the Wolf had to attack Carthage on its territory.

The person who had to face this task was Publius Cornelius Scipio, radiant with the fame of the victor of Baecula and New Carthage, who drove the Carthaginian army from the Iberian Peninsula. Having overcome the resistance of some members of the Senate (including the aged Fabius Maximus), Scipio received Sicily as a province with the possibility of conducting operations in Africa. The core of his army consisted of two “Cannen legions”. After the old and the sick were sent away and supplemented with volunteers, this resulted in two units of 6,200 infantry and 300 cavalries. By adding two units (_alae)_ allies, we get a total of 25-30,000 people. The ratio of cavalry to the rest of the army was no greater than 1 to 10. Scipio did not immediately move to Carthage. He had to train an expeditionary army on the island and prepare supplies for it. When this goal was achieved, the chief sailed from Sicily.

African warfare
---------------

The Roman landing party reached the shores of Africa on the second day after leaving Sicily. The legionaries disembarked near Utica. Already at the beginning, Roman outposts clashed with 500 Punic cavalrymen. The Romans easily prevailed over the enemy – the higher commander Hanno and the commander of the Carthaginian cavalry died. Soon, Massynis joined the Romans with his entourage of 200 men. It was not a large group, but the Numidian prince was valuable because of his knowledge of the local areas. When another detachment of enemy cavalry (about 4,000 men) consisting of Numidians and citizens of Carthage challenged the Romans, they set an ambush for him. In accordance with the order of Scipio Massynis, he got involved in the fight with the enemy unit, and then led him to the position where the Roman cavalry was hidden. The Carthaginian commander was killed, 1,000 Punic soldiers were killed or captured during the preliminary fighting, and 2,000 during the pursuit. Then the Romans began the siege of Utica, which also lasted through the winter of 204-203 BCE. Meanwhile, two armies – Hasdrubal Gisgo and Syfax built separate camps 7-8 miles from the Romans. The forces of both allies were definitely more numerous than Scipio’s army, especially because this disproportion was visible in the cavalry. Showing his commitment to besieging the city, Scipio prepared night attacks on both camps. One attack, targeting Syfax’s camp, took the enemy by surprise, as did a second aimed at Hasdrubal’s camp. After this double victory, Scipio directed part of his army against Utica and sent part of it to ravage the area.

Battle of the Great Plains in 203 BCE
-------------------------------------

This defeat frightened the inhabitants of Carthage. The Punic authorities ordered Syfax to join the forces of Hasdrubal, who brought with him newly enlisted Celtiberian warriors (about 4,000 men). Thirty days later, the two chieftains combined their forces, bringing a total of 30,000 men camped in a fortified position in an area called the Great Plains (today’s Souk el Kremis). The Roman commander, having received a report about these forces, moved against them. Leaving the fleet and part of the army to besiege Utica, he moved towards the enemy’s whereabouts. He reached the slopes of the Great Plains after five days.

The size of his army is difficult to determine, but it was probably smaller than the combined army of Syfax and Hasdrubal. Scipio set up camp 4 miles from the enemy and on the first day let his soldiers rest. The next day the Romans marched towards the enemy on the plain, forming a formation less than a mile from the enemy. Initially, there were customary skirmishes from both sides with the participation of cavalry and light-armed men from both sides, However, on that day and probably for the next two days there was no major battle. Only on the fourth day did the two chieftains bring their armies so close that a fight became inevitable. The centre of the Punic formation was occupied by the Celtiberians, to the right of the infantry from Hasdrubal’s old army, covered on the right flank by cavalry. To the left of the Celtiberians stood the Numidians of Syfax. The Roman formation took the traditional form – with two legions in the centre and _alae_ formations on either side. The right flank of the Roman formation was occupied by the Roman and Italian cavalry, the left by the Numidians of Massinis. The battle was quickly settled.

In the beginning, the Italian cavalry and the Numidian infantry of Massinissa defeated their opponents. Most of the Punic and Numidian infantry in Carthage’s service were scattered by the _alae_ soldiers. For they were the same warriors, demoralized by recent defeats, facing the same soldiers who had taken their toll in previous clashes. The abandoned Celtiberians remained on the battlefield and stood firm against the Roman legionaries. According to Livy, these brave warriors were unfamiliar with the local areas, which prevented them from joining the escape. In numbers, the Celtiberians were at least roughly equal to the _hastati_ of Scipio’s two legions fighting in the centre of the Roman formation. The Romans, lined up in _triplex acies_ formed a column of _principes and triarii_ which marched out from behind the _hastati_ and attacked the Celtiberians from both flanks. Those surrounded on all sides ceased to exist as a unit, Of the entire group of these warriors only a few survived.

The meaning of the battle
-------------------------

Battle of the Great Plains was another blow to the morale of the flagging Carthaginian forces. After these defeats, the Council in Carthage came to the conclusion that the only survivor could be Hannibal, who had victories over Rome on his account. In 203 BCE so Barcida left Italy to defend his African homeland. The culmination of these events was the defeat of the Battle of Zama, which practically ended the Second Punic War.

Battle of the Great Plains was another personal success of Scipio Africanus, who, like at Baecula and Ilipa, used bold manoeuvres with columns of troops on the enemy’s flanks. So it was like a repetition of Hannibal’s manoeuvres at Trebia and Cannae. The weakness of the opponent also enabled him to win. In the battle, the Punicians operated forces that were not coordinated with each other, but their demoralization after previous defeats also had a large impact on the outcome of the battle.
