| Third Punic War | | --- | | Part of the [Punic Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars "Punic Wars") | | [![Image 1: a map showing the defences of the city of Carthage](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/City_of_Carthage_circa_149_BC.png/330px-City_of_Carthage_circa_149_BC.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:City_of_Carthage_circa_149_BC.png) The defences of the city of [Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthage "Carthage") | |
Date149–146 BC
Location

Carthaginian territory (Modern-day Tunisia)

Result
  • Roman victory
  • Destruction of Carthage
| | Belligerents | | [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Republic "Roman Republic") | [Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Carthage "Ancient Carthage") | | Commanders and leaders | | * [Scipio Aemilianus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scipio_Aemilianus "Scipio Aemilianus") * [Manius Manilius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manius_Manilius "Manius Manilius") * [Lucius Censorinus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucius_Marcius_Censorinus_/(consul_149_BC/) "Lucius Marcius Censorinus (consul 149 BC)") * [Lucius Piso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucius_Calpurnius_Piso_Caesoninus_/(consul_148_BC/) "Lucius Calpurnius Piso Caesoninus (consul 148 BC)") | * [Hasdrubal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasdrubal_the_Boetharch "Hasdrubal the Boetharch") [![Image 2: Surrendered](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5d/White_flag_icon.svg/20px-White_flag_icon.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrender_/(military/) "Surrendered") * [Himilco Phameas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phameas "Phameas") * Diogenes | | Strength | | * 36,000–46,000 infantry * 4,000 cavalry | * 20,000 or more soldiers * Armed civilians | | Casualties and losses | | Unknown | * Up to 750,000 killed, including civilians * 50,000 [survivors enslaved](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_ancient_Rome "Slavery in ancient Rome") | The **Third Punic War** (149–146 BC) was the third and last of the [Punic Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars "Punic Wars") fought between [Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Carthage "Ancient Carthage") and [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Republic "Roman Republic"). The war was fought entirely within Carthaginian territory, in what is now northern [Tunisia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunisia "Tunisia"). When the [Second Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Punic_War "Second Punic War") ended in 201 BC one of the terms of the peace treaty prohibited Carthage from waging war without Rome's permission. Rome's ally, King [Masinissa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masinissa "Masinissa") of [Numidia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numidia "Numidia"), exploited this to repeatedly raid and seize Carthaginian territory with impunity. In 149 BC Carthage sent an army, under [Hasdrubal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasdrubal_the_Boetharch "Hasdrubal the Boetharch"), against Masinissa, the treaty notwithstanding. The campaign ended in disaster as the [Battle of Oroscopa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Oroscopa "Battle of Oroscopa") ended with a Carthaginian defeat and the surrender of the Carthaginian army. Anti-Carthaginian factions in Rome used the illicit military action as a pretext to prepare a [punitive expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punitive_expedition "Punitive expedition"). Later in 149 BC a large Roman army landed at [Utica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utica,_Tunisia "Utica, Tunisia") in North Africa. The Carthaginians hoped to appease the Romans, but despite the Carthaginians surrendering all of their weapons, the Romans pressed on to [besiege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Besiege "Besiege") the city of Carthage. The Roman campaign suffered repeated setbacks through 149 BC, only alleviated by [Scipio Aemilianus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scipio_Aemilianus "Scipio Aemilianus"), a middle-ranking officer, distinguishing himself several times. A new Roman commander took over in 148 BC and fared equally badly. At the annual election of Roman magistrates in the spring of 147 BC the public support for Scipio was so great that the usual age restrictions were lifted to allow him to be appointed [consul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_consul "Roman consul") and commander in Africa. Scipio's term commenced with two Carthaginian successes, but he tightened the siege and started to build a large [mole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mole_/(architecture/) "Mole (architecture)") to prevent supplies from getting into Carthage via [blockade runners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blockade_runner "Blockade runner"). The Carthaginians had partially rebuilt their fleet, and it [sortied](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sortie "Sortie"), to the Romans' surprise. After an indecisive engagement, the Carthaginians mismanaged their withdrawal and lost many ships. The Romans then built a large brick structure in the harbour area that dominated the city wall. Once this was complete, Scipio led a strong force that stormed the camp of Carthage's field army and forced most of the towns and cities still supporting Carthage to surrender. In early 146 BC the Romans launched their final assault and, over six days, systematically destroyed the city and killed its inhabitants; only on the last day did they take prisoners, 50,000 of them, who were sold into slavery. The conquered Carthaginian territories became the [Roman province of Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa_Province "Africa Province"), with Utica as its capital. It was a century before the site of Carthage was [rebuilt as a Roman city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Carthage "Roman Carthage"). The main source for most aspects of the Punic Wars[\[note 1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-2) is the historian [Polybius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polybius "Polybius") (c. 200 – c. 118 BC), a Greek sent to Rome in 167 BC as a hostage.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200620%E2%80%9321-3) His works include a now-lost manual on [military tactics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_tactics "Military tactics"),[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShutt193853-4) but he is best known for [_The Histories_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Histories_/(Polybius/) "The Histories (Polybius)"), written sometime after 146 BC.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200620-5)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWalbank199011%E2%80%9312-6) He accompanied his patron and friend,[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAstin20065-7) the Roman general [Scipio Aemilianus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scipio_Aemilianus "Scipio Aemilianus"), in North Africa during the Third Punic War;[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChampion201596,_108-8) this causes the normally reliable Polybius to recount Scipio's actions in a favourable light.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200621-9)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAstin20065%E2%80%936-10)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWalbank1979662-11) In addition, significant portions of _The Histories_' account of the Third Punic War have been lost.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200621-9)[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos20152-12) The account of the Roman annalist [Livy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Livy "Livy"), who relied heavily on Polybius, is much used by modern historians of the Punic Wars,[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChampion201595-13) but all that survives of his account of events after 167 BC is a list of contents.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200622-14)[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMineo2015123-15) Other ancient accounts of the Third Punic War or its participants which have also been largely lost include those of [Plutarch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plutarch "Plutarch"), [Dio Cassius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dio_Cassius "Dio Cassius")[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMineo2015126-16) and the Greek [Diodorus Siculus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diodorus_Siculus "Diodorus Siculus").[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMineo2015119-17) Modern historians also use the account of the 2nd-century AD Greek [Appian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appian "Appian").[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015430-18)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMineo2015125-19) The modern historian Bernard Mineo states that it "is the only complete and continuous account of this war".[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMineo2015126-16) It is thought to have been largely based on Polybius's account, but several problems with it have been identified.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWalbank1979662-11)[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200622%E2%80%9323-20) These issues mean that of the three Punic Wars, the third is the one about which the least is reliably known.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200624-21) Other sources include coins, inscriptions, [archaeological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology "Archaeology") evidence and empirical evidence from reconstructions.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy200623,_98-22) In the mid-2nd century BC [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Republic "Roman Republic") was the dominant power in the [Mediterranean region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_Basin "Mediterranean Basin"),[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHolland200410-23) while [Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Carthage "Ancient Carthage") was a large [city-state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City-state "City-state") in the north east of what is now Tunisia.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011324%E2%80%93325-24)[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEUNESCO2020-25) Carthage and Rome had fought the 23-year-long [First Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Punic_War "First Punic War") from 264 to 241 BC and the 17-year-long [Second Punic War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Punic_War "Second Punic War") between 218 and 201 BC. Both wars ended with Roman victories; the Second when the Roman general [Scipio Africanus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scipio_Africanus "Scipio Africanus") defeated [Hannibal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hannibal "Hannibal"), the premier Carthaginian general of the war, at the [Battle of Zama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama "Battle of Zama"), 160 kilometres (100 mi) south-west of Carthage.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999289,_295%E2%80%93298-26) Africanus imposed a [peace treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_treaty "Peace treaty") on the Carthaginians which stripped them of their overseas territories and some of their African ones. An indemnity of 10,000 silver [talents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talent_/(measurement/) "Talent (measurement)")[\[note 2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-29) was to be paid over 50 years.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTELazenby1998228-27) Hostages were taken and Carthage was prohibited from waging war outside Africa—and could wage war in Africa only with Rome's express permission. Many senior Carthaginians wanted to reject the treaty, but Hannibal spoke strongly in its favour and it was accepted in spring 201 BC.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011317-30)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006308%E2%80%93309-31) Henceforth, it was clear that Carthage was politically subordinate to Rome.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999303,_305%E2%80%93306-32) [![Image 3: a map of the western Mediterranean with the territories of Numidia, Carthage and Rome shown](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Western_Mediterranean_territory%2C_150_BC.svg/330px-Western_Mediterranean_territory%2C_150_BC.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Western_Mediterranean_territory,_150_BC.svg) Map of approximate extent of Numidian, Carthaginian and Roman territory in 150 BC At the end of the war [Masinissa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masinissa "Masinissa"), an ally of Rome, emerged as by far the most powerful ruler among the [Numidians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numidians "Numidians"), the indigenous population which controlled much of what is now Algeria and Tunisia.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKunze2015398-33) Over the following 50 years, he repeatedly took advantage of Carthage's inability to protect its possessions. Whenever Carthage petitioned Rome for redress or permission to take military action, Rome backed Masinissa and refused.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKunze2015398,_407-34) Masinissa's seizures of and raids into Carthaginian territory became increasingly flagrant. In 151 BC Carthage raised a large army commanded by the previously unrecorded[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999307-35) general [Hasdrubal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasdrubal_the_Boetharch "Hasdrubal the Boetharch") and, the treaty notwithstanding, counter-attacked the Numidians. The campaign ended in disaster at the [Battle of Oroscopa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Oroscopa "Battle of Oroscopa") and the army surrendered.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKunze2015407-36)[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006336%E2%80%93337-37) Many Carthaginians were subsequently massacred by the Numidians.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999307-35) Hasdrubal escaped to Carthage, where, in an attempt to placate Rome, he was condemned to death.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999308-38) Carthage paid off its indemnity in 151 BC[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006332-39) and was prospering economically[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKunze2015405,_408-40) but was no military threat to Rome.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKunze2015408-41) Nevertheless, there had long been a faction within the [Roman Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Senate "Roman Senate") that had wished to take further military action against Carthage.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKunze2015399-42) For example, the dislike of Carthage by the senior senator [Cato](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cato_the_Censor "Cato the Censor") was so well known that since the 18th century (AD), he has been credited with ending all of his speeches with _[Carthago delenda est](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthago_delenda_est "Carthago delenda est")_ ("Carthage must be destroyed").[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011336-43)[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVogel-Weidemann198979-44) The opposing faction included [Scipio Nasica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scipio_Nasica_Corculum "Scipio Nasica Corculum"), who argued that fear of a strong enemy such as Carthage would keep the common people in check and avoid social division.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999307-35)[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006333-45) Cato was a member of an embassy to Carthage, probably in 153 BC, and noted her growing economy and strength;[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006333-45) Nasica was likely a member of the same embassy.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVogel-Weidemann198980-46) Using the illicit Carthaginian military action as a pretext,[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKunze2015399-42) Rome began preparing a punitive expedition.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006337-47) [![Image 4: the obverse and reverse of a slightly corroded siver coin](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/22/Carthage_-_Double_Shekel_-_c.160-149_BC.jpg/250px-Carthage_-_Double_Shekel_-_c.160-149_BC.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Carthage_-_Double_Shekel_-_c.160-149_BC.jpg) A silver [double shekel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthaginian_coinage "Carthaginian coinage") from Carthage's last minting of coins before its destruction.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJenkinsLewis196353-48) Modern scholars have advanced several theories as to why Rome was eager for war.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVogel-Weidemann198981-49) These include: a Roman fear of Carthaginian commercial competition;[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015432-50)[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarris2006156-51)[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVogel-Weidemann198981%E2%80%9382-52) a desire to forestall a wider war which might have broken out with the death of Masinissa, who was aged 89 at the time;[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVogel-Weidemann198982,_85-53) the [factional](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_faction "Political faction") use of Carthage as a political "bogeyman", irrespective of its true power;[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015431%E2%80%93432-54)[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarris2006154-55) a greed for glory and loot;[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015432-50)[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarris2006155-56) and a desire to quash a political system which Rome considered anathema.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015431%E2%80%93432-54) No consensus has been reached regarding these and other hypotheses.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVogel-Weidemann198981,_87%E2%80%9388-57) Carthaginian embassies attempted to negotiate with Rome, which responded evasively.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999308-38)[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarris2006151-58) The large North African port city of [Utica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utica,_Tunisia "Utica, Tunisia"), some 55 km (34 mi) north of Carthage,[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015437-59) went over to Rome in 149 BC. Aware that Utica's harbour would greatly facilitate any assault on Carthage, the Senate and the [People's Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centuriate_Assembly "Centuriate Assembly") of Rome declared war on Carthage.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKunze2015407-36)[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006337%E2%80%93338-60) The Romans elected two men each year, known as [consuls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_consul "Roman consul"), as senior [magistrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_magistrate "Roman magistrate"), who at time of war would each lead an army; on occasion their term of office was extended.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBeard2016127-61)[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHolland2004154%E2%80%93155-62)[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall199924-63) A large Roman army landed at Utica in 149 BC under both consuls for the year, [Manius Manilius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manius_Manilius "Manius Manilius") commanding the army and [Lucius Marcius Censorinus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucius_Marcius_Censorinus_/(consul_149_BC/) "Lucius Marcius Censorinus (consul 149 BC)") the fleet. The Carthaginians continued to attempt to appease Rome and sent an embassy to Utica. The consuls demanded that they hand over all weaponry; reluctantly the Carthaginians did so. Large convoys took enormous stocks of equipment from Carthage to Utica. Surviving records state that these included 200,000 sets of armour and 2,000 [catapults](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catapult "Catapult"). Carthage's warships all sailed to Utica and were burnt in the harbour.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006338%E2%80%93339-64) Once Carthage was disarmed, Censorinus made the further demand that the Carthaginians abandon their city and relocate 16 km (10 mi) away from the sea; Carthage would then be destroyed.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006338%E2%80%93339-64)[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurcell1995134-65) The Carthaginians abandoned negotiations and prepared to defend their city.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006339-66) The city of Carthage was unusually large for the time: modern scholars give population estimates ranging from 90,000 to 800,000. Any of these would make Carthage one of the most populous cities in the Mediterranean area at the time.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHoyos2005225-67)[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011342-68) It was strongly fortified with walls of more than 35 km (20 mi) circumference.[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999313-69) Defending the main approach from the land were three lines of defences, of which the strongest was a brick-built wall 9 metres (30 ft) wide and 15–20 metres (50–70 ft) high with a 20-metre-wide (70 ft) ditch in front of it. Built into this wall was a barracks capable of holding over 24,000 soldiers.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurcell1995134-65)[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006340-70) The city had few reliable sources of ground water but possessed a complex system to catch and channel rainwater and many cisterns to store it.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011342%E2%80%93343-71) The Carthaginians raised a strong and enthusiastic force to garrison the city from their citizenry and by freeing all slaves willing to fight.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006339-66)[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015438%E2%80%93439-72)[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011341-73) They also formed a field army at least 20,000 strong,[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHarris2006159-74) which was placed under Hasdrubal, freshly released from his condemned cell. This army was based at [Nepheris](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Nepheris&action=edit&redlink=1 "Nepheris (page does not exist)"), 25 km (16 mi) south of Carthage.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015439-75) Appian gives the strength of the Roman army which landed in Africa as 84,000 soldiers; modern historians estimate it at 40,000–50,000 men, of whom 4,000 were [cavalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalry "Cavalry").[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006340-70)[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015436-76) The Roman army moved to Carthage, unsuccessfully attempted to scale the city walls, and settled down for a [siege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Carthage_/(Third_Punic_War/) "Siege of Carthage (Third Punic War)"). They set up two camps under command of [legates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legatus "Legatus"): Censorinus' had the primary role of protecting the beached Roman ships and Manilius's housed the Roman legions. Hasdrubal moved up his army to harass the Roman supply lines and foraging parties.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006341-77) The Romans launched another assault on the city but were repulsed again. Scipio Aemilianus, the adopted grandson of Scipio Africanus, who was serving as a [tribune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribune "Tribune") – a middle-ranking military position – held back his men and was able to deploy them to beat off the pursuing Carthaginians, preventing heavy losses.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999314-78)[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006342%E2%80%93343-79) [![Image 5: a colourful oil painting showing men hauling on a large siege engine](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Catapulta_by_Edward_Poynter.jpg/330px-Catapulta_by_Edward_Poynter.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Catapulta_by_Edward_Poynter.jpg) The camp established by Censorinus was badly situated and by early summer was so pestiferous that it was moved to a healthier location. This was not as defensible, and the Carthaginians inflicted losses on the Roman fleet with [fireships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fireship "Fireship").[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999314-78) The Romans then made these attacks more difficult by building additional fortifications.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006343-80) Nevertheless, the Carthaginians repeatedly attacked the camps. In often confused fighting Scipio distinguished himself further by his role in thwarting these; the discipline which he imposed on his troops was in contrast with the behaviour of most of the rest of the Roman army.[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006343%E2%80%93344-81) Manilius decided to strike against the Carthaginians' main camp near Nepheris, despite its strong position and fortifications. Arriving there, Manilius ordered an immediate assault, against Scipio's advice. This initially went well, but the Romans advanced into an untenable position. When they attempted to withdraw, the Carthaginians counterattacked, inflicting heavy casualties. Scipio led 300 cavalrymen in a series of limited and well-disciplined charges and threats which caused the Carthaginians to pause long enough for most of the infantry to complete their retreat. That night Scipio led his cavalry back to rescue a trapped group of Romans.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999314%E2%80%93315-82) The Roman column retreated to its camp near Carthage, where a committee from the Senate had arrived to evaluate Scipio and Manilius' progress. Scipio's performance was prominent in their subsequent report.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006344%E2%80%93345-83) Scipio made contact with several of the leaders of Carthage's [Numidian cavalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numidian_cavalry "Numidian cavalry"), then joined a second, better-planned expedition led by Manilius against Hasdrubal at Nepheris. Despite the greater forethought, the Romans made no progress, although one of the Numidians contacted by Scipio did defect to the Romans with 2,200 men. Manilius withdrew after the Romans ran out of food and Scipio led the Romans' new allies on a successful foraging expedition.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999315-84)[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006345%E2%80%93346-85) The Romans elected two new consuls in 148 BC, but only one of them was sent to Africa: [Lucius Calpurnius Piso Caesoninus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucius_Calpurnius_Piso_Caesoninus_/(consul_148_BC/) "Lucius Calpurnius Piso Caesoninus (consul 148 BC)"); [Lucius Hostilius Mancinus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucius_Hostilius_Mancinus_/(consul_145_BC/) "Lucius Hostilius Mancinus (consul 145 BC)") commanded the navy as his subordinate. He pulled back the close siege of Carthage to a looser [blockade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blockade "Blockade") and attempted to mop up the other Carthaginian-supporting cities in the area. He failed: [Neapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nabeul "Nabeul") surrendered and was subsequently [sacked](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Looting "Looting"), but [Aspis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelibia "Kelibia") withstood assaults from both the Roman army and navy, while [Hippo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bizerte "Bizerte") was fruitlessly besieged. A Carthaginian [sortie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sortie "Sortie") from Hippo destroyed the Roman [siege engines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_engine "Siege engine"), causing the Romans to break off the campaign and go into winter quarters. Hasdrubal, already in charge of the Carthaginian field army, overthrew the civilian leadership of Carthage and took command himself. Carthage allied with [Andriscus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andriscus "Andriscus"), a pretender to the [Macedonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macedonia_/(ancient_kingdom/) "Macedonia (ancient kingdom)") throne. Andriscus had invaded Roman Macedonia, defeated a Roman army, had himself crowned King Philip VI and sparked the [Fourth Macedonian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Macedonian_War "Fourth Macedonian War").[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006346-86)[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999315%E2%80%93316-87) [![Image 6: a glass display case containing stones and a pot](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Vitrine_3e_guerre_punique.jpg/250px-Vitrine_3e_guerre_punique.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vitrine_3e_guerre_punique.jpg) Arrowheads, remains of a dagger and stones for slingshots exhibited at the [National Museum of Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_Carthage "National Museum of Carthage") Scipio intended to stand in the 147 BC elections for the post of _[aedile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aedile "Aedile")_, which was a natural progression for him. Aged 36 or 37, he was too young to stand as consul, for which by the _[Lex Villia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lex_Villia_Annalis "Lex Villia Annalis")_ the minimum age was 41. There was considerable political manoeuvring behind the scenes. Scipio and his partisans played on his successes over the previous two years and the fact that it was his adoptive grandfather, Scipio Africanus, who had sealed Roman victory in Africa in the Second Punic War. Public demand to appoint him as consul and so allow him to take charge of the African war, was so strong that the Senate put aside the age requirements for all posts for the year. Scipio was elected consul and appointed to sole command in Africa; usually theatres were allocated to the two consuls by lot. He was granted the usual right to [conscript](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conscript "Conscript") enough men to make up the numbers of the forces there and the unusual entitlement to enroll volunteers.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006346%E2%80%93347-88)[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAstin196761%E2%80%9369-89) Scipio moved the Romans' main camp back to near Carthage, closely observed by a Carthaginian detachment of 8,000. He made a speech demanding tighter discipline and dismissed those soldiers he considered ill-disciplined or poorly motivated. He then led a successful night attack and broke into the city with 4,000 men. Panicked in the dark, the Carthaginian defenders, after an initial fierce resistance, fled. Scipio decided that his position would be indefensible once the Carthaginians reorganised themselves in daylight and so withdrew.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006348%E2%80%93349-90) Hasdrubal, horrified at the way the Carthaginian defences had collapsed, had Roman prisoners tortured to death on the walls, in sight of the Roman army. He was reinforcing the will to resist in the Carthaginian citizens; from this point, there could be no possibility of negotiation or even surrender. Some members of the city council denounced his actions and Hasdrubal had them too put to death and took full control of the city.[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015440-91)[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006349-92) [![Image 7: A black and white aerial photograph of an urban area by the sea with a water-filled, torus-shaped inlet.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2e/Carthage_view.jpg/250px-Carthage_view.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Carthage_view.jpg) A World War II [United States Army Air Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Air_Forces "United States Army Air Forces") aerial reconnaissance photograph of the remains of the naval base of the city of Carthage. The remains of the mercantile harbour are in the centre and those of the military harbour are bottom right. (North is to the bottom-right) The renewed close siege cut off landward entry to the city, but a tight seaward [interdiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interdiction "Interdiction") was all but impossible with the naval technology of the time. Frustrated at the amount of food being shipped into the city, Scipio built an immense [mole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mole_/(architecture/) "Mole (architecture)") to cut off access to the harbour via [blockade runners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blockade_runner "Blockade runner"). The Carthaginians responded by cutting a new channel from their harbour to the sea. They had built a new fleet and once the channel was complete, the Carthaginians sailed out, taking the Romans by surprise. In the ensuing [Battle of the Port of Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Port_of_Carthage "Battle of the Port of Carthage") the Carthaginians held their own, but when withdrawing at the end of the day many of their ships were trapped against the city's [sea wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_wall "Sea wall") and sunk or captured.[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006349%E2%80%93350-93)[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles20112-94) The Romans now attempted to advance against the Carthaginian defences in the harbour area, eventually gaining control of the [quay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quay "Quay"). Here, over several months, they constructed a brick structure as high as the city wall, which enabled up to 4,000 Romans to fire onto the Carthaginian [ramparts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rampart_/(fortification/) "Rampart (fortification)") from short range.[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015441-95)[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011346-96)[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006351-97) Once this feature was complete, Scipio detached a large force and led it against the Carthaginian field army at Nepheris. The Carthaginians, commanded by a Greek named [Diogenes](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diogenes_\(Third_Punic_War\)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Diogenes (Third Punic War) (page does not exist)"), had established a fortified camp for their winter quarters. Late in 147 BC Scipio directed an [assault on the camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Nepheris_/(147_BC/) "Battle of Nepheris (147 BC)") from several directions and overran it. Fleeing Carthaginians were pursued by Rome's mounted Numidian allies and few escaped. The town of Nepheris was then besieged and surrendered after three weeks. Most of the fortified positions still holding out in Carthage's hinterland now opened their gates.[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006351-97)[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBagnall1999317%E2%80%93318-98) Scipio's position as the Roman commander in Africa was extended for a year in 146 BC.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGoldsworthy2006347-99) In the spring he launched a full-scale assault from the harbour area, which successfully breached the walls.[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles20113-100) Over six days,[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles20114-101) the Romans systematically worked their way through the residential part of the city, killing everyone they encountered and setting the buildings behind them on fire.[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015441-95) On the last day Scipio agreed to accept prisoners, except for 900 Roman [deserters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deserter "Deserter") in Carthaginian service, who fought on from the Temple of [Eshmoun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eshmoun "Eshmoun") and burnt it down around themselves when all hope was gone.[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles20113%E2%80%934-102) At this point, Hasdrubal surrendered to Scipio on the promise of his life and freedom. Hasdrubal's wife, watching from a rampart, then blessed Scipio, cursed her husband and walked into the temple with her children to burn to death.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015442-103) 50,000 Carthaginian prisoners were sold into slavery.[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2002316-104) The notion that Roman forces then [sowed the city with salt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salting_the_earth "Salting the earth") is likely a 19th-century invention.[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTERidley1986144%E2%80%93145-105)[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTERipleyDana1858%E2%80%931863497-106)[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurcell1995140-107) Many of the religious items and cult-statues which Carthage had pillaged from Sicilian cities and temples over the centuries were returned with great ceremony.[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPurcell1995141%E2%80%93142-108) [![Image 8: a colour photograph of the remains today of part of ancient Carthage](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/The_Punic_Quarter%2C_Carthage.jpg/250px-The_Punic_Quarter%2C_Carthage.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Punic_Quarter,_Carthage.jpg) Ruins of the Punic Quarter, Carthage, in 2005 Rome was determined that the city of Carthage remain in ruins. The Senate despatched a ten-man commission and Scipio was ordered to carry out further demolitions. A curse was placed on anyone who might attempt to resettle the site in the future.[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011353-109) The former site of the city was confiscated as _[ager publicus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ager_publicus "Ager publicus")_, public land.[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015443-110) Scipio celebrated a [triumph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_triumph "Roman triumph") and took the _[agnomen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnomen "Agnomen")_ "Africanus", as had his adoptive grandfather.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015442-103)[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2002316-104) Hasdrubal's fate is not known, although he had surrendered on the promise of a retirement to an Italian estate.[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015442-103) The formerly Carthaginian territories were annexed by Rome and reconstituted to become the [Roman province of Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa_Province "Africa Province"), with Utica as its capital.[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015443-110)[\[109\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard2002310,_316-111) The province became a major source of grain and other food.[\[110\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMitchell2007345-112) The Punic cities which had stood by Carthage to the end were forfeit to Rome as _ager publicus_, or, as in the case of [Bizerte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bizerte "Bizerte"), were destroyed.[\[108\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015443-110)[\[107\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011353-109) Surviving cities were permitted to retain at least elements of their traditional system of government and culture.[\[111\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFantar2015455%E2%80%93456-113)[\[112\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPollard2015249-114) The Romans did not interfere in the locals' private lives and Punic culture, language and religion survived, and is known to modern scholars as "Neo-Punic civilization".[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTELe_Bohec2015443%E2%80%93445-115)[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFantar2015454-116) The [Punic language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_language "Punic language") continued to be spoken in north Africa until the 7th century AD.[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJouhaud196822-117)[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEScullard1955105-118) In 123 BC a [reformist faction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Populares "Populares") in Rome led by [Gaius Gracchus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaius_Gracchus "Gaius Gracchus") was eager to [redistribute land](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agrarian_law "Agrarian law"), including publicly held land. This included the site of Carthage and a controversial law was passed ordering the establishment of a new settlement there, called [Junonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonia_Junonia "Colonia Junonia"). [Conservatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optimates "Optimates") argued against the law and after its passage spread rumours that markers delimitating the new settlement had been dug up by wolves – a very poor omen. These rumours, and other political machinations, caused the plan to be scrapped.[\[note 3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-121)[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011354%E2%80%93355-122) In 111 BC legislation repeated the injunction against any resettlement.[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011448-123) A century after the war, [Julius Caesar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar "Julius Caesar") planned to rebuild Carthage as a Roman city, but little work was done. [Augustus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus "Augustus") revived the concept in 29 BC and brought the plan to completion. [Roman Carthage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Carthage "Roman Carthage") had become one of the main cities of Roman Africa by the time of the [Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire").[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTERichardson2015480%E2%80%93481-124)[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMiles2011363%E2%80%93364-125) Rome still exists as the capital of Italy; the ruins of Carthage lie 16 km (10 mi) east of modern [Tunis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunis "Tunis") on the North African coast; the [modern town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthage_/(municipality/) "Carthage (municipality)") is a suburb of Tunis and the site of the Tunisian [Presidential Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthage_Palace "Carthage Palace").[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Punic_War#cite_note-FOOTNOTEUNESCO2020-25) A symbolic peace treaty was signed by [Ugo Vetere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ugo_Vetere "Ugo Vetere") and [Chedli Klibi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chedli_Klibi "Chedli Klibi"), the mayors of Rome and modern Carthage, respectively, on 5 February 1985; 17.title: VGhlIEJhdHRsZSBvZiBaYW1hIOKAkyAyMDIgQi5DLiDigJMgQmF0dGxlcyBhbmQgQm9vayBSZXZpZXdz
17.content:
The Battle of Zama, fought in 202 B.C., was the culminating battle of the Second Punic War between Carthage and Rome. The short story of the battle is that a Roman army under Scipio met and destroyed the Carthaginian Army under Hannibal. The defeat forced the Carthaginian Senate to sue for peace and ended the war.

What makes the battle interesting from my perspective is that the Roman army was outnumbered and on the offensive and still won. This is not typically what happens in warfare, especially in warfare in antiquity when numbers made a rather large difference in melee combat. One thing that makes Zama stand out is the sheer number of War Elephants (80 or so) Hannibal had and made use of during the battle, and how ineffective they were. Generally war elephants are depicted in popular literature as being fearsome things akin to modern tanks. All the battles I can think of off the top of my head in which they were used, they tend to be pretty ineffective in actual use. I tend to think they were used more for psychological reasons, to spread terror, than because they had any real tactical effectiveness.

The Carthaginian army numbered about 55,000 while the Romans had about 40,000.   Of decisive importance was that the Romans had numerical superiority in cavalry.   Before the battle began the opposing armies drew up opposite each other on a plain outside the ancient city of Zama, hence the name of the battle. Both armies had three lines of infantry with cavalry on the wings. The Carthaginians had mercenaries in the first line, citizen militia in the second, and Hannibal’s Italian veterans formed his third line. Scipio arrayed his troops according to Roman doctrine with the Hastati, Principes, and Triarii forming the first through third lines respectively with his auxiliary cavalry on his flanks. The below diagram from Wikipedia is a good stylized representation of the deployment of the armies. In addition, Hannibal put his war elephants out front completely hoping to stampede them through the Roman formation and break it up before the main battle was joined.  
[![Image 1: Battle of Zama - Army Deployments](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/66/Mohammad_adil_rais-battle_of_zama-1.PNG)](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/66/Mohammad_adil_rais-battle_of_zama-1.PNG)

The course of the battle was pretty straightforward. Hannibal attempted to charge is elephants through the Roman ranks, Scipio defeated this maneuver by the simply expedient of opening gaps in his army through which the elephants charged. The disadvantage of elephants is that they were only controllable if they charged in a straight line. After the elephants passed through the Roman army reformed and the Roman cavalry attacked and defeated the Carthaginian Cavalry on the flanks driving them from the field and pursuing them. As the cavalry battle occurred the Roman infantry attacked and defeated the first and second lines of Hannibal’s army but were stopped by the veterans of the Carthaginian third line. The battle remained a virtual stalemate for a few hours until the Roman cavalry returned and attacked the Carthaginians on their flanks. The battle rapidly devolved into a rout and Hannibal was forced to flee the field.

Total casualties on both sides were somewhere in the neighborhood of 40-50,000 with the vast majority of those being Carthaginian.   The casualty ratio was about 100-1 if prisoners are included, and they should be because anyone no longer capable of fighting is essentially a killed whether they are killed, wounded, or captured.   That ratio seems incredible but it is actually not when you consider the nature of ancient melee warfare.   Hanson, goes into this in great detail in _[The Western Way of War: Infantry Battle in Classical Greece](http://www./gp/product/0520260090/ref=as_li_tf_tl?ie=UTF8&tag=patsmilhisblo-20&linkCode=as2&camp=1789&creative=9325&creativeASIN=0520260090)![Image 2](https://www.assoc-/e/ir?t=patsmilhisblo-20&l=as2&o=1&a=0520260090)_. He makes the valid and logical point that it was natural that casualty counts would be lopsided as the victors cut down their opponents as they attempted to flee. Man does not naturally act merciful in battle, that comes from discipline and civilization.

From a tactical standpoint there is really nothing to be learned from the battle except that the Carthaginians wasted their money on mercenaries, who are only loyal so long as they feel the risk is worth the pay in the first place and that citizen militias had no business standing in line of battle against an experienced foe.   It was significant that only the Italian veterans in Hannibal’s army managed to hold firm.   It is also significant that even they could not maneuver quickly enough to defend against the flank threat when the Roman cavalry was done treating the Carthaginian cavalry like step-children.   The Carthaginians tended to form up in blocks that were much more close than the Romans which robbed them of some articulation.   Hannibal also probably hoped or expected too much of his war elephants, which were blunt instruments at best and useless when faced with the simple counter that Scipio devised. The major result of the battle was that Carthage was destroyed as a military and forced to sue for peace. In granting that peace the Romans exacted such a price as to ensure that Carthage could not become a military power and rival in the future.

20.title: QmF0dGxlIG9mIFphbWEgKHN0cmF0ZWd5ICYgdGFjdGljcyk=
20.content:
The Battle of Zama took place between the Romans, accompanied by the Numidian cavalry, and the Carthaginians with Scipio as the commander of the Roman forces and Hannibal as the leader of the Carthaginian troops. This confrontation between the Romans and Carthaginians marked the end of the Second Punic War, which had been occurring for many years. It took place on the plains of Zama Regia in the fall of 202 BC.

[![Image 1](https://legioilynx.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/02/trajans-column-romans-marching-and-making-camp2.jpg?w=300&h=200)](https://legioilynx.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/02/trajans-column-romans-marching-and-making-camp2.jpg)

Romans marching and making camp- Use by permission. Copyright Peter Rockwell

Previous to the battle, the Romans utilized diverse mental tactics to psych out their opponents and prove dominance. As they won each battle, the Romans intentionally mangled the bodies of their fallen foes to demonstrate their ruthlessness and display an example of what the next enemy could expect to occur (75 Zhmodikov). They also made a camp each night, not only out of necessity, but to show their superiority as a force. The Romans had enough sophistication to build an entire village in one night and have it taken down by morning in order to be ready to march.

Both the Romans and the Carthaginians used similar battle layouts, but each tweaked their tactics with personal techniques. Hannibal utilized a traditional phalanx line of troops consisting of three rows with a cavalry on the wings, but also had war elephants as a unique weapon of war. Scipio, on the other hand, used a maniple formation of troops consisting of three lines with a large cavalry on the wings. The first two lines consisted of lighter infantry men known as the Hastati and the Principes (67 Zhmodikov). The last row consisted of heavy infantry men called Triarii; they were only used as back-up so they rarely saw much fighting. Although the Romans had fewer infantry troops, they made up for it in number and skill of cavalry troops. This became an important factor in the outcome of the battle; the terrain highly favored cavalry troops.

As the battle commenced, Hannibal unleashed his elephants on the Roman lines, which Scipio had anticipated. Scipio then used the maniple formation in order to allow his troops to move apart and permit the elephants to run right past them; it worked. In addition, the Romans blew loud horns as the elephants approached in an attempt to scatter them from their charge (Scullard 1930). As the lines clashed, they met in deadlock and each side repeatedly gained and lost ground with their opponent. It wasn’t until the superior Roman cavalry joined the battle, victorious over the Carthaginian cavalry, that the Romans were able to surround the Carthaginians and slaughter them. Roughly 20,000 Carthaginians were killed and another 20,000 were taken prisoner, while only 5,000 Romans were slain during the battle of Zama.

[http://www.stoa.org/trajan/buildtrajanpage.cgi?261](http://www.stoa.org/trajan/buildtrajanpage.cgi?261)

15.title: QmF0dGxlIG9mIFphbWEgfCBCaW9ncmFwaHkgJiBGYWN0cw==
15.content:
Top Questions

*   What was the Battle of Zama?
    
*   Which countries fought in the Battle of Zama?
    
*   Who were the main leaders during the Battle of Zama?
    
*   Why was the Battle of Zama important in Roman and Carthaginian history?
    
*   How did Roman and Carthaginian tactics differ at Zama?
    
*   What were the effects of the Battle of Zama on the people of Rome and Carthage?
    

**Battle of Zama**, (202 bce), victory of the Romans led by [Scipio Africanus the Elder](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Scipio-Africanus) over the Carthaginians commanded by [Hannibal](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hannibal-Carthaginian-general-247-183-BCE). The last and [decisive](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/decisive) battle of the [Second Punic War](https://www.britannica.com/event/Second-Punic-War), it effectively ended both Hannibal’s command of Carthaginian forces and also [Carthage](https://www.britannica.com/place/Carthage-ancient-city-Tunisia)’s chances to significantly oppose [Rome](https://www.britannica.com/place/ancient-Rome). The battle took place at a site identified by the Roman historian [Livy](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Livy) as Naraggara (now Sāqiyat Sīdī Yūsuf, [Tunisia](https://www.britannica.com/place/Tunisia)). The name Zama was given to the site (which modern historians have never precisely identified) by the Roman historian [Cornelius Nepos](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Cornelius-Nepos) about 150 years after the battle.

By the year 203 [Carthage](https://www.britannica.com/place/Carthage-ancient-city-Tunisia) was in great danger of attack from the forces of the Roman general [Publius Cornelius Scipio](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Publius-Cornelius-Scipio), who had invaded Africa and had won an important battle barely 20 miles (32 km) west of Carthage itself. The Carthaginian generals Hannibal and his brother [Mago](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Mago-Carthaginian-general) were accordingly recalled from their campaigns in Italy. Hannibal returned to Africa with his 12,000-man veteran army and soon gathered a total of 37,000 troops with which to defend the approaches to Carthage. Mago, who had [sustained](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/sustained) battle wounds during a losing engagement in [Liguria](https://www.britannica.com/place/Liguria) (near [Genoa](https://www.britannica.com/place/Genoa-Italy)), died at sea during the crossing.

Scipio, for his part, marched up the Bagradas ([Majardah](https://www.britannica.com/place/Wadi-Majardah)) River toward Carthage, seeking a decisive battle with the Carthaginians. Some of Scipio’s Roman forces were reinvigorated veterans from [Cannae](https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Cannae) who sought redemption from that disgraceful defeat. Once his allies had arrived, Scipio had about the same number of troops as Hannibal (around 40,000 men), but his 6,100 cavalrymen, led by the [Numidian](https://www.britannica.com/place/Numidia) ruler [Masinissa](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Masinissa) and the Roman general [Gaius Laelius](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Gaius-Laelius), were superior to the Carthaginian cavalry in both training and quantity. Because Hannibal could not transport the majority of his horses from Italy, he was forced to [slaughter](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/slaughter) them to keep them from falling into Roman hands. Thus, he could field only about 4,000 [cavalry](https://www.britannica.com/topic/cavalry), the bulk of them from a minor [Numidian](https://www.britannica.com/place/Numidia) ally named Tychaeus.

Hannibal arrived too late to prevent Masinissa from joining up with Scipio, leaving Scipio in a position to choose the battle site. That was a reversal of the situation in Italy, where Hannibal had held the advantage in cavalry and had typically chosen the ground. In addition to utilizing 80 war [elephants](https://www.britannica.com/animal/elephant-mammal) that were not fully trained, Hannibal was also compelled to rely mostly upon an army of Carthaginian recruits that lacked much battle experience. Of his three battle lines, only his seasoned veterans from Italy (between 12,000 to 15,000 men) were accustomed to fighting Romans; they were positioned at the rear of his formation.

Before the battle, Hannibal and Scipio met personally, possibly because Hannibal, perceiving that battle conditions did not favour him, hoped to negotiate a generous settlement. Scipio may have been curious to meet Hannibal, but he refused the proposed terms, stating that Carthage had broken the truce and would have to face the [consequences](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/consequences). According to Livy, Hannibal told Scipio, “What I was years ago at [Trasimene](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Battle-of-Trasimene) and [Cannae](https://www.britannica.com/event/Battle-of-Cannae), you are today.” Scipio is said to have replied with a message for Carthage: “Prepare to fight because evidently you have found peace intolerable.” The next day was set for battle.

As the two armies approached each other, the Carthaginians unloosed their 80 elephants into the ranks of the Roman [infantry](https://www.britannica.com/topic/infantry), but the great beasts were soon dispersed and their threat neutralized. The failure of the elephant charge can likely be explained by a trio of factors, with the first two being well documented and most important. First, the elephants were not well trained. Second—and perhaps even more vital to the outcome—Scipio had arranged his forces in maniples (small, flexible infantry units) with broad alleys between them. He had trained his men to move to the side when the elephants charged, locking their shields and facing the alleys as the elephants passed by. That caused the elephants to run unimpeded through the lines with little, if any, engagement. Third, the loud shouts and blaring trumpets of the Romans may have disconcerted the elephants, some of which swerved to the side early in the battle and instead attacked their own infantry, causing [chaos](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/chaos) on the front line of Hannibal’s recruits.

Scipio’s cavalry then charged the opposing Carthaginian cavalry on the wings; the latter fled and were pursued by Masinissa’s forces. The Roman infantry legions then advanced and attacked Hannibal’s infantry, which consisted of three consecutive lines of defense. The Romans crushed the soldiers of the first line and then those of the second. However, by that time the legionnaires had become nearly exhausted—and they had yet to close with the third line, which consisted of Hannibal’s veterans from his Italian campaign (i.e., his best troops). At that crucial juncture, Masinissa’s Numidian cavalry returned from their [rout](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/rout) of the enemy cavalry and attacked the rear of the Carthaginian infantry, who were soon crushed between the combined Roman infantry and the cavalry assault. Some 20,000 Carthaginians died in the battle, and perhaps 20,000 were captured, while the Romans lost about 1,500 dead. The Greek historian [Polybius](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Polybius) states that Hannibal had done all that he could as a general in battle, especially considering the advantage held by his opponent. That Hannibal was fighting from a position of weakness does not in any way diminish Scipio’s victory for Rome, however. With the defeat of Carthage and Hannibal, it is likely that Zama awakened in Rome a vision of a larger future for itself in the [Mediterranean](https://www.britannica.com/place/Mediterranean-Sea).

The Battle of Zama left Carthage helpless, and the city accepted Scipio’s peace terms whereby it [ceded](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/ceded) Spain to Rome, surrendered most of its warships, and began paying a 50-year indemnity to Rome. Scipio was awarded the surname Africanus in tribute of his victory. Hannibal escaped from the battle and went to his estates in the east near [Hadrumetum](https://www.britannica.com/place/Hadrumetum) for some time before he returned to Carthage. For the first time in decades, Hannibal was without a military command, and never again did he lead Carthaginians into battle. The indemnity Rome set as payment from Carthage was 10,000 silver talents, more than three times the size of the indemnity demanded at the conclusion of the [First Punic War](https://www.britannica.com/event/First-Punic-War). Although the Carthaginians had to publicly burn at least 100 ships, Scipio did not [impose](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/impose) harsh terms on Hannibal himself, and Hannibal was soon elected as suffete (civil magistrate) by popular vote to help administer a defeated Carthage.

Conclusively ending the Second Punic War with a decisive Roman victory, the Battle of Zama must be considered one of the most important battles in ancient history. Having staged a successful invasion of Africa and having vanquished its canniest and most-implacable foe, Rome began its vision of a Mediterranean empire.

[Patrick Hunt](https://www.britannica.com/contributor/Patrick-Hunt/9539405)

Such was Scipio’s impact upon the Romans that even during his lifetime, [legends](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/legends) began to cluster around him; he was regarded as favoured by Fortune or even divinely inspired. Many believed not only that he had received a promise of help from Neptune in a dream on the night before his assault on [Carthago Nova](https://www.britannica.com/place/Cartagena-Spain) but also that he had a close connection with [Jupiter](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Jupiter-Roman-god). He used to visit Jupiter’s temple on the Capitol at night to commune with the god, and later the story circulated that he was even a son of the god, who supposedly had appeared in his mother’s bed in the form of a snake.

[Polybius](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Polybius) thought that this popular view of Scipio was mistaken and argued that Scipio always acted only as the result of reasoned foresight and worked on men’s superstitions in a calculating manner. But Polybius himself was a rationalist and probably underestimated a streak of religious confidence, if not mysticism, in Scipio’s character that impressed so many of his contemporaries with its magnanimity and generosity. Thus, although Polybius had an intense admiration for Scipio, whom he called “almost the most famous man of all time,” the existence of the [legend](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/legend), a unique phenomenon in [Rome’s](https://www.britannica.com/place/Rome) [history](https://www.britannica.com/topic/history), may indicate that Polybius’s portrait is too one-sided.

Significance and influence
--------------------------

A man of wide sympathies, [cultured](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/cultured) and [magnanimous](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/magnanimous), Scipio easily won the friendship of such men as [Philip V](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Philip-V-king-of-Macedonia), king of Macedonia, and the native princes of Spain and Africa while he secured the devotion of his own troops. Though he was essentially a man of good planning and practical action, he may also have been something of a mystic in whom [contemporary legend](https://www.britannica.com/topic/urban-legend), at any rate, saw a favourite of Jupiter as well as a spiritual descendant of [Alexander the Great](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Alexander-the-Great). Scipio was one of the greatest soldiers of the ancient world; by his tactical reforms and strategic insight, he created a new army that defeated even [Hannibal](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Hannibal-Carthaginian-general-247-183-BCE) and asserted Rome’s supremacy in Spain, Africa, and the Hellenistic East. He had a great appreciation of [Greek](https://www.britannica.com/place/ancient-Greece) [culture](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/culture) and enjoyed relaxing in the [congenial](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/congenial) atmosphere of the Greek cities of Sicily, conduct that provoked the anger of old-fashioned Romans such as Cato. Indeed, he was outstanding among those Roman nobles of the day who welcomed the civilizing influences of Greek culture that were beginning to permeate Roman society. His Greek sympathies led him to champion Rome’s mission in the world as protector of Greek culture; he preferred to establish Roman protection rather than direct conquest and annexation. For 10 years (210–201) he commanded a devoted army at the people’s wish. His position might seem almost kingly; he had been hailed as king by Spanish tribes, and he may have been the first Roman [general](https://www.britannica.com/topic/general) to be acclaimed as imperator (emperor) by his troops. But, though he was convinced of his own powers, he offered no challenge to the dominance of the Roman nobility ensconced in the Senate except by normal political methods (in which he showed no outstanding ability). Reaction against his generous foreign policy—with possible [clemency](https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/clemency) to Hannibal after Zama—and against his encouragement of Greek culture in Roman life led to his downfall amid personal and political rivalries. His career, however, had shown that Rome’s destiny was to be a Mediterranean, not merely an Italian, power.

Scipio’s influence outlived the Roman world. Great interest was shown in his life during the early [Renaissance](https://www.britannica.com/event/Renaissance), and it helped the early [humanists](https://www.britannica.com/topic/humanism) to build a bridge between the classical world and Christendom. He became an idealized perfect hero who was seen to have served the ends of Providence. [Petrarch](https://www.britannica.com/biography/Petrarch) glorified him in a Latin epic, the _[Africa](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Africa-by-Petrarch)_, which secured his own coronation as [poet laureate](https://www.britannica.com/art/poet-laureate) in 1341 on the Capitol, where, some 1,500 years earlier, the historical Scipio used to [commune](https://www.britannica.com/dictionary/commune) in the temple of Jupiter.

[Howard Hayes Scullard](https://www.britannica.com/contributor/Howard-Hayes-Scullard/2653) [Patrick Hunt](https://www.britannica.com/contributor/Patrick-Hunt/9539405) [The Editors of Encyclopaedia Britannica](https://www.britannica.com/editor/The-Editors-of-Encyclopaedia-Britannica/4419)
