Introduction
------------

The Battle of Zama, fought in 202 BC, stands as one of the most significant military engagements of the ancient world. This climactic confrontation between the [Roman Republic](https://www.unrv.com/roman-republic.php) and Carthage effectively ended the Second Punic War, a 17-year struggle that had seen the fortunes of both empires rise and fall dramatically.

Commanded by [Publius Cornelius Scipio](https://www.unrv.com/military/roman-generals/scipio-africanus.php) - later honored with the agnomen of _Africanus_ in recognition of his military success in Carthage and [North Africa](https://www.unrv.com/provinces/africa.php) - for Rome, and the legendary Hannibal Barca for Carthage, the battle was not just a clash of armies but a meeting of two of history's greatest military strategists.

Their tactics and decisions at Zama have been studied by military leaders and historians for centuries, offering timeless lessons on warfare, leadership, and strategy.

![Image 1: A map of the western Mediterranean Sea in 218 BC, showing Roman and Carthaginian territory at the start of the Second Punic War](https://www.unrv.com/images/1200width/cc/second-punic-war.jpg)

[Grandiosederivative work: Augusta 89](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Map_of_Rome_and_Carthage_at_the_start_of_the_Second_Punic_War_2.svg), [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0), via Wikimedia Commons

**A map of the western Mediterranean Sea in 218 BC, showing Roman and Carthaginian territory at the start of the Second Punic War**

Background
----------

  

### The Second Punic War

[The Second Punic War (218–201 BC)](https://www.unrv.com/empire/second-punic-war.php) was the second in a trilogy of conflicts between Rome and Carthage, two burgeoning powers competing for dominance over the Mediterranean. The war was rooted in the rivalry that followed the [First Punic War](https://www.unrv.com/empire/first-punic-war.php), particularly over control of strategic territories like [Sicily](https://www.unrv.com/provinces/sicilia.php) and the Iberian Peninsula.

Carthage, under the Barcid family, sought to expand its influence in Iberia to compensate for losses elsewhere, while Rome was determined to curtail Carthaginian power.

  

### Causes of the War

The immediate cause of the war was the siege of Saguntum, a city in Iberia allied with Rome but located south of the Ebro River which, according to a previous treaty, was the boundary of Carthaginian influence.

Hannibal's attack on Saguntum in 219 BC was seen by Rome as a breach of the treaty, prompting declarations of war. However, underlying this was a deeper animosity and competition for supremacy.

  

### Hannibal's Campaign in Italy

Hannibal's invasion of [Italy](https://www.unrv.com/provinces/italia.php) is renowned for its audacity and strategic brilliance. Defying conventional logistics, he led an army - including war elephants - across the Pyrenees, through [Gaul](https://www.unrv.com/provinces/gallia.php), and over the snow-covered Alps, facing treacherous terrain and hostile tribes along the way.

His surprise arrival in Italy caught the Romans off-guard, leading to a series of stunning victories at the battles of Trebia, Lake Trasimene and, most notably, Cannae in 216 BC, where he annihilated a much larger Roman force using a double envelopment tactic.

Despite these victories, Hannibal faced challenges. He lacked sufficient reinforcements and [siege equipment](https://www.unrv.com/military/roman-siegecraft.php) to attack Rome directly. His strategy shifted to weakening Rome by encouraging its allies to defect, hoping to erode the Roman confederation from within.

While some southern Italian cities did switch sides, Rome's core allies remained loyal, and [the Roman Senate](https://www.unrv.com/empire/the-senate.php) adopted a strategy of attrition, avoiding direct confrontations and focusing on smaller engagements and disrupting Carthaginian supply lines.

  

### Scipio Africanus and His Rise

Publius Cornelius Scipio emerged as Rome's foremost military leader during this critical period. After surviving Cannae, where many of Rome's commanders perished, Scipio was appointed to command Roman forces in [Hispania](https://www.unrv.com/provinces/hispania.php) at a young age. Demonstrating exceptional leadership, he captured New Carthage (Cartagena) in 209 BC, securing a vital base and cutting off Carthaginian resources from Iberia.

Scipio's success in Spain not only deprived Carthage of silver mines and manpower, but also bolstered his reputation. He recognized that to defeat Carthage, Rome needed to shift the war's theater. Advocating for an invasion of North Africa, he believed that threatening Carthage directly would force Hannibal to defend his homeland, leveling the playing field.

His proposal was initially met with skepticism but eventually gained support, setting the stage for the decisive confrontation at Zama.

  

Prelude to Battle
-----------------

  

### Scipio's Invasion of North Africa

In 204 BC, Scipio launched his daring invasion of North Africa. Landing near Utica, he forged alliances with local Numidian rulers, most notably Masinissa, who commanded a formidable cavalry force. Masinissa's support was crucial; his knowledge of the terrain and mobile cavalry units provided Scipio with a significant tactical advantage.

Scipio's campaign in Africa was methodical. He won several engagements against Carthaginian forces and their Numidian allies, including a notable victory at the Battle of the Great Plains. These successes undermined Carthaginian confidence and pressured the city-state into recalling Hannibal from Italy as their situation grew increasingly dire.

  

### Negotiations Between Rome and Carthage

Facing invasion, Carthage initiated peace negotiations. The initial terms were harsh but manageable, requiring Carthage to surrender its fleet and Iberian territories.

However, during the armistice, Carthaginian forces attacked a Roman supply fleet, which Rome interpreted as a breach of faith. This incident reignited hostilities and hardened Roman resolve, leading both sides to prepare for a final showdown.

  

### Hannibal's Return to Africa

After 16 years in Italy, Hannibal was summoned back to defend Carthage. Returning with his seasoned veterans, he faced the daunting task of assembling a new army. The Carthaginian forces were a mix of experienced troops and hastily recruited soldiers, including mercenaries and recently levied citizens.

Despite these challenges, Hannibal's presence rejuvenated Carthaginian morale. He sought to leverage his tactical expertise to overcome Scipio's forces, aware that the fate of Carthage hung in the balance.

  

### Pre-Battle Maneuvers

In the days leading up to the battle, both commanders engaged in strategic positioning. Hannibal attempted to negotiate with Scipio, proposing peace terms that would restore the status quo. Scipio, confident in his army's strength, declined, insisting on unconditional surrender.

Hannibal studied the Roman formations and adjusted his tactics accordingly. He understood that Scipio had countered the elephants effectively in previous battles and sought ways to exploit any weaknesses.

Both armies made camp near Zama Regia, an area suitable for the large-scale engagement that was about to unfold.

  

The Armies
----------

  

### Composition of Roman Forces

Scipio's army was a well-balanced force of approximately 30,000 infantry and 6,000 [cavalry](https://www.unrv.com/military/roman-cavalry.php). The infantry comprised [Republican legionaries](https://www.unrv.com/military/roman-republican-legion.php) and allied Italian troops, organized into _maniples_ - a flexible formation allowing for maneuverability. The Roman soldiers were battle-hardened and [disciplined](https://www.unrv.com/military/discipline.php), trained to operate cohesively under Scipio's command.

The cavalry, a crucial component of Scipio's strategy, included about 4,000 Numidian horsemen under Masinissa and 2,000 Roman and Italian cavalry led by Gaius Laelius. The Numidian cavalry was especially renowned for its speed and agility, capable of executing swift flanking movements and harassing enemy units.

  

### Composition of Carthaginian Forces

Hannibal's forces numbered around 36,000 infantry and 4,000 cavalry, supplemented by 80 war elephants. The infantry was a diverse mix:

*   **First Line**: Mercenaries from Gaul, Liguria, and the Balearic Islands. They were experienced but lacking cohesion.
*   **Second Line**: Carthaginian citizens and Libyan levies, motivated to defend their homeland.
*   **Third Line**: Hannibal's veteran troops from Italy, highly disciplined and loyal.

The cavalry was composed of Numidian units loyal to Carthage and other allied horsemen. The war elephants, a traditional Carthaginian asset, were intended to disrupt Roman formations and sow panic.

  

Tactics and Strategies
----------------------

  

### Scipio's Strategy

Anticipating Hannibal's use of war elephants, Scipio devised specific countermeasures to neutralize this threat.

He arranged his manipular formations with wide lanes between the units, creating clear paths that would allow the elephants to pass through without causing significant damage to his infantry lines. Soldiers were instructed to create loud noises and visual disturbances - such as shouting, blowing trumpets, and waving their weapons - to frighten and confuse the elephants.

This tactic aimed to cause the elephants to panic, veer off course, or even turn back against their own troops.

Scipio also planned to leverage his superior cavalry forces. He intended for his cavalry, particularly the Numidian horsemen under Masinissa, to quickly engage and defeat the Carthaginian cavalry. By doing so, they could then circle back to attack the enemy infantry from the rear, creating a pincer movement that would disrupt Hannibal's formations and morale.

In terms of infantry deployment, Scipio organized his troops into the traditional Roman _triplex acies_, consisting of three lines: the _hastati_ in the front, the _principes_ in the middle, and the _triarii_ at the rear.

This arrangement provided both depth and flexibility, allowing the Roman army to absorb initial assaults and reinforce or replace front-line units as necessary. The formation also enhanced communication and command control, enabling Scipio to quickly adapt to the unfolding dynamics of the battle.

  

### Hannibal's Strategy

Hannibal aimed to break the disciplined Roman lines by utilizing his war elephants as a shock force. He planned for the elephants to charge directly at the Roman infantry, intending to create gaps and sow chaos within their ranks. These breaches would then be exploited by his following infantry units, allowing them to penetrate and dismantle the Roman formations.

For his infantry assault, Hannibal deployed his less reliable troops - comprising mercenaries and newly recruited soldiers - in the front lines. His strategy was to have these forces engage the Romans first, wearing them down and causing attrition before his seasoned veterans entered the fight. By holding his most experienced soldiers in reserve, Hannibal hoped they would deliver a decisive blow once the enemy was fatigued and their formations disrupted.

Acknowledging the inferiority of his cavalry compared to the Roman and Numidian horsemen, Hannibal intended to engage them as long as possible to prevent them from influencing the main infantry battle. By delaying the Roman cavalry, he aimed to protect his infantry's flanks and rear, reducing the risk of encirclement.

Hannibal understood that maintaining the cohesion of his infantry was crucial, and keeping the enemy cavalry occupied was essential to this aspect of his strategy.

  

The Battle
----------

  

### Deployment and Initial Moves

At dawn, both armies arrayed themselves on the plains near Zama. The terrain was open, favoring maneuverability for both infantry and cavalry. Scipio's manipular formations stood ready, with the cavalry units positioned on the flanks. Hannibal's forces mirrored this, with his elephants at the forefront.

As the armies prepared for battle, both commanders understood the gravity of the confrontation; the outcome would significantly impact the future of Rome and Carthage.

  

### Use of War Elephants

The battle commenced with Hannibal ordering the elephant charge. The massive beasts moved forward, their handlers urging them into a thunderous advance. Scipio's preparations paid off; Roman soldiers blew trumpets and shouted, creating a cacophony that unsettled the elephants. Some panicked and veered away, running into the Carthaginian left-wing cavalry and causing disorder.

Others charged through the gaps in the Roman lines, where they were met with volleys of [javelins](https://www.unrv.com/military/pilum.php) and attacks by skirmishers. The disciplined Roman troops allowed the elephants to pass, minimizing casualties and preventing disruption of their formations.

  

### Cavalry Engagement

Simultaneously, the cavalry units engaged on the flanks. Masinissa's Numidian cavalry clashed with their Carthaginian counterparts, leveraging their superior tactics and familiarity with the enemy. On the opposite flank, Laelius led the Roman and Italian cavalry against the Carthaginian horsemen.

The Roman-allied cavalry gained the upper hand, eventually driving the Carthaginian cavalry from the field.

  

### Infantry Clash: First Phase

With the elephants neutralized and the cavalry battle temporarily resolved, the infantry engagement began in earnest.

Hannibal's first line of mercenaries advanced, meeting the Roman _hastati_ (front-line soldiers). The mercenaries fought fiercely, motivated by pay and personal valor. However, lacking the cohesion and discipline of the Romans, they struggled to make significant headway.

As the Romans pushed forward, the mercenaries began to fall back, colliding with Hannibal's second line of Carthaginian citizens. This retreat caused confusion and resentment; the Carthaginian soldiers accused the mercenaries of cowardice, while the mercenaries felt betrayed by the lack of support.

  

### Infantry Clash: Second Phase

The disarray in Hannibal's front lines presented an opportunity for Scipio. He ordered a temporary halt to reorganize his forces, before advancing on the combined Carthaginian first and second lines. The renewed Roman assault capitalized on the enemy's confusion. Hannibal's attempts to rally his troops were only partially successful.

Despite the turmoil, the Carthaginian veterans remained steadfast. As the Romans approached, Hannibal committed his third line. These seasoned soldiers from the Italian campaigns were well-trained and experienced, matching the Romans in discipline and skill.

  

### The Decisive Moment

The battle reached its climax as the Roman and Carthaginian veterans engaged. The fighting was intense and evenly matched, with neither side gaining a clear advantage. Scipio recognized that without intervention, the battle could turn into a costly stalemate.

At this critical juncture, the Roman and Numidian cavalry, having chased the Carthaginian horsemen off the field, returned. Charging into the rear of Hannibal's forces, they executed a classic pincer movement. This attack sowed panic among the Carthaginians, who found themselves surrounded.

Hannibal's troops began to falter under the pressure of attacks from both front and rear. The encirclement was reminiscent of Hannibal's own tactics at Cannae, but this time the Romans were the executors. Recognizing defeat, some Carthaginian soldiers attempted to flee, while others fought desperately to the end.

  

Aftermath
---------

  

### Casualties and Losses

The battle resulted in heavy losses for Carthage. Estimates suggest that up to 20,000 Carthaginian soldiers were killed, with an additional 15,000 captured. Roman casualties were significantly lower, though still substantial, reflecting the ferocity of the fighting.

  

### Consequences for Carthage

The defeat at Zama was catastrophic for Carthage. With its army decimated and resources depleted, Carthage was defenseless against Roman demands. The city sued for peace, accepting terms that effectively ended its status as a major power.

The psychological impact was profound. Carthage, once Rome's equal, was humbled. The loss also marked the end of Hannibal's military career in Carthage; he later fled into exile to avoid Roman retribution, spending his remaining years advising other kingdoms, and ultimately taking his own life to avoid capture.

  

### Rise of Rome as a Superpower

Rome emerged from the Second Punic War as the unchallenged master of the Western Mediterranean. The victory at Zama allowed Rome to consolidate its holdings and pursue further expansion into new [provinces and territories](https://www.unrv.com/provinces/provincetable.php). The war had tested Rome's [political](https://www.unrv.com/government.php) and [military](https://www.unrv.com/military.php) institutions, which proved resilient and adaptable.

The experience gained during the war, particularly in logistics and long-term campaigning, would serve Rome well in future conflicts. The Republic began to transition into an Imperial entity, with ambitions extending beyond Italy and into Greece, North Africa, and the Near East.

  

### Terms of the Peace Treaty

The Treaty of Zama imposed harsh conditions on Carthage:

*   **Territorial Losses**: Carthage ceded all territories outside the immediate vicinity of the city, including Iberia and Mediterranean islands.
  
*   **Military Restrictions**: The Carthaginian navy was limited to ten ships, effectively ending its maritime power.
  
*   **Financial Indemnity**: Carthage agreed to pay a war indemnity of 10,000 talents of silver over 50 years, a crippling economic burden.
  
*   **Political Limitations**: Carthage was prohibited from waging war on others without Roman permission, reducing it to a client state.

These terms ensured that Carthage could not recover militarily or economically, thereby securing Roman dominance.

  

Legacy
------

  

### Impact on Future Roman Military Tactics

As alluded to above, the Battle of Zama had a lasting influence on Roman military doctrine going forward. Scipio's emphasis on adaptability, combined arms tactics, and psychological warfare became staples of Roman strategy. The successful integration of allied forces, such as the Numidian cavalry, demonstrated the value of incorporating diverse units.

Roman commanders learned the importance of intelligence, logistics, and the strategic use of diplomacy. The experience gained would inform military training and campaigns for generations, contributing to Rome's ability to maintain and expand [its empire](https://www.unrv.com/empire.php).

  

### Hannibal's Legacy

Hannibal's legacy transcends his defeat. He is remembered as one of history's greatest military commanders, renowned for his tactical genius and daring strategies. His campaigns in Italy showcased the potential of maneuver warfare, the element of surprise, and the effective use of diverse troops.

Hannibal's crossing of the Alps became legendary, symbolizing determination against overwhelming odds. His teachings influenced not only his contemporaries, but also future military leaders like Napoleon Bonaparte (1769–1821) and Carl von Clausewitz (1780–1831), a Prussian general and military theorist, who studied his tactics extensively.

  

Historiographical Perspectives
------------------------------

  

### Ancient Historians and Their Accounts

The primary sources of information about the Battle of Zama come from the works of ancient historians such as Polybius and Livy. Their detailed narratives have been instrumental in shaping the modern understanding of this pivotal event, despite the limitations and biases inherent in their accounts.

[Polybius](https://www.unrv.com/culture/polybius.php), a Greek historian and statesman who lived from around 208 to 125 BC, provides one of the most reliable accounts of [the Punic Wars](https://www.unrv.com/empire/punic-wars-and-expansion.php) in his work, _The Histories_. As a result of becoming closely associated with many influential Roman families, he had access to Roman records and firsthand testimonies, which he utilized to construct a comprehensive history.

Polybius is noted for his rigorous approach to historiography, emphasizing eyewitness testimony and critical analysis, while also striving for objectivity. His proximity to the events - writing within a few decades of the battle - and his connections with prominent Roman families, including the Scipios, lent credibility to his work.

In his account, Polybius highlights the exceptional leadership of both Scipio and Hannibal. He admires Scipio's strategic foresight, diplomatic skills, and ability to inspire his troops. Similarly, he acknowledges Hannibal's tactical genius, resilience, and innovative use of diverse forces.

Polybius provides detailed descriptions of the military tactics employed at Zama, explaining Scipio's innovative formation to counter the elephants and his effective use of the Numidian cavalry. He delves into Hannibal's strategic deployment of his infantry and the challenges he faced with his heterogeneous army.

Polybius often reflects on the moral dimensions of warfare, discussing the virtues and vices of the commanders, the ethical implications of their decisions, and the role of fate and fortune in human affairs. His analysis offers insights into the values and philosophical perspectives of the period.

[Titus Livius, known as Livy](https://www.unrv.com/culture/livy.php), was a Roman historian who lived from 59 BC to 17 AD and wrote _Ab Urbe Condita Libri_ (Books from the Foundation of the City), a monumental history of Rome from its [mythical origins](https://www.unrv.com/empire/founding.php) to his own time.

Livy's work is characterized by a dramatic and rhetorical style, aiming not only to record events but also to moralize and inspire patriotism among his readers. He often included speeches and dramatized scenes to highlight moral lessons and exemplify Roman virtues.

Livy presents Scipio as a paragon of Roman excellence; brave, pious, and favored [by the gods](https://www.unrv.com/culture/roman-gods.php). He emphasizes Scipio's magnanimity and strategic brilliance. Hannibal, while acknowledged as a formidable opponent, is often depicted with a degree of Roman bias, highlighting his cunning and attributing his ultimate failure to moral shortcomings.

While less technical than Polybius, Livy also provides substantial information on the strategies and tactics of the battle. He describes Scipio's clever use of the manipular formation and the pivotal role of the cavalry. Livy also recounts the psychological aspects of warfare, such as the impact of the war elephants and the morale of the troops.

As mentioned, his narrative is imbued with reflections on destiny, virtue, and the moral fiber of nations, using the Battle of Zama to illustrate the triumph of Roman discipline and righteousness over Carthaginian guile.

The works of Polybius and Livy have significantly shaped the modern interpretation of the Battle of Zama. Their accounts offer complementary perspectives: Polybius's analytical approach appeals to modern historians seeking a critical understanding of the events, while Livy's engaging storytelling provides cultural and ideological context.

However, both historians wrote with their own biases; Polybius with a Greek perspective influenced by his Roman associations, and Livy with a patriotic Roman viewpoint. Modern scholars must critically assess these biases to extract reliable historical information.

  

### Modern Historians and Ongoing Debates

Contemporary historians continue to analyze the Battle of Zama, utilizing a variety of sources and methodologies to deepen our understanding of this historical event.

For example, there is ongoing debate regarding the exact numbers of troops and casualties involved, as estimates vary due to discrepancies in ancient sources and the tendency of historians like Livy to use numbers symbolically or rhetorically.

Modern historians apply knowledge of logistics, supply chains, and the capabilities of ancient societies to assess the plausibility of the reported figures, examining the capacity of the terrain to support large armies and the limitations of ancient [transportation](https://www.unrv.com/articles/transportation.php).

Assessing the reliability of sources is a critical aspect of modern scholarship. By comparing different historical accounts, including those of [Appian of Alexandria](https://www.unrv.com/culture/appian-alexandria.php) and [Plutarch](https://www.unrv.com/culture/plutarch.php) for instance, historians identify consistencies and discrepancies, aiding in forming a more accurate picture of the events.

While archaeological evidence from so long ago is limited, findings contribute to understanding the battle's context; artifacts, inscriptions, and remains can corroborate or challenge the literary sources.

Modern historians explore how the victory at Zama had profound effects on Roman politics, [the economy](https://www.unrv.com/economy.php), and Roman society in general. They investigate how the war contributed to Rome's expansionist policies, shifts in governance, and the accumulation of wealth and [slaves](https://www.unrv.com/slavery.php).

Unsurprisingly, [the defeat and fall of Carthage](https://www.unrv.com/empire/fall-of-carthage.php) led to significant changes in Carthaginian society, including economic hardship due to war indemnities, loss of territories, and internal political strife. Studies examine how these factors influenced Carthage's eventual downfall in the [Third Punic War](https://www.unrv.com/empire/third-punic-war.php).

The prolonged conflict also impacted cultural exchanges between Rome and Carthage, and historians investigate how this interaction affected [art](https://www.unrv.com/culture/roman-art.php), [religion](https://www.unrv.com/religion.php), technology and commerce in the Mediterranean region.

Advancements in research and new findings lead historians to re-assess established narratives. Alternative theories on the battle's location have been proposed based on interpretations of ancient texts and geographical studies.

Some modern analyses suggest that Hannibal's decisions at Zama may have been constrained by factors beyond his control, such as the quality of his troops and political pressures, prompting re-evaluation of his tactics. The impact of Numidian alliances is scrutinized to understand how local dynamics influenced the battle's outcome.

  

### Cultural and Educational Significance

The enduring interest in the Battle of Zama extends beyond academia. The battle is frequently included in military history courses and classical studies programs, serving as a case study for strategy, leadership, and ancient history.

It also features prominently in popular media; books, documentaries, and works of historical fiction often depict the battle, bringing the story to a wider audience and sparking public interest in ancient history.

Symbolically, the battle represents themes of perseverance, the rise and fall of powers, and the impact of individual leaders on historical events.

  

Final Thoughts
--------------

The Battle of Zama was more than just the culmination of the Second Punic War; it was a decisive moment that shaped the trajectory of Western civilization. By defeating Carthage and ending Hannibal's threat, Rome not only secured its own survival, but also laid the foundation for an era of unprecedented expansion and influence.

The victory at Zama allowed Rome to transition from a regional power confined to the Italian peninsula into a Mediterranean superpower with far-reaching ambitions.

The success of Roman civilization in the centuries that followed can be traced back to this pivotal battle. With Carthage neutralized, Rome faced fewer obstacles in consolidating control over the Western Mediterranean. This expansion facilitated the spread of [Roman law](https://www.unrv.com/government/laws.php), [culture](https://www.unrv.com/culture/daily-life.php), [language](https://www.unrv.com/culture/latin-language.php), and infrastructure across vast territories.

The integration of diverse peoples under Roman governance led to a period of relative peace and stability known as the _[Pax Romana](https://www.unrv.com/early-empire/pax-romana.php)_. This era saw advancements in [engineering](https://www.unrv.com/military/engineering-marvels-of-the-roman-army.php), [architecture](https://www.unrv.com/architecture.php), [literature](https://www.unrv.com/culture/literature.php), and philosophy, many of which have left a lasting legacy on modern societies.

Moreover, the lessons learned from the Punic Wars, particularly the importance of naval power, logistics, and adaptable military tactics, strengthened Rome's military institutions. The professionalization of the Roman army and the emphasis on discipline and innovation made it a formidable force for centuries.

The psychological impact of the victory cannot be understated. Rome's triumph over a formidable adversary like Hannibal instilled a sense of destiny and confidence in Roman leaders and [the general populace](https://www.unrv.com/empire/roman-population.php). This belief in Rome's preeminence fueled further conquests and the spread of Roman ideals.

The cultural exchange that ensued from Rome's expansion enriched its civilization, incorporating elements from conquered peoples and fostering a cosmopolitan society.

In the broader context of history, the Battle of Zama represents the decisive turning point where the balance of power in the ancient Mediterranean shifted irrevocably. It set in motion the rise of an empire that would shape the political, legal, and cultural frameworks of the Western world. The institutions and ideas developed during Rome's ascendancy continue to influence modern governance, law, engineering, and language.

The enduring significance of the Battle of Zama lies not only in the military victory but also in its profound impact on the course of human history. It underscores how the outcomes of pivotal conflicts can alter the destiny of civilizations. The legacy of Rome, cemented by successes like Zama, serves as a testament to the far-reaching consequences of strategic vision, effective leadership, and the relentless pursuit of a nation's aspirations.

By examining the Battle of Zama, we gain insights into the factors that contribute to the rise and fall of great powers. It reminds us that the confluence of strategy, leadership, and opportunity can shape the world in enduring ways. The echoes of Rome's victory resonate through time, highlighting the battle's importance not just as a historical event, but as a cornerstone in the foundation of Western civilization.

*   [Outbreak of the Second Punic War](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/wars/punic-wars/second-punic-war/#outbreak-of-the-second-punic-war)
*   [Hannibal’s Expedition](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/wars/punic-wars/second-punic-war/#hannibals-expedition)
*   [Battles in Italy](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/wars/punic-wars/second-punic-war/#battles-in-italy)
*   [Mago’s mission to Carthage with request for support for Hannibal](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/wars/punic-wars/second-punic-war/#magos-mission-to-carthage-with-request-for-support-for-hannibal)
*   [After Cannae](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/wars/punic-wars/second-punic-war/#after-cannae)
*   [Roman counteroffensive](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/wars/punic-wars/second-punic-war/#roman-counteroffensive)
*   [Battle of Zama](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/wars/punic-wars/second-punic-war/#battle-of-zama)
*   [Consequences](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/wars/punic-wars/second-punic-war/#consequences)
*   [Important battles of the Second Punic War](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/wars/punic-wars/second-punic-war/#important-battles-of-the-second-punic-war)

Second Punic War took place in the years 218-201 BCE between Carthage and Rome. The conflict decided about the primacy in the Mediterranean.

Background of events
--------------------

Humiliated after the [First Punic War](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/wars/punic-wars/first-punic-war/), [Carthage](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/roman-geography/neighboring-lands-around-ancient-rome/carthage/) thought of taking revenge on the Romans. After losing the war, Carthage lost its influence in Sicily, and later also in Sardinia and Corsica. Rome strengthened its rule in the western Mediterranean and significantly limited the hegemony of the Phoenicians, who had to additionally pay off a huge compensation – 3,200 talents. Despite the harsh conditions of peace, Carthage still remained a strong player in the region and sought to expand its spheres of influence in the Mediterranean basin and create a hinterland in the event of a war with Rome. The Carthaginian family of the Barcids played an important role in regaining strength in Carthage after the First Punic War.

The head of the Barcids family during the first Roman-Carthaginian conflict was Hamilcar Barkas. This talented leader and an important figure on the Carthaginian political scene was never defeated in an open battle by the Romans. Despite his relative successes, however, he could not come to terms with the defeat of Carthage and the shameful terms of peace. Certainly, his aversion to the Romans had a large impact on the further policy of Carthage, as well as the attitude of his sons towards the Roman state.

Carthage directed its expansion to the Iberian Peninsula, which became for it a source of mercenaries and income. She conquered its south-eastern part, and the acquired loot and mines allowed the Romans to pay off a huge contribution in record time. Naturally, Rome was anxiously watching the events in Spain and the growing influence of the Carthaginians. Rome established strategic alliances with several tribes and cities, incl. Sagunt and defined the Ebro River as the boundary of the Roman and Carthaginian spheres of influence.

Outbreak of the Second Punic War
--------------------------------

The immediate cause of the new conflict between the states was the siege and the capture of Saguntu, a city in alliance with Rome, by Carthaginian forces. The Romans, who had been preparing for the conflict for a long time, demanded the release of the chief provocateur – the [Carthaginian chief, Hannibal](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/article/hannibal-barcas-great-enemy-of-romans/), son of the aforementioned Hamilcar, who became after his and his uncle’s death head of the Barcids family. In the event of failure to fulfil its obligation, Rome threatened to declare war on the Carthaginian state. However, the ultimatum was refused.

The plan, prepared in detail by the Roman command, assumed a simultaneous attack on Carthage in North Africa and Spain (with the help of a strong fleet), which was the granary of the African state. These plans, however, could not come into force because the initiative was taken over by Hannibal. He was aware of the small Carthaginian fleet compared to the Romans, and could only count on his well-trained ground army, which over the years had led to the expansion of the Carthaginian state in Spain.

His plan was to quickly transfer hostilities to Italy and threaten Rome directly. Unable to transport troops directly by the sea, he decided to reach Italy by land via Spain and the Alps. He also hoped that he would be able to win over to his side the Gallic tribes of northern Italy, Latin vassals of the Romans and Greek cities in the south of the Apennine Peninsula. Hannibal realized that the loss of southern Spain to Rome would mean the definitive defeat of Carthage. It was certainly the weakest point of the Carthaginian state, which, as it turned out, was later ruthlessly used by the Romans. Hannibal, in order to secure Spain during the campaign, left troops led by the brothers Hasdrubal and Magon.

![Image 1: Hannibal's Expedition to Italy during the Second Punic War](https://imperiumromanum.pl/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/Hannibal_route_of_invasion-en.png)

[](https://imperiumromanum.pl/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/Hannibal_route_of_invasion-en.png "Hannibal’s Expedition to Italy during the Second Punic War.")

Author: Abalg | Under Creative Commons Attribution license - On the same terms 3.0.

Hannibal’s Expedition
---------------------

In 218 BCE Hannibal, at the head of his great army of nearly 60,000 soldiers, crossed the Ebro and headed for the Pyrenees. After crossing the mountain massif, he found himself in unfamiliar territory, belonging to the arrogant and distrustful Gallic tribes. Hannibal had to use his command skills and wits to defeat the brave, though undisciplined Gallic troops. In the vicinity of Massalia (today’s Marseille in the south of France), the first clash between the Punic and Roman armies took place, but it brought nothing more than that the Romans realized how close the enemy army was to Italy.  
Then Hannibal, with a smaller army, entered the Alps. It should be noted that both the Romans and the Carthaginians did not have much to do with the mountains and the harsh conditions that prevail there. This is how Hannibal’s expedition is described by the Roman historian [**Titus Livius**](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/biographies/titus-livius/):

![Image 2: Hannibal, genius Carthaginian commander](https://imperiumromanum.pl/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/hanibal-400x400.jpg)

[](https://imperiumromanum.pl/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/hanibal.jpg "Hannibal, genius Carthaginian commander. After losing the Second Punic War, Hannibal took refuge at the Seleukid court. After Antiochus’ defeat in the war with Rome, he committed suicide so as not to be placed in a cage during his triumph in Rome.")

[**Hannibal**](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/article/hannibal-barcas-great-enemy-of-romans/), genius Carthaginian commander. After losing the Second Punic War, Hannibal took refuge at the Seleukid court. After Antiochus’ defeat in the war with Rome, he committed suicide so as not to be placed in a cage during his triumph in Rome.

Creative Commons Attribution license - On the same terms 3.0.

> From the Druentia, by a road that lay principally through plains, Hannibal arrived at the Alps without molestation from the Gauls that inhabit those regions. Then, though the scene had been previously anticipated from report, (by which uncertainties are wont to be exaggerated,) yet the height of the mountains when viewed so near, and the snows almost mingling with the sky, the shapeless huts situated on the cliffs, the cattle and beasts of burden withered by the cold, the men unshorn and wildly dressed, all things, animate and inanimate, stiffened with frost, and other objects more terrible to be seen than described, renewed their alarm. To them, marching up the first acclivities, the mountaineers appeared occupying the heights over head; who, if they had occupied the more concealed valleys, might, by rushing out suddenly to the attack, have occasioned great flight and havoc. \[…\]  
> On the ninth day they came to a summit of the Alps, chiefly through places trackless; and after many mistakes of their way, which were caused either by the treachery of the guides, or, when they were not trusted, by entering valleys at random, on their own conjectures of the route. For two days they remained encamped on the summit; and rest was given to the soldiers, exhausted with toil and fighting: and several beasts of burden, which had fallen down among the rocks, by following the track of the army arrived at the camp. A fall of snow, it being now the season of the setting of the constellation of the Pleiades, caused great fear to the soldiers, already worn out with weariness of so many hardships. On the standards being moved forward at daybreak, when the army proceeded slowly over all places entirely blocked up with snow, and languor and despair strongly appeared in the countenances of all, Hannibal, having advanced before the standards, and ordered the soldiers to halt on a certain eminence, whence there was a prospect far and wide, points out to them Italy and the plains of the Po, extending themselves beneath the Alpine mountains; and said “that they were now surmounting not only the ramparts of Italy, but also of the city of Rome; that the rest of the journey would be smooth and down-hill; that after one, or, at most, a second battle, they would have the citadel and capital of Italy in their power and possession.
> 
> – **Titus Livius**, _Ab urbe condita_, XXI.32-35

Hannibal’s expedition (the crossing of the mountains took 15 days), which lasted from May to October 218 BCE, became legendary for posterity, and Hannibal’s boldness and military genius continue to delight today.

The quick crossing of the Alps was a complete surprise for the Romans, who were preparing to implement their own plan. In this situation, the Romans were forced to defend Italy in the north. Commander-in-chief of the Roman army, consul Publius Cornelius Scipio (father of the later victorious commander Scipio Africanus the Elder) sent his brother Gnaeus to Spain in order to cut off the way back for the great Carthaginian army, and thus force Hannibal’s tired army into a battle in northern Italy.

It should be noted that the harsh conditions of the march led to large losses in Hannibal’s army, which was additionally abandoned by newly recruited soldiers with low morale. Hannibal, however, managed to obtain reinforcements, backed by staunch rivals of the Romans – the Gauls.

Battles in Italy
----------------

The first step after crossing the Alps was to break the camp and allow the troops to recover after a hard march. Then Hannibal headed for the lands of the Taurines, who were hostile to him. After conquering their main centre and a short rest, the Punics set off to the lands of the allied Insubres and Boii.

After gathering an army, Consul Publius Cornelius Scipio set out to the armies of Hannibal to cut his way. To the surprise of the Senate and the Roman people, Hannibal managed to win further victories over the River Ticinus and [Trebia](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/battles/battle-of-the-trebia/) in 218 BCE, and in the first clash, Consul Scipio was badly wounded, rescued according to one source by his son, the future winner Hannibal. Subsequent defeats forced the Roman army to abandon the defence line on the Po River in northern Italy. The next blow struck the Roman legions in 217 BCE, when consul Gaius Flaminius, wanting to prevent the looting of Hannibal’s army, was ambushed in the narrow passage between the mountain range and [Lake Trasimene](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/battles/battle-of-lake-trasimene/).

![Image 3: Battles of the Second Punic War](https://imperiumromanum.pl/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/battles_druga23.jpg)

[](https://imperiumromanum.pl/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/battles_druga23.jpg "Battles of the Second Punic War.")

Battles of the Second Punic War.

Creative Commons Attribution license - On the same terms 3.0.

The defeats of the Roman army forced the Senate to act violently. It was decided to appoint [Quintus Fabius Maximus](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/biographies/fabius-maximus-cunctator/) as dictator. He adopted a new way of fighting – avoiding direct clashes with the enemy – which was aimed at rebuilding the morale of soldiers and gathering forces for a decisive battle. This tactic was effective for a certain period of time, but with time it ceased to appeal to the impetuous aristocracy, which lost its fortune as a result of the plunder of Carthaginian soldiers. The Senate decided that the time of manoeuvres was over and we should strive for the fastest possible victory. The power over the army was taken over by: **Gaius Terentius Varro** and **Lucius Aemilius Paulus**. Success was to be ensured by the largest army that was established in the history of the republic. They were ordered to finally liquidate Hannibal’s army. Both commanders: Paulus and Varro, led by their mighty army, marched to the city of Cannae (_Cannae_) in Apulia, in the south-eastern part of Italy.

**On August 2, 216** there was the [**battle of Canna**](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/battles/battle-of-cannae/ "The Battle of Canna"). The Romans suffered a defeat that they had not experienced in their history so far. Their huge army, of at least 55,000 soldiers, was completely wiped out by half the size of Hannibal’s army. Despite the great victory, Hannibal could not use it strategically. He was too weak to continue the hostilities, and most of all he was unable to win Rome, the heart of Italy. The Romans, realizing that they would not be able to oppose the enemy in open combat, began to harass the enemy with short driveways and light infantry attacks, provoking the enemy to bolder movements. This tactic turned out to be very beneficial at this point in time when the Roman legions were “morally decayed” after a series of defeats.

![Image 4: Hannibal accepting the Romans’ surrender](https://imperiumromanum.pl/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/hannibal.jpg)

[](https://imperiumromanum.pl/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/hannibal.jpg "Hannibal accepting the Romans’ surrender.")

Hannibal accepting the Romans’ surrender.

Autor: Aleksander Jeżow

Mago’s mission to Carthage with request for support for Hannibal
----------------------------------------------------------------

Despite the great victory of [at Cannae](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/battles/battle-of-cannae/) in 216 BCE, [Hannibal](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/article/hannibal-barcas-great-enemy-of-romans/) still needed both material and military support to defeat the Romans. To this end, Hannibal, before the battle, sent his younger brother Magon to [Carthage](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/roman-geography/neighboring-lands-around-ancient-rome/carthage/) to negotiate additional troops to Italy.

Mago asks the Carthaginian “senators” to supply Hannibal with grain, money, and military meals. Mago stresses the plight of Hannibal, who is at the heart of a hostile country and yet has won many victories so far, defeating six consular armies led by six different chiefs; moreover, he killed over 200,000 enemies and took 50,000 prisoners. In order to emphasize Hannibal’s achievements, Mago has the numerous rings obtained from his opponents thrown to the floor. Mago also points out that other peoples and cities of Italy, including some Samnites and Capua, are passing over to Hannibal.

As it turned out, Mago’s speech was successful, despite the objections of one of Hannibal’s opponents – Hannon. The Council of Elders unanimously agreed to send support to Italy: 4,000 Numidian cavalries, 40 elephants1 and money.

After the mission in Carthage, Mago went to Spain to organize a new army, thus becoming an independent commander.

After Cannae
------------

![Image 5: Hannibal's elephant attack](https://imperiumromanum.pl/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/slonie.jpg)

[](https://imperiumromanum.pl/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/slonie.jpg "Hannibal’s elephant attack.")

Hannibal’s elephant attack.

Creative Commons Attribution license - On the same terms 3.0.

Despite the difficult situation in which Rome found itself, no one thought of surrendering. A heroic effort was made to recreate the army – in a size that exceeded any mobilization achievements to date. New taxes were passed to support these efforts. When looking for reserves, it was even decided to enlist slaves to the army, who were guaranteed freedom, or criminals by offering amnesty. The abandoned tactic of Maximus was returned to – avoiding a clash with Hannibal, while trying to destroy smaller enemy groups, systematically cracking down on treacherous Italian allies; an example may be dealing with Kapua, who entered into an agreement with the Punics.

Rome’s position deteriorated further when the alliance between Carthage and Macedonia was formed. This forced the Romans to send an additional contingent to Greece and fight also outside Italy. In practice, however, the Romans supported only, for example, the Aetolian Union and Greek cities, and the battles between themselves were mainly fought by the Greeks. In addition, Hannibal, plundering Italy, encouraged other peoples and cities to rebel against Roman authority, promising protection and full freedom in exchange for military support and supplies. In this way, he managed to gain allies, and the Romans, beyond the control of Hannibal’s actions, were forced to suppress another arrogant former ally. Hannibal tried to involve Rome in various conflicts, reduce its combat strength and lead to destruction, and in the long run, force them to seek peace.

The economic situation of Rome also deteriorated. The financial system was undermined, forcing the Senate to increase taxes. Destroyed Italy was unable to produce the right amount of food. The main source of grain harvesting, Sicily was dominated by Carthage. This situation forced Rome to import grain from Ptolemaic Egypt. It is also worth mentioning the decline in the number of citizens able to bear arms following successive disasters.

Roman counteroffensive
----------------------

Defensive actions were mainly carried out in Italy; there they tried to bind Hannibal’s forces and avoid open clashes with his army. The entanglement of the main Carthaginian forces in the Apennine Peninsula allowed the Romans to launch an offensive in Sicily, which was key to any plans to invade Africa. Within two years, from 214 to 212 BCE, Syracuse was captured, which was controlled by the allies of Carthage. There, the great ancient [scientist and inventor Archimedes](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/article/archimedes-man-who-put-himself-against-romans/), who designed subsequent war machines, contributed to the effective defence of the city for a long time. The capture of Syracuse was a breakthrough in the fighting in Sicily and finally allowed the Carthaginian army to be driven out of the island.

![Image 6: Portion of Servius Wall](https://imperiumromanum.pl/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/800px-Servian_Wall.jpg)

[](https://imperiumromanum.pl/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/800px-Servian_Wall.jpg "Portion of Servian Wall. It was this wall that prompted Hannibal to reject the idea of an immediate attack on Rome.")

Portion of **Servian Wall**. It was this wall that prompted Hannibal to reject the idea of an immediate attack on Rome.

Creative Commons Attribution license - On the same terms 3.0.

The situation of the Romans in Spain was less favourable. The Roman armies were defeated and two Roman chieftains were killed. As a result, the command over the troops in Spain was entrusted to the young [**Publius Cornelius Scipio**](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/biographies/scipio-africanus-the-elder/ "African Scipio"), who acted as proconsul in 210 BCE This decision turned out to be a brilliant solution for the rest of the war. First, the young commander trained and disciplined the soldiers, rebuilding the conviction of their combat value. His goal in the war was to drive the Carthaginians from the Iberian Peninsula, or rather brother of Hannibal, Hasdrubal. Scipio had a relatively small army – up to 30,000 men – which unfortunately was not able to compete with all three Punic armies at once. Luckily for the Roman leader, all armies were far away from the Carthaginian capital of the region – New Carthage. Scipio made the decision to boldly enter the hostile territory and besiege the city in 209 BCE, from which the Carthaginian chiefs drew their supplies. Using the information about the shallow lagoon, it was possible to lead an attack on the unprotected city ramparts and capture the city. The loss of New Carthage was a blow to the Punics. The Romans took the initiative; Scipio also managed to win the friendship of the Iberian tribes that were ready to support the Roman troops under his command.

There was also some success in Italy, where Hannibal had trouble securing and protecting many of the cities that passed over to his side. The Romans, instead of creating one large army, operated several armies at once, in different regions, gaining an advantage over their rivals. Capua was captured in 211, and then Tarentum was recaptured from the Carthaginians in 209 BCE, which allowed Hannibal to be pushed south and limited supplies from Africa.

The Romans gradually began to take the lead in the Second Punic War. The Carthaginians then decided to take the bold step of supporting Hannibal’s troops stationed in Italy. After the fall of New Carthage and the victory of the Romans in 208 BCE at Baecula, it was decided to send an army to Italy, headed by Hasdrubal – Hannibal’s brother. He set out with the troops by land, crossing the Alps along the path previously marked out by Hannibal. The Romans, however, took over the letters Hasdrubal had sent to his brother and learned about his plans. He was beaten in the summer of 207 BCE [on the Metaurus River](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/battles/battle-of-metaurus-river/) in Umbria. On his way stood the Roman army under the command of two consuls: Gaius Claudius Nero and Marcus Livius Salinator. The Carthaginian commander was killed in battle, his body was found on the battlefield and his head was cut off. Then she was thrown behind the embankments of the Hannibal camp. According to Florus, the Carthaginian chief was then supposed to pronounce the prophetic words: “I recognize the ill-luck of Carthage”2.

Eventually, the Carthaginians were expelled from Spain after the victorious Battle of Ilipa in 206 BCE, where Scipio defeated Hasdrubal Giskon. The advantage of the Carthaginian commander did not bring him victory, he had to flee to Africa after the battle.

Thanks to decisive successes, Scipio in 205 BCE received the governorship of Sicily, which was to serve him as a base for the planned invasion of North Africa. His idea of a direct threat to Carthage in Africa was not fully accepted in the Senate. It was still believed that Hannibal should be expelled from Italy first, as he still posed a real threat. Ultimately, however, there was a consensus and Scipio began preparations for the invasion. Supplies were collected, the army was supplemented and trained, the fleet was brought in, and alliances were concluded, among others with [Massinisa](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/biographies/massinissa/), a contender to the throne of Numidia who previously fought for Carthage. Masinissa, noticing that the Romans had gained the advantage in the Punic War, decided to form an alliance with the “sons of the she-wolf” and promised Scipio to support him in the invasion of North Africa.

Interestingly, there were legions stationed in Sicily, which consisted of the surviving soldiers from Kann. After the defeat in 216 BCE, the Senate, as a punishment, sent fighting legionaries to the island to repent of their sins and regain Roman power in the region. Scipio in his invasion of Africa was to use the “Cannabis veterans”.

Scipio was elected the chief commander of the expedition and set off in 204 BCE for Africa. The consul used his experience and cunning to gain successive victories in Africa. In 203 BCE there was a Battle of the Bagradas River, defeated by Hasdrubal and Syphax, rivals to the throne of Numidia Masynissa.

[Battle of Zama](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/battles/battle-of-zama/)
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

The Carthaginian authorities, terrified by the turn of events, forced Hannibal to leave Italy and return with the army to his homeland in 203 BCE. Italy, devastated after almost 16 years of Hannibal’s presence, was finally in the hands of Rome again. After arriving in Africa, the invincible Carthaginian commander gave the young Roman consul a fighting battle. That battle was the [**battle of Zama**](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/battles/battle-of-zama/ "The Battle of Zama") in 202 BCE

The meeting of the two armies took place exactly on October 19, 202 BCE, on the plain near Zama, south of Carthage. Hannibal was aware of the weakness of his cavalry and the poor training of most of the soldiers but accepted the fight. Before the clash, he met with Scipio. The greatest commanders of the time looked at each other for the first time. We know this conversation from Livy’s message, which probably reflects its content well. Carthaginian tried to convince the Romans to make peace, arguing that Carthage had already been defeated and that Scipio’s victories so far and the fact that he, Hannibal, asked for a truce, ensured sufficient fame.

Hannibal was to address Scipio:

> \[…\] Peace once established is a better and safer thing than hoping for victory; that is in your hands, this in the hands of the gods. Do not expose so many years’ good fortune to the hazard of a single hour. You think of your own strength, but think too of the part which fortune plays and the even chances of battle. On both sides there will be swords and men to use them, nowhere does the event less answer expectation than in war. Victory will not add so much to the glory which you can now win by granting peace, as defeat will take away from it. The chances of a single hour can annihilate all the honours you have gained and all you can hope for. If you cement a peace, P. Cornelius, you are master of all, otherwise you will have to accept whatever fortune the gods send you. \[…\]
> 
> – **Titus Livius**, _Ab urbe condita_, XXX.30

Roman commander replied:

> Our fathers were not the aggressors in the war for Sicily, nor were we the aggressors in Spain, but the dangers which threatened our Mamertine allies in the one case and the destruction of Saguntum in the other made our case a righteous one and justified our arms. That you provoked the war in each case you yourself admit, and the gods bear witness to the fact; they guided the former war to a just and righteous issue, and they are doing and will do the same with this one. As for myself, I do not forget what weak creatures we men are; I do not ignore the influence which Fortune exercises and the countless accidents to which all our doings are liable. Had you of your own free will evacuated Italy and embarked your army before I sailed for Africa and then come with proposals for peace, I admit that I should have acted in a high-handed and arbitrary spirit if I had rejected them. But now that I have dragged you to Africa like a reluctant and tricky defendant I am not bound to show you the slightest consideration. So then, if in addition to the terms on which peace might have been concluded previously, there is the further condition of an indemnity for the attack on our transports and the ill-treatment of our envoys during the armistice, I shall have something to lay before the councils. If you consider this unacceptable. then prepare for war as you have been unable to endure peace
> 
> – **Titus Livius**, _Ab urbe condita_, XXX.31

The last attempt to make peace has failed. The chiefs returned to their armies and began to form lines.

![Image 7: Titus Livius mentions that Scipio Africanus and Hannibal reportedly met in Ephesus](https://imperiumromanum.pl/wp-content/uploads/2015/10/Scypion-i-Hannibal.jpg)

[](https://imperiumromanum.pl/wp-content/uploads/2015/10/Scypion-i-Hannibal.jpg "Titus Livius mentions that African Scipio and Hannibal reportedly met in Ephesus in 193 BCE when the Roman was a member of the Senate delegation. Then Scipio asked Hannibal who he thought was the best commander in history. Hannibal replied that Alexander the Great had conquered all of Persia with a much smaller army. The Roman then asked who he would name in second place. The Carthaginian replied that Pyrrhus. After this question, Scipio asked who he would see in 3rd place. Hannibal exchanged himself. Scipio laughed and asked him what he would say if he defeated him. Hannibal replied that then he would have put himself in 1st place.")

[**Titus Livius**](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/biographies/titus-livius/ "Titus Livius") mentions that [**African Scipio**](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/biographies/scipio-africanus-the-elder/ "African Scipio") and [**Hannibal**](https://imperiumromanum.pl/en/article/hannibal-barcas-great-enemy-of-romans/) reportedly met in Ephesus in 193 BCE when the Roman was a member of the Senate delegation. Then Scipio asked Hannibal who he thought was the best commander in history. Hannibal replied that Alexander the Great had conquered all of Persia with a much smaller army. The Roman then asked who he would name in second place. The Carthaginian replied that Pyrrhus. After this question, Scipio asked who he would see in 3rd place. Hannibal exchanged himself. Scipio laughed and asked him what he would say if he defeated him. Hannibal replied that then he would have put himself in 1st place.

Photo: pa/akg-images

Scipio used a tactic almost identical to that used by Hannibal in the battle of Cannae. Using the help of the Numidian prince Masinissa, in the form of Numidian cavalry, he managed to outflank the Carthaginian army and then destroy it. During the battle, Hannibal had war elephants at his disposal, which, however, did not do much harm to the army, as they ran through specially designated streets in an array of manipulators.

Consequences
------------

Carthage, after losing the battle, was no longer able to wage war. In 201 BCE, peace was signed under which the Carthaginians could only keep their possessions in Africa. They could not wage wars without Rome’s consent, and moreover, they were forced to pay a gigantic contribution of 10,000 silver talents in 50 years and had to hand over their entire fleet to Rome, except 10 guard ships, and give hostages as a guarantee to fulfil the conditions of the treaty. The actions of Carthage in Africa were to be guarded by Masinissa, king of Numidia, who assisted Scipio in the battle of Zama.

The fate of Hannibal himself is interesting. For some time he remained in Carthage:

> Well, after this as if the last act of his valour, Hannibal took refuge in Hadrumetum and from there was summoned to Carthage. He returned to her in the thirty-sixth year after he had left her as a child. Here in the Carthaginian Senate he openly confessed that he had lost not only this battle but the entire war and that there was no hope of salvation other than peace.
> 
> – **Titus Livius**, _Ab urbe condita_, IX.35

Ultimately, Roman intrigues forced Hannibal to flee. He took refuge in the court of the Seleukid ruler, Antiochus III the Great. After Antiochus’ defeat in the war with Rome in 189 BCE, he fled to Bithynia, where he committed suicide, drinking the poison he had received from his father and always carried in a ring so as not to fall into the hands of the Romans and be put in a cage during his triumph. Before he died, he said, “Let us now relieve the Romans of their fears by the death of a feeble old man”.

The defeat at Zama marked the end of the strong Carthaginian state. Thanks to the reform of the Roman army by Scipio, it became almost unbeatable from that moment. Rome became the greatest power in the Mediterranean and having no worthy competitors, it began its expansion to become the great Roman Empire in the future.

Important battles of the Second Punic War
-----------------------------------------

![Image 8: Major battles of the Second Punic War](https://imperiumromanum.pl/wp-content/uploads/2015/02/Battles_second_punic_war.png)
